title: How Anansi Brought Stories to the World
subtitle: a folktale from Ghana, about one very small spider and one very large bargain
moral: Granny’s whisper: cleverness is a kind of courage.
script_en:
Long ago, in the time when the world was young, there were no stories on the earth. All of the stories belonged to Nyame, the Sky God, who kept them in a great golden box up above the clouds.

Down below lived Anansi the spider, who was clever and small, and more than a little fond of mischief. One day Anansi climbed up his web, all the way to the sky, and said, “Nyame, great Sky God, what is the price of your stories? I would like to buy them for the people of the earth.”

Nyame laughed a deep thunder-laugh. “My stories are not cheap, little spider. Their price is Onini the python, who swallows goats whole; Osebo the leopard, with teeth like knives; the Mmoboro hornets, who sting like fire; and Mmoatia, the fairy whom no one has ever seen.” Most creatures would have gone home. But Anansi stroked his chin and said, “It shall be done.”

First, Anansi cut a long branch and walked through the forest muttering, “My wife says a python is shorter than this branch. I say a python is longer.” Onini the python heard him and uncoiled himself with a hiss. “I am longer,” he said. “Measure me.” So Onini stretched out along the branch, and quick as a blink, Anansi wrapped him head to tail in silk, and carried him up to Nyame.

Next, Anansi dug a deep pit and covered it with leaves. When Osebo the leopard fell in, Anansi pretended to be surprised. “What are you doing down there?” he asked. “I fell,” growled Osebo. “Then let me help,” said Anansi, and he lowered a web so sticky that the moment the leopard climbed out, he was tangled like a fly. Up to Nyame went Osebo.

For the hornets, Anansi filled a gourd with water and poured it over their nest. “Rain!” he cried. “Why do you sit out in the rain? Come into my dry gourd.” The hornets flew in to thank him, and Anansi corked the gourd tight.

Last came Mmoatia, the unseen fairy. Anansi carved a little wooden doll, covered it with sticky sap, and set a bowl of mashed yams in its lap. When the fairy came by, she smelled the yams. “May I eat?” she asked the doll. The doll said nothing. “I said, may I eat?” The doll said nothing. Annoyed, the fairy slapped the doll, and her hand stuck fast. She struck it with the other hand, then kicked it, and stuck all over, she was carried up to the sky.

Nyame looked at the python, the leopard, the hornets, and the fairy, and he laughed until the clouds shook. “Never has anyone paid my full price,” he said. “Take the golden box. The stories belong to the earth now.”

And that is why, when the fire crackles and the evening grows quiet, we have stories to tell. They came down from the sky on the back of a small, clever spider. And some people say Anansi is still listening, in the corner, smiling his small smile.
script_original:
Te’ nse se, ’nse se o

SE ’YOYE A ANYANKONSEM YE BE FRE NO ANANSESEM

KWAKU ANANSE na okoo Nyankonpon ho se omfa ’Nyankonsem mma no nto. Nyame see, “Wo betimi ato?” Ananse see, “Ei! metimi.” Nyame see, “Akuro akantinka be ye se Kokofu, Bekwai, Asumengya aba, ye’antimi anto, na wo Kwafwiaban na wo betimi?” Ananse see, “Edieben na ye to ma?” Nyame see, “Ye nto mma fwe gye se, Aboa Onini, Osebo, Mmoatia, Mmoboro.” Ananse see, “Me de nnooma nnyina bi meba, me de m’aberewa, Nsia, meka ho.” Nyame see, “Ko fa bra e.” Ananse baye, na oboo oni amanie se, “Nyankonsem me pe se me to, na Nyame se me mfa Onini, Osebo, Mmoatia, Mmoboro mmera, na me see, me de wo be ka ho ma ko ma Nyankonpon.” Na Ananse bisaa ne ye’ Aso se, “Ebeye den na ye’anya Onini?”. Na Aso ka kyeree no se, “Wodie ko twa tonton na twa demere ka ho, na fa bra.” Na Ananse de baye. Na Aso see, “Fa ko asuom’.” Na Ananse de ekoro no, osee, “Esene no, ensene no; woboa, esene no.” Ananse see, “Ono na oda doo no.” Onini see, “Aden?” Ananse see, “Nye Aso na ogye me akyinnyie, se tonton yi kyen wo tenten, na me se oboa.” Onini see, “Fra bra, be susu me.”

Ode tonton no too Onini ho. Osee, “Twe wo mu.” Na Onini twe no mu, na Ananse de demere no too no so, nwenene! nwenene! nwenene! na esii tire. Ananse see, “Kwasea, me de wo ko gye Anyankonsem.” Ananse de no ko maa Nyame. Nyame see, “Me nsa aka, aka dee aka.” Ananse san baye be boo ne ye’ amanie se, “Aka Mmoboro.” Ne yere see, “Pe towa, fa nsuo gum’, na fa ko.” Ananse koo wuram’ obefwe se Mmoboro sen ho, na ofwiee nsuo no bi na opete guu Mmoboro no so. Ananse fwiee dee aka guu ono ara so na otwaa brodee-ahan de kataa no ti. Efei na oka kyeree Mmoboro no se, “Osuo eba yi, ankra mo ba na mo be hyee me toa yim’a s’ankra osuo yi emmo mo, mo nfwe se me de brodee ahahan akata me soo?” Ena Mmoboro no see, “Ye’da w’ase Aku, ye’da w’ase Aku.” Mmoboro no nnyina tuo toa nom’, fom! Agya Ananse tuaa ano. Osee, “Nkwaseafuo m’anya mo, me de mo ko gye Anyankonsem.” Ode Mmoboro ko maa Nyame. Nyame see, “Me nsa aka, aka dee aka.”

Ananse baa bio, be ka kyeree ne yere see, “Aka Osebo.” Aso see, “Ko tu amana.” Ananse see, “Gyae na mahu.” Enie Ananse ko pee Osebo kyeneno na otu amana tententen, na okataa so, na obaa ’fie. Adeekyeye anopa, Ananse se oko, obekoro, Osebo na oda amanam’. Ananse see, “Agyawa ’ba! Enawa ’ba! se maka akyere wo se nnom nsa, sese wo nokwa wako nom abo, nti na w’abe to amanam’; se me kaase me beyi wo a, addekye wo ko hu me a, se nso me ’ba biara a, na wo ko kye no.” Osebo se, “O! me ntimi.” Ananse ko twaa nnua mmienu, de bako too ha, de bako too ha. Osee, “Fa wo nsa bako to ha, na fa wo nsa bako soso to ha.” Na Osebo de totoye. Ose ofo’ na Ananse ama sekan so, na wa ma n’anyam, ne tirim’ gao! Osebo gyee amanam’ fom! Ananse faa atwedee de sii amanam’ ko yii Osebo. Oko yii Osebo de no baye, osee, “Kwasea me de wo ko gye Anyankonsem.” Omaa Osebo so, ko maa Nyame. Nyame see, “Me nsa aka, aka dee aka.”

Ananse baye na osenee Akua Ba, na oboo amane de tetaree Akua Ba no ho: na ofufuu to, na ode bi hyee Akua Ba no nsam’, na ofufuu bi de guu ayowam’; ode homa soo Akua Ba asen, na ode no kosii odum ase babi a mmoatia bedi agoro. Na mmoatia bako baye. Osee, “Akua, me nni eto yi bi?” Na Ananse atwe homa no, na Akua Ba no abo ne tiri nko. Mmoatia ka kyeree onua bako se, “Ose me nni bi.” Osee, “Di bi e.” Na odii aduane no wieye, na odaa n’ase. Oda n’ase ommua. Na Mmoatia no ka kyeree onua se, “Me da n’ase a, ommua.” Mmoatia no nua ka kyeree no se, “Bo no sum.” Na wabo, pa! Na ne nsa aka ho. Oka kyeree onua se, “Me nsa aka ho.” Osee, “Fa bako a aka, bo no sum bio.” Na ode boo no pa! na ’yi no so aka ho. Na Mmoatia ka kyeree onua se, “Me nsa mmienu aka ho.” Osee, “Fa w’afu sum no.” Ode sum no, na n’afu aka ho. Na Ananse baye na obe kyekyeree no; osee, “Kwasea m’anya wo, me de wo ko gye Anyankonsem.”

Na ode koo ’fie. Na Ananse ka kyeree oni, Ya Nsia se, “Sore, ma yen ko, me mfa wo nka Mmoatia yi ho nko gye Anyankonsem.” Omaa yen so, koo Nyame ho. Osee, “Nyame, Mmoatia ni, m’aberewa a me kaye no, nso ni.” Nyame so free Ko’ntire ne Akwam’, ne Adonten, ne Gyase, ne Oyoko, ne Ankobea, ne Kyidom. Na ode too ye’anim se, “Ahene akesie akesie aba, ye’antimi anto Anyankonsem, Kwaku Ananse dee watimi ato; m’agye no Mmoboro; m’agye no Mmoatia; m’agye no Osebo; m’agye no Onini; ono ara Ananse de oni ato so; nnooma no nnyina na egu ho yi.” Osee, “Mo mpene no.” Ye see, “Eee!” Nyankonpon see, “Kwaku Ananse, efiri nne ekoro yi, me de Anyankonsem me kye wo, kose! kose! kose! Ye’mmfre no Anyankonsem bio, na ye’mfre no Anansesem.”

M’anansesem a metooye yi, se eye de o, se ennye de o, momfa bi nko, na momfa bi mmera.

Akan text as published in R. S. Rattray’s 1930 field collection Akan-Ashanti Folk-Tales, transcribed from Akan storytellers (pp. 53–57).
alternate_title: Sɛnea Ananse De Anansesɛm Brɛɛ Wiase

title: The Legend of the Bluebonnet
subtitle: a legend of the Comanche people of the southern plains, about the hardest gift of all
moral: Granny’s whisper: the dearest gifts are the hardest ones to give.
script_en:
Long ago, in a wide country of tall grass and big sky, there was a season when the rain forgot to come. The creeks dried to dust, the grass turned the color of straw, and the People, who belonged to that land the way the wind belongs to the sky, grew hungry and thin.

Day after day the dancers danced, asking the Great Spirits for rain. Day after day the sky stayed blue and empty. At last the dancers heard a drum-voice in the silence between their own drumming, and it said: “The rain will return when the People return to themselves. You have each been living for yourself alone. A sacrifice must be made — one person must give up the most precious thing they own, burn it, and scatter the ashes to the four winds.”

Everyone looked at their own possessions. A fine bow? A warm robe? A string of shining shells? Surely the Spirits did not mean anything that precious. And so everyone went home, still waiting for the rain.

Now there was a little girl in the camp whose name was She-Who-Is-Alone, for her parents and her grandparents had all been taken by a sickness, and she lived quietly at the edge of the village. She had no sisters, no brothers, and only one possession in the whole world: a little doll.

It was a small warrior doll, sewn by her mother and beaded by her grandmother, and on its head it wore a tiny bonnet of blue jay feathers, the color of the sky at dusk. When she held it, she could almost remember her mother singing. It was her family now. It was the most precious thing she had — and perhaps, she thought, the most precious thing anyone had.

That night, while the camp slept, She-Who-Is-Alone wrapped her doll in her arms and climbed the hill. She built a small fire from dry brush. Her hands were shaking, but her heart was steady. “For my people,” she whispered, and she laid her doll into the flames. She watched it burn — the beads, the little bonnet, the last blue feather — and when morning came, she walked around the hill scattering the cold gray ashes to the north, to the south, to the east, and to the west. Then, exhausted, she fell asleep on the hillside in the early sun.

She woke to beauty. As far as she could see, every hill and valley was covered in blue flowers — the color of blue jay feathers, the color of the dusk sky, the color of the shawl her grandmother once wore. The People came out of the village and stood among the flowers, too amazed to speak. And that very afternoon, soft generous rain began to fall, and it fell on everyone alike.

From that day on, the little girl had a new name. The People called her One-Who-Dearly-Loves-Her-People. And every spring, after the winter passes, the hills bloom again with the flowers called bluebonnets — little bonnets of blue — so that nobody forgets what one small girl gave, and what one small act of love can bring back to a thirsty land.
script_alternate:
Hace mucho tiempo, una larga sequía cayó sobre las llanuras. Los arroyos se secaron, los animales se alejaron y el pueblo comanche pidió ayuda al Gran Espíritu. Los ancianos dijeron que la lluvia regresaría cuando alguien ofreciera aquello que más amaba.

Una niña llamada La-Que-Está-Sola escuchó en silencio. Sus padres habían muerto y su único tesoro era una muñeca de piel con plumas azules, recuerdo de su familia. Nadie le pidió que la entregara, pero esa noche la niña comprendió lo que significaba la promesa.

Subió sola a la colina, encendió un pequeño fuego y sostuvo la muñeca contra el corazón. «Por mi pueblo», susurró. La dejó arder, guardó las cenizas y, cuando llegó el amanecer, las esparció hacia los cuatro vientos.

Al volver la luz, toda la colina estaba cubierta de flores azules, suaves como las plumas de su muñeca. Entonces llegaron las nubes. La lluvia cayó sobre la tierra sedienta, llenó los arroyos y despertó el pasto.

El pueblo cambió el nombre de la niña por La-Que-Ama-a-Su-Pueblo. Y cada primavera, cuando los bluebonnets pintan de azul las llanuras, cuentan su historia con respeto: la de una niña cuyo regalo hizo sitio para que la vida regresara.
alternate_note: Published Spanish text for a Comanche legend.

title: The Clever Mountain Woman
subtitle: a Bohemian tale about plain truth, impossible riddles, and a young woman who sees the whole circle
moral: Granny’s whisper: a quiet answer can travel farther than a loud horse.
script_en:
In the Czech mountains, two farmers stopped at an inn on their way to market. One drove a mare, the other an ox. During the night the mare gave birth to a foal, and by morning the little animal had wandered beneath the ox.

The rich farmer claimed it at once. “The foal was found beside my ox,” he said. The poor farmer protested, but the dispute reached the village judge, who cared more for fine gifts than for plain sense. He awarded the foal to the rich man.

On his way home, the poor farmer met a hunter who was really the local prince in disguise. Hearing the story, the prince summoned both farmers and asked three questions: what was swiftest, sweetest, and richest in the world?

The rich farmer answered that his own horse was swiftest, his honey sweetest, and his land richest. The poor farmer carried the questions to his daughter, a young woman known for listening carefully before she spoke.

“Thought is swiftest,” she said, “because it crosses the world in an instant. Sleep is sweetest, because every weary person seeks it. The earth is richest, because all life draws nourishment from it.”

The prince recognized the wisdom behind the answers. He ordered the daughter to visit him neither dressed nor undressed, neither walking nor riding, and carrying neither a gift nor empty hands.

She wrapped herself in a fishing net, set one foot upon a goat while the other touched the road, and carried a live hare. When the prince reached for it, she opened her arms and the hare bounded away. Thus she arrived neither clothed nor bare, neither walking nor riding, and neither bearing a gift nor empty-handed.

The prince asked how her poor household lived. “My father fishes on dry hills,” she replied, “and I gather fruit from the river.”

“Fish do not live on hills, and fruit does not grow in rivers,” said the prince.

“Then an ox cannot give birth to a foal,” she answered.

The prince laughed at the neat way truth had closed the circle. He returned the foal to the poor farmer and punished the dishonest judge. Impressed by the young woman’s wisdom, he asked her to become his wife, with one condition: she must not interfere in his judgments.

For a time she kept her promise. Then, when an innocent farmer was condemned, she quietly advised him how to reveal the truth. The prince learned what she had done and angrily told her to leave the palace, though she might take one thing she loved most.

At supper she gave him a sleeping drink. When he woke in her humble home, she explained, “You allowed me to take what I loved most, so I brought you.” The prince’s anger melted. He brought her home again and listened to her counsel thereafter.

Faithfully retold from the public-domain Bohemian tale “The Clever Mountain Woman” in The Shepherd and the Dragon. Read the source text.
script_original_note: Only an English telling is published for this tale; no alternate-language script.

title: How Coyote Brought Fire to the People
subtitle: a Karuk and Pacific Northwest fire-bringing tale, about planning together and passing a gift onward
moral: Granny’s whisper: a great gift reaches home because many small paws keep it moving.
script_en:
Long ago, before people had fire, nights were cold and meals were eaten raw. High on a mountain, three powerful beings guarded the only flame. They fed it through every season and would not share even one coal.

Coyote saw children shiver beneath blankets. He saw elders rub stiff hands together. “Fire should travel,” he said. “Warmth grows when it is given.” So he climbed the mountain to watch the guardians.

For three nights Coyote hid among the rocks. He learned that two guardians slept while the third watched. At dawn they changed places. The fire never stood alone. Coyote knew that taking it would require more than speed. It would require everyone.

He called a council beside the river. Cougar came, and Bear, Deer, Squirrel, Frog, and Woodpecker. Coyote placed them along a path from the mountain to the villages. “Each runner carries the ember only as far as the next,” he explained. “No one needs to be fastest all night. We only need to be faithful for our part.”

Near midnight Coyote climbed again. He crept close, stretched one paw toward the glowing logs, and caught a burning twig between his teeth. The waking guardian shouted. Coyote ran.

Down the stony slope he flew, sparks snapping behind him. At the first bend he tossed the twig to Cougar. Cougar bounded over fallen trees and passed it to Bear. Bear crashed through berry thickets and gave it to Deer. Deer’s hooves rang along the ridge until she reached Squirrel.

The guardians were close now. Squirrel seized the ember and raced from branch to branch. The heat curled his beautiful long tail over his back, and squirrels have carried that curl ever since. At the river he dropped the coal to Frog.

Frog held it carefully in his mouth and dove. One guardian struck the water, but Frog swam beneath reeds and stones. When he reached the far bank, the ember was nearly hidden in his throat, which is why Frog’s voice became rough and why he still sings at the water’s edge.

Woodpecker took the last turn. He tucked the ember into the soft heart of a cedar and tapped the bark shut. The guardians searched everywhere, but the fire had disappeared into wood.

Coyote showed the people how to turn a dry stick against a cedar board until the hidden ember woke. They fed it grass, bark, and patient breath. Soon a small flame stood in every lodge.

No animal claimed the gift alone. Coyote had made the plan, but Cougar’s leap, Bear’s strength, Deer’s feet, Squirrel’s courage, Frog’s swim, and Woodpecker’s wisdom had carried it home. Ever after, people treated fire as a relative: never carelessly, never greedily, and always with thanks for every helper along the way.
alternate_title: How Coyote Brought Fire to the People
script_alternate:
Long ago, before people had fire, the nights were cold. Coyote watched the guardians of the only flame and made a careful plan. He placed Cougar, Bear, Deer, Squirrel, Frog, and Woodpecker along the path from the mountain to the villages.

Coyote stole one burning twig and ran. Each animal carried it only as far as the next. Squirrel’s tail curled from the heat. Frog hid the ember in his mouth and swam beneath the river. Woodpecker tucked it into the heart of cedar wood, where the guardians could not find it.

Coyote taught the people how to wake the hidden ember by rubbing dry wood together. Soon every lodge was warm. No one helper had brought fire alone; the gift arrived because each one kept faith with the next.

This Karuk and Pacific Northwest story is presented in English only. No invented Native-language script or voice has been added.
alternate_note: Second English telling as published ('Original telling (English)' / 'Oral-tradition note').

title: The Grateful Crane
subtitle: a folktale from Japan, about a rescued bird and a debt of feathers
moral: Granny’s whisper: some gifts must not be watched while they are made.
script_en:
Long ago, in the snow country of Japan, there lived a poor old man and his wife. One winter’s day, the old man heard a terrible crying in the forest. He followed the sound and found a great crane, her wing caught fast in a hunter’s trap. Gently, gently, the old man opened the trap and freed the crane’s wing. The bird bowed her long neck once, then rose into the grey sky and was gone.

That night, as the old couple sat by their small fire, there came a tap, tap, tapping at the door. Outside stood a young girl, trembling in the snow. “I have lost my way,” she said. “May I stay until the storm passes?”

They welcomed her in and gave her rice and a warm place by the fire. The storm did not pass for three days, and when it did, the girl smiled and said, “You have been kinder to me than anyone in the world. Let me be your daughter.” And so she stayed.

One evening the girl said, “Father, Mother, I will weave you a cloth to sell at the market. But you must promise me one thing. While I weave, you must never, never look into my room.” They promised.

For three days the loom went click-clack, click-clack, and when the girl came out she was thin and pale, but in her arms she held a cloth more beautiful than any ever seen: cranes flying across it as if they were alive, feathers shining like moonlight. The cloth sold for a great price at the market.

The old couple were happy, but the girl began weaving again. Click-clack, click-clack. And again she grew thinner and paler. “Do not look,” she begged, and they promised once more. But curiosity is a heavy stone in a person’s heart. One evening the old woman could bear it no longer, and she peeped through the crack in the door. And there at the loom sat not a girl, but a great white crane, plucking her own feathers, one by one, and weaving them into the cloth.

The crane turned, and her eyes were sad. “I was the crane you saved that winter day,” she said. “I came to repay your kindness. But now that you have seen my true shape, I cannot stay.”

“We are sorry,” cried the old couple. “Please, do not go.” But it was too late. The crane spread her wings, few as they were, and flew out beneath the evening sky, circling the house three times: once for the trap, once for the rice, and once for goodbye.

The old couple never forgot her. And they say that in the snow country, when a crane flies over calling, someone always looks up and whispers, “Thank you. Safe journey home.”
script_original:
むかしむかし、雪深い村に、貧しいけれど心のやさしいおじいさんとおばあさんが暮らしていました。ある冬の日、おじいさんは森で罠にかかった一羽の鶴を見つけました。おじいさんがそっと罠を外すと、鶴は長い首を一度下げ、白い翼で空へ飛んでいきました。

その晩、戸をたたく音がしました。雪の中に若い娘が立っています。「道に迷いました。泊めてくださいませんか。」二人は娘を温かく迎えました。娘はやがて、「私を娘にしてください」と言い、三人は仲よく暮らし始めました。

ある日、娘は「布を織ります。でも、決して部屋の中を見ないでください」と頼みました。三日三晩、機の音が続き、娘は月の光のように美しい布を持って出てきました。その布は高く売れましたが、娘はひどくやつれていました。

娘がもう一度織り始めると、おばあさんは心配と好奇心に負け、戸の隙間からのぞきました。そこには娘ではなく、一羽の白い鶴がいました。鶴は自分の羽を抜き、その羽で布を織っていたのです。

鶴は悲しそうに振り返りました。「私は、あの日助けていただいた鶴です。ご恩を返しに来ました。でも姿を見られたから、もうここにはいられません。」二人が泣いて謝っても、鶴は夕空へ飛び立ちました。家の上を三度まわり、感謝と別れの声を残して、雪の向こうへ消えていきました。

title: The Crystal Heart
subtitle: a Vietnamese legend, about a beautiful song, an unkind laugh, and a heart finally heard
moral: Granny’s whisper: listen for the heart before you judge the face.
script_en:
Long ago in Vietnam, the daughter of a powerful mandarin lived in rooms overlooking a broad river. Her name was Mi Nương. She had silk robes, carved screens, and servants for every need, but she knew little of the world beyond her garden wall.

Every evening a poor fisherman named Trương Chi rowed past in his weathered boat. His face was plain and his clothes were patched, but his singing voice was clear enough to make the river seem to pause and listen. High at her window, Mi Nương heard him and imagined the singer must be a handsome prince.

When the song did not come for several days, she grew pale and restless. Her father sent people along the river to find the singer, and at last Trương Chi was brought into the great house.

Mi Nương hurried forward, eager to meet the man from her dreams. But when she saw a shy fisherman in worn clothes, she laughed in surprise and turned away. The sound of that laugh hurt more deeply than any storm. Trương Chi bowed and returned alone to his small boat.

His songs faded. His sorrow grew until, one quiet day, his life ended. The villagers who prepared him for burial found that his faithful heart had become a clear crystal. They placed it gently in the river, and the current carried it away.

Much later, the crystal washed ashore near the mandarin’s home. A craftsman found it and shaped it into a delicate cup. When Mi Nương lifted the cup, the river shimmered inside it. She saw a small fishing boat and heard the song that had once risen to her window.

At last she understood the person she had refused to see. “Forgive me,” she whispered. A tear fell into the cup. At once the crystal dissolved into clear water, and the fisherman’s song floated once around the room before slipping free through the open window.

From then on, Mi Nương listened before she judged. And when songs rose from the river, she welcomed them for the truth they carried, never again measuring a heart by the coat worn over it.
script_original:
Ngày xưa ở Việt Nam, nàng Mỵ Nương, con gái một vị quan, sống trong ngôi nhà nhìn ra sông rộng. Mỗi chiều, một chàng đánh cá nghèo tên Trương Chi chèo thuyền ngang qua. Áo chàng vá nhiều chỗ, gương mặt bình thường, nhưng giọng hát trong trẻo đến nỗi dòng sông dường như cũng dừng lại lắng nghe.

Từ cửa sổ cao, Mỵ Nương nghe tiếng hát và tưởng người hát phải là một chàng hoàng tử khôi ngô. Khi tiếng hát vắng đi nhiều ngày, nàng buồn bã. Cha nàng sai người tìm, và Trương Chi được đưa vào nhà.

Mỵ Nương chạy ra gặp người trong mộng. Nhưng thấy một ngư phủ rụt rè trong bộ áo cũ, nàng bật cười rồi quay đi. Tiếng cười ấy làm Trương Chi đau đớn. Chàng trở về chiếc thuyền nhỏ, tiếng hát dần im, và chẳng bao lâu chàng qua đời vì buồn.

Người làng tìm thấy trái tim chàng đã hóa thành một khối pha lê trong suốt. Dòng nước đưa nó đến gần nhà Mỵ Nương, nơi một người thợ làm thành chiếc chén nhỏ. Khi nàng nâng chén, mặt sông hiện ra bên trong và tiếng hát xưa lại vang lên.

Mỵ Nương cuối cùng hiểu ra tấm lòng mà nàng từng không nhìn thấy. Một giọt nước mắt rơi vào chén. Pha lê tan thành nước trong, và bài hát lướt quanh căn phòng rồi bay qua cửa sổ. Từ đó, nàng luôn lắng nghe trước khi phán xét, không bao giờ đo trái tim bằng chiếc áo khoác bên ngoài.

title: The Donkey Driver of Cairo
subtitle: an Egyptian Goha tale, about a father, a son, a donkey, and far too much advice
moral: Granny’s whisper: if you try to please every voice, you may end up carrying the donkey.
script_en:
One market morning in Cairo, Goha set out with his son and their patient grey donkey. They had baskets to sell, a long road ahead, and exactly one plan: Goha would ride until the road grew hot, then his son would take a turn.

They had not gone far when a passerby frowned. “Look at that selfish father! He rides while the poor child walks.” Goha did not wish to seem selfish, so he climbed down and put his son on the donkey.

A little later two shopkeepers saw them. “What manners children have these days!” one cried. “The strong boy rides while his old father walks!” The son blushed and slid down. “You ride, Father.”

“Perhaps we should both ride,” said Goha, and they did. At the next corner a woman gasped. “That poor donkey! Two people on one small back!” So both jumped off and walked beside it.

Near the city gate, a group of men burst out laughing. “They own a donkey and neither one rides! Have you ever seen such foolishness?” Goha stopped. His son looked at him. “Father, there is only one thing left that nobody has complained about.”

So they tied the donkey’s feet gently to a strong pole, lifted the pole to their shoulders, and carried the astonished animal toward Cairo. The donkey brayed, the baskets swung, and soon the whole road was laughing. Even Goha began to laugh.

He lowered the donkey and untied it. “My son,” he said, “we have ridden, walked, shared, and carried. Every choice pleased one person and annoyed another. What should we do now?”

“What is kind to the donkey and sensible for us,” said the boy. “Exactly.” They placed the light baskets on the donkey, walked together in the cool morning, and took turns riding when they grew tired.

At the market people still had opinions — people always do. But Goha and his son had stopped borrowing every opinion they heard. The donkey, who had known this wisdom from the beginning, flicked his ears and led them home.
script_original:
في صباح يوم من أيام السوق في القاهرة، خرج جحا مع ابنه وحمارهما الرمادي الصبور. اتفقا أن يركب جحا أول الطريق، ثم يركب الصبي حين يشتد الحر.

مرّ بهما رجل وقال: «يا له من أب أناني! يركب ويترك الطفل يمشي.» فنزل جحا وأركب ابنه. بعد قليل قال تاجران: «ما أقل أدب هذا الصبي! يركب وأبوه الكبير يمشي.» خجل الصبي ونزل.

قال جحا: «لنركب معاً.» لكن امرأة صاحت: «مسكين هذا الحمار! رجلان فوق ظهره الصغير!» فنزلا ومشيا إلى جانبه. قرب باب المدينة، ضحك قوم وقالوا: «يملكان حماراً ولا يركب أحدهما!»

نظر الابن إلى أبيه وقال: «بقي أمر واحد لم ينتقده الناس.» فربطا الحمار برفق إلى عصا وحملاه على كتفيهما. نهق الحمار، وتأرجحت السلال، وضحك الطريق كله. حتى جحا ضحك.

أنزلا الحمار. قال جحا: «جرّبنا كل شيء، وكل اختيار أرضى شخصاً وأغضب آخر. ماذا نفعل الآن؟» أجاب الصبي: «نفعل ما هو رحيم بالحمار ومعقول لنا.» فوضعا السلال الخفيفة على ظهره ومشيا معاً، يتبادلان الركوب عند التعب. ظل للناس آراء، لكن جحا وابنه توقفا عن استعارة كل رأي يسمعانه. أما الحمار، فهز أذنيه كأنه كان يعرف هذه الحكمة منذ البداية.

title: The Drum That Sang by Itself
subtitle: an Akan wonder tale from Ghana, about a truth-telling drum and the trouble with wanting every gift for yourself
moral: Granny’s whisper: a song may be borrowed, but its truth still belongs to everyone.
script_en:
Long ago in an Akan village, a girl named Abena gathered fallen branches at the forest edge. Her family had little, but each evening her grandmother made a warm place by the fire and filled it with songs.

One day Abena heard a soft voice beneath an odum tree: tum, tum, ta-tum. In a hollow lay a small carved drum no larger than a cooking pot. No drummer sat beside it, yet it sang:

“Kind hands lifted me from the rain. Kind feet carry me home again.”

Abena looked all around. “If you wish to come,” she said, “you may share our hearth.” She carried the drum home, where Grandmother welcomed it as politely as any visitor.

That night the drum sang everything it had seen: the moon caught in plantain leaves, a lost goat led home by two children, and Abena leaving the straightest branches for an elder who walked slowly. It never praised wealth or fine clothing. It sang only what was true.

Soon neighbors gathered outside the little house. They brought soup, stools, and their own verses. The drum answered each honest song with a rhythm. But when someone boasted, the drum fell silent until laughter softened the boast.

The village chief heard of the wonder and sent guards. “A drum that sings by itself belongs in my courtyard,” he declared. Abena bowed. “It came freely. Perhaps ask whether it wishes to go.”

The chief laughed and carried the drum away.

That evening he invited important guests. “Sing of my wisdom,” he commanded.

The drum replied:

“A wide stool is not a wide heart. The hand that grabs has the smallest part.”

The guests hid smiles behind their cups. The chief ordered a louder song about his generosity.

The drum sang:

“He stores ten baskets behind one door, while a hungry neighbor searches the floor.”

Now no one could hide their laughter. Furious, the chief covered the drum with cloth, but its voice came through. He locked it in a chest, but the chest thumped in perfect time. He buried it, and the earth beneath his courtyard hummed until even the chickens danced.

At last the chief dug it up and carried it back to Abena. “Make it stop embarrassing me,” he begged.

“I cannot order truth to stop,” she said. “But you can give it a kinder song to learn.”

The chief opened his storehouse. He shared yams during the lean weeks, repaired the widow’s roof, and listened when children spoke at the village meeting. Slowly the drum’s verses changed.

“A closed hand opened; the village ate. A proud ear listened before too late.”

From then on, the drum stayed in the meeting house, where no one person owned it. Anyone could play beside it, but it answered best when deeds and words matched. Abena became its keeper, not its master, and taught every child its oldest rhythm: tum, tum, ta-tum—the sound of a truth arriving home.
script_original:
Tete no, abeawa bi a wɔfrɛ no Abena kɔfaa mmabaa a ahwe ase wɔ kwae ano. Na n’abusua nni pii, nanso anadwo biara ne nanabea sɔ gya, na ɔde nnwom ma fie no yɛ hyew.

Da bi, Abena tee nne ketewa bi wɔ odum dua bi ase: tum, tum, ta-tum. Ɔhunuu sankuo ketewa bi wɔ dua tokuru mu. Obiara nni hɔ a ɔrebɔ no, nanso sankuo no too dwom sɛ:

“Nsa pa ayi me afi osuo mu. Anan pa de me rekɔ fie bio.”

Abena kae sɛ, “Sɛ wopɛ sɛ wokɔ a, bra ne yɛn ntena gya ho.” Ɔde sankuo no kɔɔ fie, na Nanabea gyee no sɛ ɔhɔho pa.

Saa anadwo no, sankuo no kaa nea na ahu nyinaa: ɔsram a ɛda kwadu nhaban mu, mmofra baanu a wɔde abirekyi a wayera baa fie, ne Abena a ɔgyaa mmabaa pa maa ɔpanin bi a ɔnam brɛoo. Sankuo no ankamfo sika anaa ntade pa. Ɛkaa nokware nko ara.

Ɛnkyɛ na afipamfo hyiaa ofie no anim. Wɔde nkwan, akongua ne wɔn ankasa nnwom bae. Sɛ dwom no yɛ nokware a, sankuo no gye so. Sɛ obi hoahoa ne ho a, ɛyɛ komm kosi sɛ serew bɛma ahantan no abrɛ ase.

Ɔhene tee anwonwade no ho asɛm, na ɔsoma maa wɔkɔfaa sankuo no. Ɔkae sɛ, “Sankuo a ɛto dwom ankasa no wɔ sɛ ɛtena m’abangua mu.” Abena buu ne mu na ɔkae sɛ, “Ɛbaa yɛn nkyɛn ne pɛ mu. Bisa no sɛ ɔpɛ sɛ ɔkɔ anaa.” Ɔhene serewee na ɔfaa no kɔe.

Anadwo no, ɔfrɛɛ ahɔhoɔ. Ɔhyɛɛ sankuo no sɛ, “To dwom fa me nyansa ho.” Sankuo no buae sɛ:

“Akongua kɛse nyɛ koma kɛse. Nsa a ɛfa nyinaa nya kyɛfa ketewa.”

Ɔhene hyɛɛ no sɛ ɔnto dwom fa ne ayamye ho. Sankuo no kaa sɛ:

“Ɔde nkɛntɛn du ahyɛ pon baako akyi, bere a ɔyɔnko kɔm de no.”

Ɔhene de ntama kataa so, nanso nne no fii mu bae. Ɔde no guu adaka mu, nanso adaka no bɔɔ twene. Ɔsiee no fam, na asase no hyee dwom kosi sɛ nkokɔ mpo sawee.

Afei ɔhene de sankuo no san brɛɛ Abena. Abena kae sɛ, “Merentumi nhyɛ nokware sɛ ɛnyɛ komm. Nanso wubetumi ayɛ ade pa ama no anya dwom pa.”

Ɔhene buee n’akorade. Ɔkyɛɛ bayere, osiesiee ɔbea kunafo fie, na ɔtiee mmofra wɔ asafo mu. Sankuo no dwom sesae:

“Nsa a na ato mu abue; kurow no adidi. Aso a na ɛyɛ ahantan atie ansa na akyɛ.”

Efi saa bere no, sankuo no tenaa asafo fie. Obiara anni no nko ara. Abena bɛyɛɛ ne hwɛfo, na ɔkyerɛɛ abofra biara ne nnyigyei dedaw no: tum, tum, ta-tum—nokware a ɛresan aba fie.

title: The Empty Pot
subtitle: a folktale from China, about a seed, a year, and the truth
moral: Granny’s whisper: an honest empty pot outshines a dishonest garden.
script_en:
Long ago in China there lived a boy named Ping, who loved growing things more than anything in the world. Give him a seed, any seed at all, and he could make it grow. His garden was the pride of the village — though Ping himself was a shy and quiet boy.

Now in those days the Emperor was growing old, and he had no son or daughter to rule after him. So he made an announcement that traveled to every corner of the land: “Let every child in the kingdom come to the palace. Each of them shall be given one seed. In a year’s time, they shall return with what they have grown, and the child worthy of the finest flower will be worthy of the kingdom.”

When Ping’s turn came, he took his seed home as carefully as if it were an egg. He chose his best pot, his best soil, and his best spot of morning sun. He planted the seed, and he watered it, just a little, every single day.

But the seed did not sprout. Weeks passed. Ping gave it richer soil. Nothing. He moved it into better light. Nothing. He even sang to it, because you never know. Still nothing. Other children were already boasting about their little green shoots, but Ping’s pot stayed stubbornly, mysteriously empty.

The seasons turned, and the day came to return to the palace. Down every road walked children carrying tall chrysanthemums, sweet peonies, and roses as red as lanterns. And behind them all came Ping, holding a pot of plain brown earth, with hot tears in his eyes.

At the palace the Emperor walked slowly down the line, and as he looked at all the beautiful flowers, his face grew darker and darker, which puzzled everyone. Then he came to Ping. “And what is this?” he asked. “Did you forget your flower?” Ping hung his head. “No, Your Majesty. I gave my seed the best of everything, and I watered it every day. But it would not grow, and I cannot tell you why. So I have brought you my empty pot, and I am sorry.”

The Emperor was quiet for a long moment. Then he smiled, lifted Ping’s chin gently, and turned to the crowd. “I gave every one of you a seed that had been boiled,” he said. “No boiled seed can ever grow. I do not know where all these flowers came from — but I know this one child came back with the truth, an empty pot, and a brave heart.”

And so the empty pot became the most famous pot in the whole kingdom — and shy Ping, the boy who could grow anything except a lie, grew up to tend an entire land.
script_original:
从前，中国有一位年老的皇帝。他没有孩子，便决定从全国的孩子中选一位继承人。皇帝给每个孩子一粒种子，说：“一年以后，把你们种出的花带到宫里来。谁种得最好，谁就成为继承人。”

一个叫平的男孩最爱种花。他把种子放进最好的土里，每天浇水，让花盆晒太阳。可是一天过去，一月过去，什么也没有长出来。他换了土，也换了花盆，种子仍旧没有发芽。

一年后，孩子们都捧着开满鲜花的花盆去见皇帝。平只捧着一个空花盆。他的父亲说：“你已经尽了最大的努力。诚实地把结果带去吧。”

皇帝看过一盆盆艳丽的花，却一直皱着眉。看到平的空花盆时，他问：“你为什么什么也没种出来？”平低着头，把自己如何照料种子的事情全说了。

皇帝终于笑了。“我给你们的种子都煮过，根本不可能发芽。”他说，“只有平带来了真话。”于是皇帝选择平做继承人。那一天，全国的人都明白了：诚实看起来也许像一只空花盆，里面却装着最珍贵的勇气。

title: The Fisherman and the Jinni
subtitle: a tale from the Arabian Nights, about a copper pot and a very patient temper
moral: Granny’s whisper: a cool head outlasts four hundred years of temper.
script_en:
Long ago, on the shores of a warm and glittering sea, there lived a poor fisherman who cast his net into the waves four times every day — no more, no less, for that was his rule.

One morning he waded out at sunrise and threw his net for the first time. When he hauled it in, it was so heavy he could barely lift it. “A fine catch!” he cried. But when the net opened, out flopped a dead donkey, soggy and smelling dreadful. “Well,” sighed the fisherman, “at least the day can only improve.”

The second cast brought an old basket packed with mud. The third brought stones and bleached white bones, clicking at his feet. And the fisherman looked up at the bright sky and said, “Once more, then. The fourth throw decides the day.”

He cast the net wide, and it sank down, down, down. When he pulled, he had to wade back to shore and drag it up the sand. Inside there was not a single fish — only a round copper pot, plugged tight with a lead seal, and on the seal the mark of a great and ancient king.

“A pot is better than bones,” said the fisherman. “I shall sell it for a few coins at the market.” But when he turned it over, it felt strangely light — and strangely warm. And curiosity, which is a fisherman of its own kind, got the better of him. He picked the seal open with his knife.

Out poured a column of smoke — thick, dark, and taller than the tallest tower. It climbed and curled until it covered the sun, and then it gathered itself into a gigantic jinni, with eyes like lamps and a voice like thunder in a mountain cave. “The time has come!” roared the jinni. “Choose how you wish to die!”

The fisherman trembled. “But why? I have let you out!” The jinni crossed his enormous arms. “For four hundred years I lay in that pot. In the first century I swore to shower my rescuer with riches. In the second, with palaces. In the third, with wishes. But no one came. So in my fourth century I grew angry, and swore to grant whoever freed me only the choice of how to die. Choose quickly!”

Now the fisherman was a poor man, but he was not a slow one. He looked at the tiny pot, and he looked at the mountain-sized jinni, and he said, “Forgive me, great one. Before I choose, I must settle a doubt in my heart. How could a jinni as grand as you ever fit inside this little pot? I simply do not believe it.”

“Not believe it?” thundered the jinni. “Then watch!” He turned himself back into smoke, thinner and thinner, and spiraled down into the copper pot — and the moment the last wisp had vanished inside, the fisherman slapped the lead seal back on and held it tight. “Now,” he said, “I shall throw you back into the sea, and tell every fisherman to beware your promises.”

From inside the pot, the jinni’s voice came very small and very polite. “Wait. Promise to let me out, and I swear by the great seal upon this pot that I shall not harm a hair of your head. Instead, I shall make you rich.” The fisherman thought. “A jinni of honor keeps his oath, I hope.” And he opened the seal once more.

Out came the jinni, who bowed until his forehead nearly touched the sand. “You are wiser than I,” he said. “Come.” And he led the fisherman over the hills to a hidden lake, where the water shone like glass. “Cast your net here.” The fisherman threw his net, and when he pulled it in, it held four fish the color of jewels: a white one, a red one, a blue one, and a yellow one, glittering like stars.

The jinni told him to carry the fish to the palace and offer them to the sultan — and they were so marvelous that the sultan filled the fisherman’s hands with gold, and his family was comfortable all the rest of their days. And that is why the grandmothers of the old ports say: keep a cool head when the smoke rises, dear. A clever question can bottle a mountain.
script_original:
كان يا ما كان، في قديم الزمان، صياد فقير لا يرمي شبكته في البحر أكثر من أربع مرات كل يوم. في صباحٍ ما، ألقى الشبكة ثلاث مرات فلم يجد إلا حماراً ميتاً وجرّة مكسورة وحجارة ثقيلة. بقيت له رمية واحدة، فرفع يديه إلى السماء وألقى الشبكة.

خرجت من الماء جرّة نحاسية مختومة بخاتم الملك سليمان. فتح الصياد الغطاء، فتصاعد دخان كثيف حتى ملأ السماء، ثم صار عفريتاً هائلاً. قال العفريت إنه ظل محبوساً أربعمئة عام، وإنه أقسم في غضبه أن يقتل من يحرره. ارتجف الصياد، لكنه لم يفقد عقله.

قال: «لا أصدق أنك كنت داخل هذه الجرّة الصغيرة. قدمك وحدها أكبر منها.» غضب العفريت وتحول إلى دخان، ثم دخل الجرّة ليبرهن على كلامه. وما إن صار كله في الداخل حتى أغلق الصياد الغطاء بسرعة وأعاد الخاتم إلى مكانه.

صرخ العفريت وطلب الرحمة. قال الصياد: «كما كنت تريد قتلي بعد أن أنقذتك، سأعيدك إلى البحر.» فأقسم العفريت أن يكافئه وألا يؤذيه. لم يثق به الصياد حتى كرر عهده، ثم أطلقه.

قاد العفريت الصياد إلى بحيرة خفية مليئة بأسماك عجيبة، ومن هناك بدأت مغامرات أخرى. أما الصياد فتعلم أن القوة الكبيرة قد تهزمها فكرة هادئة، وأن الرحمة لا تكون عمياء: تُمنح بعد عهد صادق، لا قبل الحذر.

title: The Four Harmonious Friends
subtitle: a Himalayan Jātaka tale about respect, shared work, and four friends who stand together
moral: Granny’s whisper: harmony does not make every friend the same; it gives every gift a place to stand.
script_en:
In the forest of Kashika stood a clear spring and, beside it, a young fruit tree. Four animals made their homes nearby: a partridge, a hare, a monkey, and an elephant. They drank from the same water and rested in the same shade, yet they often disagreed over who should speak first and who should be honoured as the eldest.

The partridge remembered carrying a seed in her beak and dropping it beside the spring. The hare remembered watering the first tender shoot. The monkey had brought rich leaves and fruit peel to feed the soil. The elephant had guarded the sapling, turning aside branches and heavy feet that might crush it.

Season followed season. The tree grew tall, its crown bright with fruit. The partridge could flutter among the lower twigs, the monkey could climb higher, the hare could nibble fallen leaves, and the elephant could reach with his trunk. But the sweetest fruit hung beyond every one of them. Alone, each friend came up short.

Before deciding what to do, they settled their old question of age. The elephant said, “When I first passed this place, the tree was a young sapling. Its top brushed my belly.” The monkey said, “When I first played here, it was only a shrub. I stepped across it without lifting my tail.”

The hare said, “When I first came, it was a fresh green sprout. I licked the dew from its two little leaves.” At last the partridge said, “Before there was a sprout, I ate fruit from an older tree far away. I carried this seed inside me and left it here beside the spring.”

The others bowed to the partridge as the eldest. From that day, age did not make her a ruler who took more. It made her a guide whose long memory helped the friends care for one another. The partridge listened to the elephant’s strength, the monkey’s quickness, and the hare’s patient attention to the ground.

Then they found a way to reach the fruit. The elephant stood firm beneath the branches. The monkey climbed onto his broad back. The hare balanced on the monkey, and the partridge perched at the very top. Together they reached the highest fruit. They passed it down and divided it equally, including the softest pieces for neighbours who had done no climbing.

The four friends promised to protect life, take only what was freely given, speak truthfully, keep faith with one another, and guard their minds from heedlessness. Their harmony spread through the forest. Quarrels softened. The spring stayed clean. The fruit tree fed travellers as well as those who tended it.

People still picture the elephant carrying the monkey, the monkey carrying the hare, and the hare carrying the bird. The image teaches that respect is not standing below because one matters less. It is choosing a strong place for every gift. When wisdom, patience, playfulness, and strength support one another, goodness grows higher than any one friend could reach.
script_original:
ཀ་ཤི་ཀའི་ནགས་ཚལ་ནང་དུ་ཆུ་མིག་དྭངས་མོ་ཞིག་དང་། དེའི་འགྲམ་དུ་ཤིང་ཏོག་གི་སྡོང་པོ་གཞོན་ནུ་ཞིག་ཡོད། བྱ་སྲེག་པ། རི་བོང་། སྤྲེའུ། གླང་ཆེན་བཅས་སེམས་ཅན་བཞི་པོ་དེའི་ཉེ་འགྲམ་དུ་གནས་བཅས། ཁོང་ཚོས་ཆུ་གཅིག་འཐུང་ཞིང་གྲིབ་མ་གཅིག་ཏུ་ངལ་གསོ་ཡང་། སུ་རྒན་པ་ཡིན་མིན་ཐད་རྩོད་པ་བྱེད།

བྱ་སྲེག་པས་ས་བོན་ཞིག་ཁ་ནས་ཁྱེར་ཏེ་ཆུ་མིག་འགྲམ་དུ་བཞག་པ་དྲན། རི་བོང་གིས་མྱུ་གུ་ཆུང་ངུ་ལ་ཆུ་བླུགས། སྤྲེའུས་ལོ་མ་དང་ཤིང་ཏོག་གི་པགས་པ་ཁྱེར་ནས་ས་གཞི་གསོས། གླང་ཆེན་གྱིས་སྡོང་ཕྲུག་སྲུང་ཞིང་། རྐང་པ་ལྕི་མོས་མི་རྫི་བར་བྱས།

དུས་ཚིགས་རིམ་པར་འདས། སྡོང་པོ་མཐོ་རུ་སྐྱེས་ཤིང་ཤིང་ཏོག་གིས་གང་། བྱ་སྲེག་པ་ཡལ་གའི་བར་དུ་འཕུར་ཐུབ། སྤྲེའུ་མཐོ་སར་འཛེག་ཐུབ། རི་བོང་གིས་སར་ལྷུང་བའི་ལོ་མ་ཟ་ཐུབ། གླང་ཆེན་གྱིས་སྣ་བརྐྱངས་ཐུབ། འོན་ཀྱང་ཤིང་ཏོག་ཞིམ་ཤོས་ནི་ཚང་མའི་ལག་ལས་མཐོ།

གླང་ཆེན་གྱིས། “ང་འདིར་ཐོག་མར་ཡོང་དུས། སྡོང་པོ་ནི་སྡོང་ཕྲུག་ཡིན་ཞིང་ངའི་གྲོད་པ་ལ་ཐུག་གི་ཡོད།” ཟེར། སྤྲེའུས། “ང་འདིར་རྩེད་མོ་རྩེ་དུས། དེ་ནི་ཤིང་ཕྲན་ཆུང་ངུ་ཙམ་ཡིན། ངས་མཇུག་མ་མ་བཀྱགས་པར་མཆོངས་ཐུབ།” ཟེར།

རི་བོང་གིས། “ང་ཐོག་མར་ཡོང་དུས། དེ་ནི་ལོ་མ་གཉིས་ཅན་གྱི་མྱུ་གུ་གསར་པ་ཞིག་ཡིན། ངས་དེའི་སྟེང་གི་ཟིལ་པ་ལྡག་མྱོང་།” ཟེར། མཐར་བྱ་སྲེག་པས། “མྱུ་གུ་མ་སྐྱེས་གོང་། ངས་རྒྱང་གི་སྡོང་པོ་རྙིང་པའི་ཤིང་ཏོག་ཟོས། ས་བོན་འདི་ངས་ཁྱེར་ཡོང་བ་ཡིན།” ཟེར།

གཞན་གསུམ་གྱིས་བྱ་སྲེག་པ་རྒན་ཤོས་སུ་བཀུར། རྒན་པ་ཡིན་པས་དབང་ཆ་མང་བ་མ་བླངས། དྲན་པ་རིང་པོས་གྲོགས་པོ་རྣམས་ལ་ལམ་སྟོན་བྱས། བྱ་སྲེག་པས་གླང་ཆེན་གྱི་སྟོབས། སྤྲེའུའི་མྱུར་བ། རི་བོང་གི་བཟོད་པ་བཅས་ལ་ཉན།

ཁོང་ཚོས་མཐོ་སའི་ཤིང་ཏོག་ལེན་པའི་ཐབས་ཤེས་རྙེད། གླང་ཆེན་ཡལ་གའི་འོག་ཏུ་བརྟན་པོར་ལངས། སྤྲེའུ་ཁོའི་རྒྱབ་ཏུ་འཛེགས། རི་བོང་སྤྲེའུའི་སྟེང་དུ་བསྡད། བྱ་སྲེག་པ་ཆེས་མཐོ་སར་བབས། དེ་ལྟར་ཁོང་ཚོས་ཤིང་ཏོག་བླངས་ཏེ་ཆ་སྙོམས་སུ་བགོས།

གྲོགས་པོ་བཞིས་སྲོག་སྐྱོབ་པ། མ་བྱིན་པ་མི་ལེན་པ། བདེན་པར་སྨྲ་བ། ཕན་ཚུན་ཡིད་ཆེས་སྲུང་བ། བག་མེད་ལས་སེམས་སྲུང་བའི་དམ་བཅས། ཁོང་ཚོའི་མཐུན་པ་ནགས་ཚལ་ཡོངས་ལ་ཁྱབ། ཆུ་མིག་གཙང་མར་གནས། སྡོང་པོས་ལམ་འགྲུལ་པའང་གསོས།

ད་ལྟའང་མི་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་གླང་ཆེན་གྱིས་སྤྲེའུ་ཁུར་བ། སྤྲེའུས་རི་བོང་ཁུར་བ། རི་བོང་གིས་བྱ་ཁུར་བའི་རི་མོ་བྲིས། གུས་ཞབས་ནི་རང་ཉིད་གལ་ཆུང་བར་བལྟ་བ་མིན། ཡོན་ཏན་རེ་རེ་ལ་གནས་འོས་པ་སྟེར་བ་ཡིན། ཤེས་རབ་དང་བཟོད་པ། སྤྲོ་བ། སྟོབས་བཅས་མཉམ་དུ་གནས་ན། དགེ་བ་མཐོ་རུ་སྐྱེ།

title: The Fox and the Condor
subtitle: an Andean folktale from Peru, about a sky feast, a boastful fox, and borrowed wings
moral: Granny’s whisper: every old story grows warmer when we listen with care.
script_en:
High in the Andes, where the mountains wear snow and the valleys fold into green terraces, Fox loved to boast. He said he could outrun the wind, outtalk the river, and outwit any creature beneath the sun. Condor usually listened in silence, for the sky teaches patience.

One evening Condor mentioned a feast among the stars. There would be music, golden maize, roasted potatoes, and bowls of sweet drink. Fox’s ears stood straight. “Take me,” he begged. “No one enjoys a feast as wisely as I do.” Condor warned him, “The road is made for wings.” Fox promised to obey.

At dusk Fox climbed onto Condor’s broad back. They rose above stone walls and llama paths, above clouds glowing rose in the sunset, until the villages became tiny sparks. Fox trembled but shouted, “Higher! I was born for the sky!” Condor spread his wings and carried him to the bright hall of the stars.

At first Fox behaved politely. Then the music quickened. He ate one bowl, then three, then seven. He danced on the tables and told everyone he had flown there by himself. Condor shook his head. “We leave before dawn,” he said. But Fox answered, “Go ahead. I know every road.”

When the sky grew pale, Fox searched for a path down. There was none. He called for Condor, but the great bird was already far below. At last Fox braided a rope from dry grass and lowered himself toward the earth.

The rope was long, but the mountains were farther. Halfway down, a flock of parrots passed. Fox could not resist teasing them. Angry at his insults, one parrot snipped the grass rope. Fox tumbled through the cold morning air.

“Spread blankets below!” he cried. “Pile soft wool and flower petals!” The people looked up, but the wind twisted his words. Fox landed in a patch of thorny scrub. He was bruised, scratched, and very quiet for several days.

The people who pulled Fox from the thorns washed his scratches and gave him a warm potato. For once he did not claim he had planned the fall. He thanked them plainly. That simple truth felt lighter than any boast and steadier than a rope of grass.

Condor found him limping home. “The sky gave me wings,” Condor said. “The earth gave you quick feet. Neither gift needs boasting.” Fox looked at the high white peaks and nodded. After that, when he spoke of the feast among the stars, he praised Condor’s strength, the beauty of the mountains, and the kindness of those who helped him from the thorns. He still loved a good story, but he learned to leave room in it for the gifts of others.
script_alternate:
En lo alto de los Andes, donde las montañas llevan nieve y los valles se doblan en terrazas verdes, el Zorro era muy amigo de presumir. Decía que podía correr más que el viento, hablar más que el río y engañar a cualquier criatura bajo el sol. El Cóndor solía escucharlo en silencio, porque el cielo enseña paciencia.

Una tarde, el Cóndor mencionó una fiesta entre las estrellas. Habría música, maíz dorado, papas asadas y cuencos de bebida dulce. Las orejas del Zorro se levantaron. “Llévame”, rogó. “Nadie sabe disfrutar una fiesta como yo.” El Cóndor le advirtió: “Ese camino fue hecho para alas.” El Zorro prometió obedecer.

Al anochecer, el Zorro subió sobre la espalda ancha del Cóndor. Volaron por encima de muros de piedra y senderos de llamas, por encima de nubes rosadas, hasta que las aldeas parecieron pequeñas chispas. El Zorro temblaba, pero gritó: “¡Más alto! ¡Yo nací para el cielo!” El Cóndor extendió sus alas y lo llevó al salón brillante de las estrellas.

Al principio, el Zorro se portó con educación. Luego la música se hizo rápida. Comió un plato, después tres y finalmente siete. Bailó sobre las mesas y contó a todos que había llegado volando por su propia fuerza. El Cóndor movió la cabeza. “Nos vamos antes del amanecer”, dijo. Pero el Zorro respondió: “Vete tú. Yo conozco todos los caminos.”

Cuando el cielo empezó a aclarar, el Zorro buscó una senda para bajar. No había ninguna. Llamó al Cóndor, pero el gran ave ya estaba muy abajo. Por fin, trenzó una cuerda con paja seca y comenzó a descender hacia la tierra.

La cuerda era larga, pero las montañas estaban todavía más lejos. A mitad del camino pasó una bandada de loros. El Zorro no pudo evitar burlarse de ellos. Enojado por sus insultos, uno de los loros cortó la cuerda de paja. El Zorro cayó dando vueltas por el aire frío de la mañana.

“¡Pongan mantas abajo!”, gritó. “¡Amontonen lana suave y pétalos!” La gente miró hacia arriba, pero el viento revolvió sus palabras. El Zorro aterrizó en unos matorrales llenos de espinas. Quedó golpeado, arañado y muy callado durante varios días.

La gente que sacó al Zorro de las espinas lavó sus arañazos y le dio una papa caliente. Por una vez no afirmó que la caída había sido parte de su plan. Les dio las gracias con sencillez. Aquella verdad pesaba menos que cualquier alarde y era más firme que una cuerda de paja.

El Cóndor lo encontró caminando con dificultad. “El cielo me dio alas”, dijo. “La tierra te dio pies veloces. Ningún regalo necesita presumir.” El Zorro miró las altas cumbres blancas y asintió. Desde entonces, cuando contaba la fiesta de las estrellas, alababa la fuerza del Cóndor, la belleza de las montañas y la bondad de quienes lo sacaron de las espinas. Seguía amando una buena historia, pero aprendió a dejar espacio para los dones de los demás.
alternate_note: Published ‘Adaptación en español andino’ — a Spanish adaptation.

title: The Three Billy Goats Gruff
subtitle: a folktale from Norway, about grass, greed, and minding the bridge
moral: Granny’s whisper: never wrestle a troll before breakfast.
script_en:
Once upon a time, on a green mountainside in Norway, there lived three billy goats, and all three were called Gruff. There was Little Billy Goat Gruff, Middle-Sized Billy Goat Gruff, and Great Big Billy Goat Gruff.

On their side of the river the grass had been nibbled down to the roots, but across the bridge, on the far hillside, the grass grew tall and sweet and green. The trouble was the bridge. Under the bridge lived a troll, a great ugly troll, with eyes as big as saucers and a nose as long as a poker, and he ate whatever tried to cross.

First came Little Billy Goat Gruff. Trip, trap, trip, trap went his little hooves on the bridge. “Who’s that tripping over my bridge?” roared the troll. “It is only I, Little Billy Goat Gruff,” said the smallest goat, in a voice no bigger than a whisper, “and I am going up to the hillside to make myself fat.” “Then I am coming up to eat you!” said the troll. “Oh please don’t eat me,” said the little goat. “I am far too small. Wait for my brother. He is much bigger.” “Very well,” said the troll. “Be off with you.”

Then came Middle-Sized Billy Goat Gruff. Trip, trap, trip, trap, trip, trap. “Who’s that tramping over my bridge?” roared the troll. “It is I, Middle-Sized Billy Goat Gruff,” said the second goat, “and I am going up to the hillside to make myself fat.” “Then I am coming up to eat you!” said the troll. “Oh no,” said the second goat. “Don’t eat me. Wait for my big brother. He is much, much bigger.” “Very well,” said the troll.

Then came Great Big Billy Goat Gruff. TRIP, TRAP, TRIP, TRAP. The bridge groaned under his weight. “Who’s that tramping over my bridge?” roared the troll. “It is I, Great Big Billy Goat Gruff,” said the biggest goat, in a voice as deep as a drum. “Then I am coming up to eat you!” “Well, come along!” said Great Big Billy Goat Gruff.

Up flew the troll, roaring and waving his arms. But the big goat lowered his head, and his horns were as sharp as spears. He charged, and he butted the troll so hard that the troll flew up into the air and splashed down into the river, and was carried away, and that was the end of him.

Then Great Big Billy Goat Gruff trotted up the hillside, and there the three goats munched the tall sweet grass until they were so fat they could hardly walk home. And if the grass hasn’t run out, they are eating there still. Snip, snap, snout. This tale is told out.
script_original:
Det var en gang tre bukker som alle het Bruse. Den minste var liten og lett på foten, den mellomste var sterkere, og den største hadde horn som kunne flytte en stein. På deres side av elven var gresset spist helt ned. På den andre siden lå seteren grønn og frodig, men for å komme dit måtte de over en bro. Under broen bodde et troll med øyne som tallerkener og en nese lang som et kosteskaft.

Først gikk den minste bukken. «Tripp, trapp, tripp, trapp», sa hovene. «Hvem er det som tramper på min bro?» brølte trollet. «Det er bare den minste bukken Bruse. Jeg skal til seters og gjøre meg fet.» Trollet ville spise ham, men bukken ba ham vente på den mellomste, som var mye større. Trollet lot ham gå.

Så kom den mellomste bukken: «Tripp, trapp, tripp, trapp.» Trollet fór opp igjen. Men også denne bukken ba ham vente på storebroren. «Han er mye, mye større.» Det likte det grådige trollet å høre, så den mellomste fikk gå.

Til slutt kom den største bukken Bruse. Broen knaket: «TRIPP, TRAPP!» Trollet sprang opp for å spise ham. Den store bukken senket hodet, satte de sterke hornene fram og stanget trollet rett ut i elven. Strømmen førte det langt bort.

De tre bukkene gikk til seters og spiste det søte, grønne gresset til de knapt kunne gå hjem. Og er ikke gresset borte, så går de der ennå. Snipp, snapp, snute — så er eventyret ute.

title: Grandmother Spider Brings the Fire
subtitle: a Cherokee First Fire story, told of the small helper whose courage warmed the world
moral: Granny’s whisper: never mistake small for powerless; one careful ember can warm a whole circle.
script_en:
In the first days, the world was cold. People and animals huddled close, but they had no fire for warmth, no flame for cooking, and no glowing coal to guide a traveller home. The Creator heard every shiver and knew it was time for fire to come into the world.

Great Thunder rolled across the sky. Lightning struck a hollow sycamore on an island in the middle of the water. Flames woke inside the tree, red and gold, but the water around the island was wide and deep. All the animals gathered on the shore to watch the precious light.

Raven went first. “My wings are strong,” he said. He flew through the smoke and tried to carry fire in his beak. The heat burned his feathers black, and he returned without an ember. Owl flew next. He came so near the flames that the heat scorched pale rings around his eyes. He, too, returned empty.

Snake offered to swim across. He slipped into the hollow tree, but the fire twisted and cracked around him. Smoke stung his eyes, and he wriggled back through the water. Other large and swift animals tried. Each had strength of one kind, yet the flame asked for a different gift.

At last Grandmother Water Spider stepped forward. She was tiny beside Raven, Owl, and Snake. “I will go,” she said. Some animals worried that the waves would cover her. Others wondered how such a small creature could carry a coal. Grandmother Spider simply began to work.

With patient legs she spun a little bowl called a tusti. Thread crossed thread until the bowl was light, close-woven, and strong. She fastened it to her back. Then she walked over the water, resting on its skin so gently that even the smallest ripple did not swallow her.

At the island, Grandmother Spider crept through the cool side of the sycamore. She found one quiet coal glowing beneath the ash. She placed it in her woven bowl and wrapped it safely. Some tellings say she carried the ember inside a tiny bubble of air. Slowly she crossed the water again.

The animals waited until a red point appeared on the dark shore. Grandmother Spider set down her bowl. They fed the coal dry bark, grass, and little sticks. A warm flame rose. Everyone moved close, leaving room for the smallest creatures at the front. They learned to tend the fire, share it, and never let it wander carelessly through the forest.

Raven kept his black feathers. Owl kept the marks around his eyes. Snake remembered the smoke. And the people remembered Grandmother Spider, who did not need great size or a loud voice to bring a world-changing gift. Sometimes the one who saves the whole circle is the quiet helper who knows how to weave, wait, and carry one small light home.
script_original:
ᎢᎬᏱ ᎡᎶᎯ ᎤᏴᏢ ᎤᏴᏜ ᎠᎴ ᎤᏴᏜ ᎨᏎᏍᏗ. ᏴᏫ ᎠᎴ ᎦᏓᏘ ᏚᎾᏓᏟᏌᏅ ᏗᎨᎵᏍᎩ ᎨᏒᎢ, ᎠᏎᏃ ᎠᏥᎳ ᎥᏝ ᏱᎨᎲᎢ. ᎥᏝ ᏱᎬᏩᎾᎦᎵᎢ, ᎥᏝ ᏱᎬᏩᎾᏅᏓᏗᏍᏗ, ᎥᏝ ᏱᎬᏩᎾᎪᎲ ᏗᏂᎩᏍᏗ. ᎤᏬᏢᏅᎯ ᏚᏛᎦᏁᎢ ᏂᎦᏛ ᎠᏂᎾᏫᏍᎬᎢ, ᎠᎴ ᎠᏥᎳ ᎤᏓᎴᏅᎯ ᎨᏎᏍᏗ ᎠᏓᏅᏖᎢ.

ᎤᏍᎦᏃᎵ ᎤᏃᏴᎩ ᎦᎸᎳᏗ. ᎤᎾᎦᎵᎯᏍᏗ ᎤᏩᏍᏔᏅ ᏥᎳᏁᏍᏗ ᎤᎾᏓᏛ ᎠᏰᎵ ᎠᎹ. ᎠᏥᎳ ᎤᎾᏓᏛ ᎠᏯᎸᎢ, ᎩᎦᎨ ᎠᎴ ᎠᏓᎶᏂᎨ ᎢᏳᏍᏗ, ᎠᏎᏃ ᎠᎹ ᎤᏂᏴᏢ ᎤᏍᏗᎩᏛ ᎥᏝ ᏱᎨᏎᎢ. ᏂᎦᏛ ᎦᏓᏘ ᎤᏣᏘ ᎠᏂᎪᎯ ᎤᏂᏗᏢ ᎠᎹ.

ᎪᎾ ᎢᎬᏱ ᎤᏪᏅᏎᎢ. “ᎠᏆᏤᎵ ᏗᎦᏃᎨ ᏚᎾᎵᏂᎩᏛ,” ᎤᏛᏁᎢ. ᎠᏥᎳ ᎤᏪᏅᏒ ᎤᎿᏅᏛ ᎠᎴ ᎤᏔᏅ ᎤᏃᏴᎩ. ᎤᏥᎸ ᏗᎦᏃᎨ ᏗᎬᎿᎨ ᏂᏚᏩᏁᎢ, ᎠᎴ Ꮭ ᏳᏲᏒ ᎠᏥᎳ. ᎤᎶᎩᎸᎢ ᏔᎵᏁ ᎤᏪᏅᏎᎢ. ᎤᏍᏗ ᎤᎶᎩ ᎤᎦᏔ ᎤᏓᎴᏅᎯ ᏚᏴᏍᏕᎢ. ᎾᏍᎩ ᎾᏍᏉ ᎤᏨᏎ ᎾᎩᎾ ᎠᏥᎳ.

ᎢᎾᏛ ᎤᏪᏅᏎᎢ ᎠᎹ ᎤᎵᏍᏆᏛ ᎤᏚᎵᏍᎬᎢ. ᎤᏴᎸᎩ ᏥᎳᏁᏍᏗ ᎤᎾᏓᏛ ᎠᏯᎸᎢ, ᎠᏎᏃ ᎠᏥᎳ ᎤᎵᏍᏗᎳᏁᎢ ᎠᎴ ᎤᏍᎪᎸ ᎤᎿᏫᏍᏔᏁᎢ. ᎤᏨᏎᎢ. ᎭᏫᏂ ᎠᎴ ᎤᎵᏂᎩᏛ ᎦᏓᏘ ᎤᎾᏁᎢ, ᎠᏎᏃ ᎤᏓᎴᏅᏛ ᎠᏓᏅᏙ ᎠᏥᎳ ᎤᏚᎵᏍᎨᎢ.

ᎣᏂ ᎠᎦᏴᎵ ᎠᎹ ᎤᏓᏔᏔ ᎤᎴᏅᏎᎢ. ᎤᏍᏗ ᎨᏎᎢ ᎪᎾ ᎠᎴ ᎤᎶᎩ ᎠᎴ ᎢᎾᏛ ᎠᏂᏙᎾᎥᎢ. “ᏥᎦᏘᏅᏏ,” ᎤᏛᏁᎢ. ᎢᎦᏛ ᎦᏓᏘ ᎤᏂᏍᎦᏎ ᎠᎹ ᏳᏐᏅᏍᏔᏅ. ᎢᎦᏛ ᎤᏂᏍᏆᏂᎪᏎ ᎤᏍᏗ ᎦᏓᏘ ᎦᎾᏄᎪᎬ ᎬᏩᏒ ᎤᎵᏍᎦᏍᏙᏗ ᎠᏥᎳ. ᎠᎦᏴᎵ ᎤᏓᏔᏔ ᎤᎴᏅᏎ ᎤᏃᏢᏍᎬᎢ.

ᎤᏁᎬ ᎠᏍᏓᏱᏳ ᎠᏯ ᎤᏃᏢᏎᎢ, ᏚᏙᎥ ᏚᏍᏘ. ᎠᏯ ᎠᏯ ᏚᏓᏙᎵᏍᏔᏁᎢ ᎬᏂ ᎤᏍᏗ ᎠᎴ ᎤᎵᏂᎩᏛ ᎤᏍᏆᏂᎪᏗ ᎤᏓᏃᏢᎢ. ᎤᏍᏕᏆ ᎤᏍᏆᏗᏍᏔᏁᎢ. ᎿᏉ ᎠᎹ ᎤᏪᏙᎸ ᎤᏩᏌ ᎤᏰᎸ ᎢᎬᏱ ᎤᏭᎪᏔᏁᎢ, ᎤᏍᏗ ᎠᎴ ᎤᏁᎳᎩ.

ᎤᎾᏓᏛ ᎤᎷᏨ, ᎠᎦᏴᎵ ᎤᏓᏔᏔ ᎤᏴᎸᎩ ᎤᏁᏍᏗ ᎾᎿ ᏥᎳᏁᏍᏗ. ᏌᏊ ᎠᏥᎳ ᎤᏍᏗ ᎤᏩᏎᎢ ᎭᏫᏂ ᎪᏍᏚᎢ. ᎤᏍᏆᏗᏍᏔᏁ ᎤᏤᎵ ᎠᏯ ᎠᎴ ᎤᏂᏴᏫᏯ ᎤᏥᎸ. ᎢᎦᏛ ᎧᏃᎮᏍᎩ ᎠᏂᏁᎪ ᎤᏍᏗ ᎤᏃᎴ ᎭᏫᏂ ᎤᏭᏓᎴᎢ. ᎤᏣᏘ ᎤᏁᎳᎩ ᎠᎹ ᎤᎶᏎᎢ.

ᎦᏓᏘ ᎤᏂᎦᏖᎢ ᎬᏂ ᎩᎦᎨ ᎤᏍᏗ ᎤᏄᎪᏨ ᎠᏍᏆᏂᎪᏗ ᎤᏲᏨᎢ. ᎠᎦᏴᎵ ᎤᏓᏔᏔ ᎤᏤᎵ ᎠᏯ ᎤᎳᏏᏕᎢ. ᎤᏂᏅᏎ ᎤᏍᏗ ᎤᎧᏲᏗ, ᎦᏚ ᎠᎴ ᏗᏀᎾ ᎠᏥᎳ. ᎠᏥᎳ ᎤᏔᎾᏗ ᎤᎵᏍᏔᏁᎢ. ᏂᎦᏛ ᎤᏂᏣᏘ ᎠᎾᏓᏟᏌᏁᎢ, ᎤᏂᏍᏗ ᎦᏓᏘ ᎢᎬᏱ ᎤᏂᏣᏘ ᎤᎾᎵᏍᏓᏁᎢ.

ᎪᎾ ᎬᎿᎨ ᏗᎦᏃᎨ ᏚᏯᎡᎢ. ᎤᎶᎩ ᎤᎦᏔ ᏚᏴᏍᏕᎢ. ᎢᎾᏛ ᎤᏅᏓᏗ ᎤᏅᏓᏛ ᎤᏬᎯᏤᎢ. ᎠᎴ ᏴᏫ ᎤᏂᎦᏔᎮ ᎠᎦᏴᎵ ᎤᏓᏔᏔ, ᎤᏍᏗ ᎠᏎᏃ ᎤᏓᏅᏘ. ᎥᏝ ᎤᏔᎾᏗ ᎤᏓᎴᏅᏛ ᏳᏚᎵᏍᎨᎢ. ᎤᏚᎵᏍᎨ ᎤᏂᏴᏫᏯ, ᎤᎦᏘᏗ, ᎠᎴ ᏌᏊ ᎤᏍᏗ ᎢᎦᎦᎵ ᎤᎾᏕᏘᏱ.

title: The Grateful Beasts
subtitle: a Hungarian tale, about Ferko and the kindness that came back threefold
moral: Granny’s whisper: kindness has a long memory and often finds the road home.
script_en:
Once there lived a poor man who had three sons. When there was no longer bread enough at home, he gave each son a single loaf and sent them out into the world to seek their fortunes.

The youngest was named Ferko, and he was as kind as he was handsome. His elder brothers were jealous of him, and one night, while he slept beneath a tree, they ate his bread down to the crumbs. When he woke, hungry, they mocked him — and in his hunger he agreed to a cruel bargain: they would share their bread only if he let them take his sight and the strength of his limbs.

They did this wicked thing, and left him by the roadside, and went on their way laughing.

Poor Ferko crawled on through the long day, and toward evening he rested beneath what he thought was a tree, though it was a gallows on a lonely hill. Above him two ravens talked together, and one said to the other, “Below this hill lies a lake whose water heals any wound — and the dew on the hillside restores sight to blind eyes.”

Ferko waited for nightfall. He washed his face in the hillside dew, and crawled down to the lake, and bathed — and rose up whole, his eyes bright and his limbs strong. He filled a little flask with the water, in case another should ever need it, and went on his way rejoicing.

As he walked, he found a wolf caught in a hunter's trap. He freed it gently and bound its leg. Further on, he lifted a drowning mouse from a stream. And on a hot afternoon, he rescued a queen bee fallen into a brook and set her on a flower to dry her wings.

“We will not forget this,” said the wolf. “We will not forget this,” squeaked the mouse. “We will not forget this,” hummed the queen bee.

At last Ferko came to a great king's city and asked for service. But his brothers were already servants there — and when they saw him alive and whole, they were afraid he would tell the king of their wickedness. So they ran to the king and whispered that Ferko was a wicked magician who had come to steal the princess.

The king summoned Ferko. “They say you are a magician,” he said. “Prove your innocence by performing three tasks — or you shall be punished.”

The brothers, grinning, named the tasks. First: before dawn, Ferko must sort a mountain of mixed grain, wheat from barley, rye from oats. Ferko despaired — but that night the mouse came with ten thousand mice, and by cockcrow every grain lay sorted in shining heaps.

Second: in a single night he must build a palace fairer than the king's own. The queen bee came with all her swarm, and by morning there stood a palace of golden wax and flowers, so lovely that the king's own looked grey beside it.

Third: the king, furious, sent his guards to seize Ferko. Then the wolf came — with a thousand wolves at his heels — and ringed the courtyard round, silent, with shining eyes.

The king turned pale and begged for peace. “Enough!” he cried. “Drive them away, and ask what you will!”

Ferko asked only for justice and kindness. The wicked brothers were sent far away, to learn better ways. And the princess — who had watched all of this with growing admiration, for she had a kind heart too — took Ferko's hand willingly, and they were married amid great rejoicing.

At the wedding feast, the old people swear, a wolf, a mouse, and a queen bee sat in the places of honor. And Ferko and his bride lived long and happily, and were much beloved by great and small throughout the land.
script_original:
Élt egyszer egy szegény ember, akinek három fia volt. Amikor már nem maradt otthon elég kenyér, mindegyik fiának adott egy-egy cipót, és elküldte őket a nagyvilágba szerencsét próbálni.

A legkisebbet Ferkónak hívták, és éppen olyan jószívű volt, mint amilyen szép legény. Bátyjai irigykedtek rá. Egy éjjel, miközben egy fa alatt aludt, megették a kenyerét az utolsó morzsáig. Amikor éhesen felébredt, csúfolni kezdték, és kegyetlen alkut ajánlottak: csak akkor osztják meg vele a kenyerüket, ha elveszik a látását és a végtagjai erejét.

Meg is tették ezt a gonoszságot. Az út szélén hagyták, és nevetve továbbmentek.

Szegény Ferkó egész nap kúszott előre. Estefelé megpihent valami alatt, amit fának gondolt, pedig akasztófa állt azon a magányos dombon. Fölötte két holló beszélgetett. Az egyik így szólt a másikhoz: „A domb alatt tó rejtőzik, amelynek vize minden sebet begyógyít, a hegyoldal harmata pedig visszaadja a vak szem világát.”

Ferkó megvárta az éjszakát. Megmosta arcát a hegyoldal harmatával, majd lekúszott a tóhoz és megfürdött benne. Épen emelkedett ki a vízből: szeme újra ragyogott, karja-lába erős volt. Megtöltött egy kis üveget a gyógyító vízzel, hátha egyszer másnak lesz rá szüksége, és örömmel folytatta útját.

Útközben egy farkast talált a vadász csapdájában. Óvatosan kiszabadította és bekötözte a lábát. Később kimentett a patakból egy fuldokló egeret. Egy forró délután pedig a vízbe esett méhkirálynőt emelte ki, és virágra tette, hogy megszáríthassa a szárnyát.

„Nem felejtjük el”, mondta a farkas. „Nem felejtjük el”, cincogta az egér. „Nem felejtjük el”, zümmögte a méhkirálynő.

Végül Ferkó egy hatalmas király városába érkezett, és szolgálatot kért. Bátyjai már ott szolgáltak. Amikor meglátták, hogy él és egészséges, félni kezdtek, hogy elmondja a királynak gonoszságukat. A királyhoz siettek, és azt suttogták, hogy Ferkó gonosz varázsló, aki el akarja rabolni a királykisasszonyt.

A király maga elé hívatta Ferkót. „Azt mondják, varázsló vagy. Három feladattal bizonyítsd be ártatlanságodat, különben megbüntetlek.”

A vigyorgó testvérek megnevezték a feladatokat. Először Ferkónak hajnalig szét kellett válogatnia egy hegyre való kevert gabonát: búzát az árpától, rozst a zabtól. Ferkó kétségbeesett, de éjjel megérkezett az egér tízezer társával. Mire megszólalt a kakas, minden szem ragyogó halmokban állt.

Másodszor egyetlen éjszaka alatt a királyénál is szebb palotát kellett építenie. Eljött a méhkirálynő az egész rajjal. Reggelre aranyviaszból és virágokból emelt palota állt ott, olyan gyönyörű, hogy mellette a király palotája szürkének látszott.

Harmadszor a dühös király elküldte őreit, hogy fogják el Ferkót. Ekkor megérkezett a farkas, nyomában ezer farkassal. Némán, fénylő szemmel körülvették az udvart.

A király elsápadt és békéért könyörgött. „Elég! Küldd el őket, és kérj, amit csak akarsz!”

Ferkó csupán igazságot és emberséget kért. Gonosz bátyjait messzire küldték, hogy jobb útra térjenek. A királykisasszony pedig, aki egyre nagyobb csodálattal figyelte Ferkót, és maga is jószívű volt, örömmel nyújtotta neki a kezét. Nagy vigasság közepette összeházasodtak.

Az öregek úgy esküsznek, hogy a lakodalomban egy farkas, egy egér és egy méhkirálynő ült a díszhelyen. Ferkó és felesége sokáig boldogan éltek, és az egész országban szerette őket kicsi és nagy.

title: The Hare and the Water
subtitle: a Swahili coast tale from Tanzania, about water, work, and the community that needs both
moral: Granny’s whisper: a shared well holds more than water; it holds the work and trust of everyone who dug.
script_en:
A hard drought came to the land. The river narrowed to a ribbon, then broke into muddy pools. Grass crackled beneath every foot. Elephant walked farther each morning for a mouthful of water, and even Jackal had no clever joke for the thirsty evenings.

Lion called all the animals beneath a baobab. “If we wait for rain, some among us will not live to see it,” he said. “We must dig where the old river once ran. Every paw, hoof, claw, and trunk will help.” The animals agreed to work at sunrise.

Only Hare laughed. “Digging water out of dry ground? You may as well dance until the clouds fall,” he said. Tortoise answered, “Perhaps our work will look foolish before it looks useful.” Hare flicked his ears. “Then be foolish without me,” and he hopped into the shade.

The next morning Elephant loosened hard earth with her tusks. Warthog pushed soil aside. Jackal and Hyena scratched. Birds carried pebbles in their beaks. Tortoise pressed the floor firm with his broad feet. To keep their courage, they stamped in rhythm and sang as they dug deeper.

On the third day, cool mud appeared. On the fourth, water gleamed at the bottom of the well. The animals danced for joy, then Lion remembered the one who had refused. “This water belongs to those who shared the work,” he said. “No water for Hare until Hare helps the community.”

That night Hare crept to the well. He drank until his belly was round, brushed away his footprints with a leafy branch, and slipped home. Yet every morning the water was lower. At the damp edge, Tortoise found one narrow print Hare had missed.

“Let me keep watch,” Tortoise said. He coated his shell with sticky tree pitch and sat beside the water as still as a dark stone. At midnight Hare arrived. “Move, little rock,” he whispered. Tortoise did not answer. Hare pushed with one paw, and the paw stuck fast.

“Release me!” Hare cried, striking with the other paw. That paw stuck too. He kicked, then leaned his body against the shell, until he was caught by all four feet. Tortoise slowly raised his head. “Water tastes sweetest after shared work,” he said.

At dawn, the animals found Hare. Lion did not throw him away from the well. Instead, Hare was asked to help widen it, carry water to the smallest creatures, and repair the path his secret visits had worn. Hare worked all day. When evening came, Tortoise washed away the pitch and offered him a clean gourd of water.

From then on, Hare brought quick ideas as well as quick feet to the community’s work. The animals kept the well shaded, clean, and open in fair measure. They remembered a truth close to ubuntu: one life becomes stronger through the lives around it. Water dug together must be guarded together, and no cleverness is wiser than helping everyone drink.
script_original:
Ukame mkali uliingia nchini. Mto ulipungua ukawa utepe mwembamba, kisha ukabaki madimbwi ya matope. Nyasi zilikauka na kupasuka chini ya miguu. Tembo alitembea mbali kila asubuhi kutafuta funda la maji, na hata Bweha hakuwa na mzaha wa kuwaambia wenzake jioni.

Simba aliwaita wanyama wote chini ya mbuyu. “Tukingoja mvua, baadhi yetu hawataiona,” alisema. “Lazima tuchimbe pale mto wa zamani ulipopita. Kila unyayo, kwato, kucha na mkonga vitasaidia.” Wanyama walikubali kuanza kazi jua litakapochomoza.

Sungura peke yake alicheka. “Kuchimba maji katika ardhi kavu? Ni sawa na kucheza mpaka mawingu yaanguke,” alisema. Kobe akajibu, “Huenda kazi yetu ikaonekana ya kipumbavu kabla haijaonekana ya maana.” Sungura akatikisa masikio. “Basi fanyeni upumbavu bila mimi,” akakimbilia kivulini.

Asubuhi iliyofuata Tembo alilegeza udongo mgumu kwa pembe zake. Ngiri alisukuma mchanga pembeni. Bweha na Fisi walikwaruza. Ndege walibeba kokoto midomoni. Kobe alikanyaga sakafu ya kisima kwa miguu yake mipana. Ili wasikate tamaa, walikanyaga kwa mdundo na kuimba walipozidi kuchimba.

Siku ya tatu matope baridi yalionekana. Siku ya nne maji yaling’aa chini ya kisima. Wanyama walicheza kwa furaha, kisha Simba akamkumbuka aliyekataa. “Maji haya ni ya wale walioshiriki kazi,” alisema. “Sungura hatakunywa mpaka asaidie jamii.”

Usiku huo Sungura alijinyemeleza hadi kisimani. Alikunywa mpaka tumbo likawa duara, akafuta nyayo zake kwa tawi lenye majani, kisha akarudi nyumbani. Lakini kila asubuhi maji yalikuwa yamepungua. Kwenye ukingo wenye unyevunyevu, Kobe aliona unyayo mmoja mwembamba ambao Sungura alikuwa ameusahau.

“Nitaweka ulinzi,” Kobe alisema. Alipaka gamba lake lami ya mti iliyonata, akaketi karibu na maji bila kusogea, kama jiwe jeusi. Usiku wa manane Sungura akafika. “Ondoka, jiwe dogo,” alinong’ona. Kobe hakujibu. Sungura akasukuma kwa mguu mmoja, nao ukakwama.

“Niachilie!” Sungura akapiga kwa mguu mwingine. Huo pia ukanata. Akapiga teke, kisha akaegemeza mwili wake kwenye gamba, mpaka miguu yote minne ikashikwa. Kobe akainua kichwa polepole. “Maji huwa matamu zaidi baada ya kazi ya pamoja,” alisema.

Alfajiri, wanyama walimkuta Sungura. Simba hakumfukuza kabisa kisimani. Badala yake, Sungura aliagizwa kusaidia kukipanua, kuwapelekea maji wanyama wadogo, na kutengeneza njia aliyoharibu katika ziara zake za siri. Sungura alifanya kazi siku nzima. Jioni, Kobe aliosha lami na kumpa kibuyu safi cha maji.

Tangu siku hiyo, Sungura alileta mawazo yake ya haraka pamoja na miguu yake kwenye kazi ya jamii. Wanyama waliweka kisima katika kivuli, safi, na wazi kwa kipimo cha haki. Walikumbuka ukweli wa ubuntu: maisha ya mmoja huimarishwa na maisha ya wengine. Maji yaliyochimbwa pamoja hulindwa pamoja, na hakuna ujanja wenye hekima kuliko kuwasaidia wote wanywe.

title: The Hodja and the Cauldron
subtitle: a Turkish folk tale, about Nasreddin Hodja and a cauldron that gave birth
moral: Granny’s whisper: a truth wrapped in laughter may travel farther than a scolding.
script_en:
In the town of Akşehir, in Turkey, there once lived a teacher named Nasreddin Hodja. He rode a little grey donkey, wore a great white turban, and was the wisest — and sometimes the most foolish — man in all the town. The children loved him, for he always had a story, and the grown-ups listened to him, for his stories always hid a truth inside, like a walnut hides its kernel.

One day a great wedding was coming, and the Hodja needed a big copper cauldron to cook the feast. So he knocked on his neighbor's door.

“Neighbor,” he said politely, “may I borrow your great cauldron for three days? I will return it washed and shining.”

The neighbor agreed — though he polished the cauldron a little nervously as he handed it over, for it was his finest.

The wedding came, the feast was cooked, and everyone ate until they could eat no more. On the third day the Hodja carried the cauldron back — washed and shining, just as he had promised. But inside it sat a tiny copper pot.

The neighbor stared. “Hodja, what is this little pot?”

The Hodja beamed. “Good news, neighbor! While your cauldron was staying with me, it had a baby. This little one is yours by right.”

The neighbor laughed until tears came. A cauldron having a baby! But the little pot was real and solid in his hands, so he kept it gladly, and told the story to everyone in the market.

Some weeks later the Hodja knocked again. “Neighbor, may I borrow the great cauldron once more?”

“Of course, Hodja, of course!” said the neighbor, thinking of the fine baby pot. “Keep it as long as you like!”

Days passed. Then a week. Then two. At last the neighbor knocked on the Hodja's door. “Hodja, my cauldron — when will you return it?”

The Hodja opened the door with the saddest face in all Akşehir. “Oh, neighbor,” he sighed, “I have terrible news. Your cauldron has died.”

The neighbor's mouth fell open. “Died? Hodja, are you mad? Cauldrons cannot die!”

The Hodja stroked his beard and looked at him mildly. “My friend,” he said, “when I told you your cauldron had given birth, you believed me gladly. Why will you not believe me now?”

The neighbor stood there with his mouth open — and then he began to laugh, and the Hodja laughed, and soon the whole street was laughing. And the neighbor never did get his cauldron back, but he got something better: a story he told for the rest of his life.

For the Hodja's truth, hidden like a kernel in the walnut, was this: people will believe anything that pleases them — and doubt anything that does not. So be careful what you believe, and be ready to laugh at yourself.
script_original:
Bir zamanlar Türkiye'nin Akşehir kasabasında Nasreddin Hoca adında bir bilge öğretmen yaşardı. Küçük boz eşeğine biner, kocaman beyaz bir sarık takardı. Kasabanın en akıllı, bazen de en şaşırtıcı adamıydı. Çocuklar onu severdi, çünkü her zaman anlatacak bir hikâyesi vardı. Büyükler de dinlerdi, çünkü hikâyelerinin içinde, cevizin içindeki öz gibi, daima bir hakikat saklanırdı.

Bir gün büyük bir düğün yapılacaktı. Hoca'nın yemek pişirmek için büyük bir bakır kazana ihtiyacı vardı. Komşusunun kapısını çaldı.

“Komşu,” dedi nazikçe, “büyük kazanını üç günlüğüne ödünç verir misin? Yıkayıp parlatır, geri getiririm.”

Komşu razı oldu. Yine de en güzel kazanını verirken onu biraz endişeyle parlatmadan edemedi.

Düğün geldi, yemekler pişti ve herkes doyuncaya kadar yedi. Üçüncü gün Hoca, söz verdiği gibi yıkanmış, ışıl ışıl kazanı geri getirdi. Fakat kazanın içinde küçücük bir bakır tencere duruyordu.

Komşu şaşkınlıkla baktı. “Hoca, bu küçük tencere de nedir?”

Hoca'nın yüzü güldü. “Müjde komşu! Senin kazan benim evimdeyken doğurdu. Bu yavru da elbette senin hakkın.”

Komşu gözlerinden yaş gelinceye kadar güldü. Kazan doğurur mu hiç! Ama küçük tencere gerçekti, eliyle tutabiliyordu. Onu sevinçle aldı ve çarşıda karşılaştığı herkese olanları anlattı.

Birkaç hafta sonra Hoca yine kapısını çaldı. “Komşu, büyük kazanını bir kez daha ödünç alabilir miyim?”

Komşu, güzel yavru tencereyi düşünerek, “Elbette Hoca, elbette! İstediğin kadar sende kalsın!” dedi.

Günler geçti. Bir hafta oldu, ardından iki hafta. Sonunda komşu Hoca'nın kapısına dayandı. “Hoca, benim kazan ne oldu? Ne zaman geri vereceksin?”

Hoca kapıyı Akşehir'deki en kederli yüzle açtı. “Ah komşum,” diye içini çekti, “sana çok kötü bir haberim var. Senin kazan öldü.”

Komşunun ağzı açık kaldı. “Öldü mü? Hoca, sen aklını mı kaçırdın? Kazan hiç ölür mü?”

Hoca sakalını sıvazladı ve yumuşak bir bakışla ona baktı. “Dostum,” dedi, “kazanının doğurduğunu söylediğimde bana sevinerek inandın. Şimdi öldüğünü söylediğimde neden inanmıyorsun?”

Komşu bir süre ağzı açık öylece kaldı. Sonra gülmeye başladı. Hoca da güldü, çok geçmeden bütün sokak onlara katıldı. Komşu kazanına bir daha kavuşamadı, ama daha iyi bir şey kazandı: ömrünün sonuna kadar anlatacağı bir hikâye.

Hoca'nın ceviz içi gibi saklı hakikati şuydu: İnsanlar hoşlarına giden şeye kolayca inanır, hoşlarına gitmeyen şeyden ise şüphe eder. Bu yüzden neye inandığına dikkat et ve gerektiğinde kendine gülmeye hazır ol.

title: How Night Came
subtitle: a Tupi tale from Brazil, recorded in a 1917 public-domain collection
moral: Granny’s whisper: the dark can be a blanket, not a fear, when it arrives in its own good time.
script_en:
In the beginning, the world knew only day. The sun stood bright over the forest, bright over the rivers, bright even when every creature longed to close its eyes. Birds sang without stopping. Flowers stayed open. People worked and worked because no darkness ever told them it was time to rest.
