The daughter of the Great Sea Serpent had grown up beneath the deep water, where her father kept night folded safely away. When she married a son of the earth and came to live on land, the endless light wearied her. She shaded her eyes and sighed, “How can anyone sleep when morning never ends?”

Her husband did not understand. “What is night?” he asked. She told him of cool darkness, the silver moon, and stars like seeds scattered over black soil. She told him how crickets sang when daylight creatures grew still. Her husband wished to bring her comfort, so he sent three faithful servants to the Great Sea Serpent.

The servants travelled by canoe to the meeting place of river and sea. Deep below, the Great Sea Serpent heard his daughter’s request. He gave them a tightly sealed bag. “Carry this to her,” he warned. “Do not open it. Only my daughter knows how to release night gently.”

They started home. Soon the bag began to murmur. “Chirr, chirr,” called the crickets inside. Something padded like a jaguar through dry leaves. Frogs croaked, owls whispered, and unseen wings brushed the woven sides. The servants became frightened, then curious. “Perhaps the bag holds treasure,” one said. “Perhaps small creatures need air,” said another.

They broke the wax seal. At once night flew out. Darkness rushed over the river, climbed the trees, and covered the earth before anyone was ready. The servants cried out. Stars sparked overhead; the moon opened like a pale flower. Creatures of the night sprang free, while day birds tucked their heads beneath their wings.

For disobeying the warning, the servants were changed into monkeys. The dark marks around their mouths remembered the wax seal they had broken. They leaped into the trees, chattering with surprise as the first true night deepened around them.

The Sea Serpent’s daughter did not panic. She lifted her hands and called the darkness by its proper name. She separated night from day, setting each in its own path. She invited the morning star to announce dawn and asked the evening birds to welcome rest. Slowly the frightened world became calm.

People lay down for the first time. Children slept while moonlight rested on their hammocks. Workers woke with strength they had forgotten. From then on, day followed night and night followed day. The forest learned two songs: one bright and busy, one dark and soft. And everyone understood that rest is not the end of living, but part of its wise and gentle rhythm.
script_alternate:
No princípio, o mundo conhecia apenas o dia. O sol brilhava sobre a floresta, sobre os rios e até quando todas as criaturas queriam fechar os olhos. Os pássaros cantavam sem parar. As flores permaneciam abertas. As pessoas trabalhavam e trabalhavam, pois nenhuma escuridão dizia que era hora de descansar.

A filha da Grande Cobra do Mar crescera sob as águas profundas, onde seu pai guardava a noite bem dobrada. Quando ela se casou com um filho da terra e foi morar em terra firme, a luz sem fim a cansou. Cobriu os olhos e suspirou: “Como alguém pode dormir quando a manhã nunca termina?”

Seu marido não compreendia. “O que é noite?”, perguntou. Ela falou da escuridão fresca, da lua de prata e das estrelas como sementes espalhadas em solo negro. Contou como os grilos cantavam quando os animais do dia ficavam quietos. Desejando confortá-la, o marido enviou três criados fiéis à Grande Cobra do Mar.

Os criados viajaram de canoa até o encontro do rio com o mar. Lá embaixo, a Grande Cobra ouviu o pedido da filha. Entregou-lhes uma bolsa muito bem fechada. “Levem-na até ela”, advertiu. “Não abram. Somente minha filha sabe soltar a noite com cuidado.”

No caminho de volta, a bolsa começou a murmurar. “Cri-cri”, cantavam os grilos lá dentro. Algo caminhava como onça sobre folhas secas. Sapos coaxavam, corujas cochichavam e asas invisíveis roçavam a palha trançada. Os criados ficaram assustados e depois curiosos. “Talvez haja um tesouro”, disse um. “Talvez criaturas pequenas precisem de ar”, disse outro.

Eles romperam o selo de cera. Imediatamente a noite escapou. A escuridão correu sobre o rio, subiu pelas árvores e cobriu a terra antes que alguém estivesse pronto. Os criados gritaram. Estrelas acenderam no alto; a lua abriu como flor pálida. Os animais da noite saltaram livres, e as aves do dia esconderam a cabeça sob as asas.

Por desobedecerem ao aviso, os criados foram transformados em macacos. As marcas escuras ao redor de suas bocas lembravam a cera que haviam rompido. Eles pularam para as árvores, tagarelando de surpresa enquanto a primeira noite verdadeira se aprofundava.

A filha da Cobra do Mar não entrou em pânico. Ergueu as mãos e chamou a escuridão pelo nome certo. Separou a noite do dia, dando a cada uma o seu caminho. Convidou a estrela-d’alva a anunciar a manhã e pediu às aves da tarde que acolhessem o descanso. Devagar, o mundo assustado se acalmou.

As pessoas se deitaram pela primeira vez. As crianças dormiram enquanto a luz da lua pousava nas redes. Os trabalhadores acordaram com uma força que haviam esquecido. Desde então, o dia segue a noite e a noite segue o dia. A floresta aprendeu duas canções: uma clara e ocupada, outra escura e suave. Todos entenderam que descansar não é deixar de viver, mas seguir o ritmo sábio da vida.
alternate_note: Published Brazilian Portuguese text for a tale from Tupi tradition.

title: Jamie Freel and the Young Lady
subtitle: an Irish folktale, about a kind son, a fairy procession, and a brave ride home
moral: Granny’s whisper: every old story grows warmer when we listen with care.
script_en:
On the edge of a small village in Donegal lived a widow and her son, Jamie Freel. They had little money, but Jamie shared his supper with travelers and never let his mother lift a basket when his hands were free. Because of this, some called him foolish. His mother called him kind, which suited him better.

One Halloween night, while the wind combed the heather, Jamie heard music on the road. It was thin and bright, like silver bells under water. He stepped outside and saw a troop of fairies riding white horses toward an old ruined castle. Curiosity tugged him after them, though he kept to the shadows and spoke no word.

Inside the roofless hall, the fairies spread a feast. Their queen lifted a hazel wand. “Where shall we ride tonight?” she asked. One cried, “To Dublin, to fetch the finest young lady there!” Before Jamie could blink, the company vanished in a rush of leaves. He seized a small horse left beside the wall and followed, holding tight as the hills streamed beneath them.

They reached a grand Dublin house where a young woman slept near the fire. The fairies lifted her gently and carried her away, leaving behind a wooden figure that looked exactly like her. Back at the castle, they laid the sleeping woman on a couch while they danced.

Jamie’s heart would not let him abandon her. During the wildest reel, he crept forward, lifted her into his arms, and mounted the little horse. “Home,” he whispered. The horse leaped over bog, hill, and dark sea-road. By dawn Jamie had brought the stranger to his mother’s cottage.

The young woman woke frightened and far from everything she knew. Jamie’s mother wrapped her in a warm shawl. They gave her the best chair, soft bread, and all the truth. Jamie promised to take her safely home, asking nothing in return.

In Dublin, her family had been mourning beside the silent wooden likeness. When Jamie led the living daughter through the door, joy filled the house like sunrise. The false figure crumbled into dry sticks. Her father offered Jamie gold, land, and horses. Jamie accepted only enough to keep his mother comfortable.

Before they parted from Dublin, Jamie returned once to the ruined castle. The moon shone through the broken roof, but no dancers appeared. He placed a small loaf on the stone sill and thanked the little horse that had carried them. Then he walked home by the ordinary road, glad for solid earth beneath his boots.

The young woman had watched his patience on the long journey and his tenderness toward his mother. In time, affection grew between them, steady and unenchanted. They married with music that belonged to human fiddlers, and every Halloween Jamie left bread and milk by the ruined castle—not from fear, but as a reminder that courage is strongest when it carries someone else toward home.
script_original:
Ar imeall sráidbhaile beag i nDún na nGall bhí baintreach agus a mac, Séamus Freel, ina gcónaí. Ní raibh mórán airgid acu, ach roinn Séamus a shuipéar le lucht siúil agus ní ligfeadh sé dá mháthair ciseán trom a iompar nuair a bhí a lámha féin saor. Dúirt daoine áirithe go raibh sé amaideach. Dúirt a mháthair go raibh sé cineálta.

Oíche Shamhna amháin, agus an ghaoth ag siúl tríd an bhfraoch, chuala Séamus ceol ar an mbóthar. Bhí sé tanaí geal, cosúil le cloigíní airgid faoin uisce. Chuaigh sé amach agus chonaic sé slua sí ag marcaíocht ar chapaill bhána i dtreo seanchaisleáin bhriste. Lean sé iad sna scáthanna agus níor labhair sé focal.

Sa halla gan díon, leag na sióga féasta amach. D’ardaigh a mbanríon slat choill. “Cá rachaimid anocht?” ar sise. D’fhreagair duine acu, “Go Baile Átha Cliath chun an bhean óg is áille a thabhairt linn!” Sula bhféadfadh Séamus análú, d’imigh siad mar dhuilleoga sa stoirm. Rug sé ar chapall beag a fágadh agus lean sé iad.

Shroich siad teach mór i mBaile Átha Cliath. Bhí bean óg ina codladh in aice leis an tine. Thóg na sióga í go réidh agus d’fhág siad dealbh adhmaid a bhí díreach cosúil léi. Nuair a d’fhill siad ar an gcaisleán, chuir siad an bhean ina luí ar leaba agus thosaigh siad ag damhsa.

Ní ligfeadh croí Shéamuis dó í a fhágáil. Nuair a bhí an rince ar mire, shiúil sé go ciúin, thóg sé an bhean ina ghéaga agus shuigh sé ar an gcapall beag. “Abhaile,” a dúirt sé. Léim an capall thar phortaigh, cnoic agus bóithre dorcha. Le breacadh an lae bhí siad ag teach a mháthar.

Dhúisigh an bhean óg eaglach agus i bhfad óna muintir. Chuir máthair Shéamuis seál te timpeall uirthi. Thug siad an chathaoir ab fhearr agus arán bog di, agus d’inis siad an fhírinne go léir. Gheall Séamus í a thabhairt abhaile slán gan luach saothair a iarraidh.

I mBaile Átha Cliath bhí an teaghlach ag caoineadh in aice leis an dealbh chiúin. Nuair a tháinig an iníon bheo isteach leis, líon áthas an teach mar éirí gréine. Thit an dealbh bhréige ina cipíní tirime. Thairg a hathair ór, talamh agus capaill do Shéamus, ach níor ghlac sé ach an méid a choinneodh a mháthair compordach.

Sular fhág siad Baile Átha Cliath, chuimhnigh siad ar gach duine a chabhraigh leo ar an mbóthar fada agus ghabh siad buíochas leo. Níor rinne Séamus laoch mór de féin. Dúirt sé gur chríochnaigh an capall beag, a mháthair, agus misneach na mná óige an obair le chéile.

Chonaic an bhean óg foighne Shéamuis ar an turas agus an cineáltas a léirigh sé dá mháthair. Le himeacht ama d’fhás grá eatarthu, mall agus fíor, gan draíocht ar bith. Phós siad le ceol fidléirí daonna. Gach Oíche Shamhna d’fhág Séamus arán agus bainne in aice leis an seanchaisleán, mar chuimhne go mbíonn misneach níos láidre nuair a iompraíonn sé duine eile abhaile.
alternate_title: Séamus Freel agus an Bhean Óg

title: Juan Bobo
subtitle: a folktale from Puerto Rico, about a boy who learns one errand at a time
moral: Granny’s whisper: every mistake is a lesson wearing a funny hat.
script_en:
Long ago in a green town in Puerto Rico, where the bananas grow and the mountains wear scarves of cloud, there lived a boy named Juan Bobo — which means, more or less, Simple John. He had a big heart, a bigger smile, and a head where ideas went marching in single file, one at a time.

One morning his mother said, “Juanito, take these coins to the market and buy me a nice clay pot.” Juan Bobo bought the finest pot in the market, admired it, and then tied it to a string and dragged it home behind him, the way you walk a little dog. “Why should my arms get tired,” he reasoned, “when the pot has such a nice bottom for walking?” By the time he reached home, the pot was in a hundred pieces.

“Ay, Juan!” cried his mother. “Look what you have done! A pot you carry on your head, all in one piece.” “Sí, Mamá,” said Juan Bobo, nodding hard, so the idea would stay put. “Next time I will carry it on my head.”

The next market day, she sent him for a suckling pig for Sunday dinner. Juan Bobo marched into the market, chose the plumpest little pig, paid politely — and hoisted it straight up onto his head, all four legs kicking. He walked the whole way home wearing a squealing hat, until at last the pig wriggled free, splashed him into the mud, and ran off squealing to be lucky somewhere else. He arrived home with only the rope and one shoe full of dirty water.

“Ay, Juan!” cried his mother. “A pig you lead home gently on a rope, talking to it kindly!” “Sí, Mamá,” said Juan Bobo, nodding even harder. “Next time I will lead it kindly on a rope.”

Now, one Sunday his mother won a fine cut of meat at the church festival, and she asked Juan Bobo to bring it home fresh and clean for dinner. Juan Bobo remembered. He found a rope, tied it around the meat, and led it down the road talking to it kindly: “Easy there, friend. Good little… meat.” Every dog in the town thought this was a wonderful parade. By the time he reached his house, what was left of that dinner would not feed a beetle — and the dogs followed him for a week, hoping he worked there.

His mother looked at the rope, and at the dogs, and at her mud-streaked son. And do you know what she did? She laughed — she laughed until she cried — because what else was there to do? “Juan Bobo,” she said, wiping her eyes, “things are not sheep, mijo. Everything carries its own way. Next time — just ask me before you invent.”

And little by little, that is just what Juan Bobo learned. He kept asking questions, and he kept the village laughing, and when he grew up there was no one quicker at saying, “Wait — is this a pot thing or a pig thing?” Which, as anyone will tell you, is a very wise question. And the grandmothers say that whenever a child makes a mistake and learns from it, somewhere in Puerto Rico, Juan Bobo is clapping.
script_original:
Juan Bobo vivía con su madre en Puerto Rico. Tenía buen corazón, pero entendía cada encargo de una manera tan especial que el barrio nunca se aburría. Un día su madre le dio una olla y le dijo: «Llévala con mucho cuidado y no la sueltes.»

El camino era largo. Juan miró sus brazos cansados y dijo: «Si yo puedo caminar, la olla también.» La puso en el suelo, le ató una cuerda y la arrastró detrás de sí. Cuando llegó, de la olla sólo quedaba el asa. «No la solté ni un momento», explicó con orgullo.

Otro día debía llevar un cerdito al mercado. Recordando la olla rota, decidió tratarlo como a un pasajero. Sentó al cerdo en una silla, puso la silla sobre su cabeza y caminó mientras el animal chillaba y las gallinas corrían. Todo el pueblo salió a mirar.

Su madre suspiró, pero Juan siempre intentaba obedecer. Con el tiempo aprendió a preguntar: «¿Quieres decir que cargue la olla? ¿Quieres decir que el cerdo camine?» Y cada pregunta evitó un pequeño desastre.

Aun así, de vez en cuando una idea de Juan Bobo recorría la calle y hacía reír hasta a su madre. Por eso sus cuentos siguen vivos: nos recuerdan que el buen corazón necesita escuchar bien, y que equivocarse con alegría también puede enseñar.

title: Kongji and Patzzi
subtitle: a Korean folktale, about kindness, patient courage, and help arriving on quiet feet
moral: Granny’s whisper: every old story grows warmer when we listen with care.
script_en:
Long ago, in a village tucked between green hills, lived a gentle girl named Kongji. After her mother died, her father married again. His new wife had a daughter named Patzzi, and from the first morning, the stepmother saved every soft cushion and sweet rice cake for Patzzi while giving Kongji the hardest work.

Kongji rose before the magpies and slept after the lamps went dark. Still, she spoke kindly, tended the kitchen garden, and never passed a hungry creature without sharing what little she had. Patzzi teased her for this. “Kind words cannot finish chores,” she said. Kongji only smiled and kept working.

One bright festival day, the stepmother and Patzzi dressed in their finest clothes. Before leaving, the woman handed Kongji a wooden hoe. “Clear the whole stony field before sunset,” she ordered. “Then fill that enormous jar by the gate. Mind you, the jar must not leak.” They walked away laughing, for the hoe was broken and the jar had a hole in its bottom.

Kongji worked until her hands ached, but the stones seemed to multiply. At last she sat beneath a tree and wept. A great black ox stepped from the shade. “You have given grass to small creatures,” he said gently. “Today kindness returns.” The ox lowered his broad head and plowed the field while sparrows followed, picking stones from every furrow.

Kongji thanked them and hurried to the well. She poured bucket after bucket into the jar, yet the water streamed out below. Then a turtle crawled from the reeds. “You once carried me from the road to the pond,” he reminded her. He pressed his sturdy back against the hole. The jar slowly filled, shining like a small moon.

When the chores were done, a woman in cloud-colored robes appeared. She placed silk shoes and a bright jacket before Kongji. “Go to the festival,” she said. “A joyful heart should not always wait at home.” Kongji bowed and ran toward the village, but at the bridge one shoe slipped into the water.

A young magistrate found the tiny shoe caught among the reeds. He asked throughout the village who had lost it. Patzzi pushed and tugged, but the shoe would not fit. When Kongji tried, it settled lightly upon her foot. She told the truth about the field, the jar, the ox, and the turtle. The magistrate admired not only her grace but the kindness that had called so many helpers.

Before she left, Kongji returned to the field and thanked every helper by name. She loosened the turtle from the jar, led the ox to fresh grass, and scattered a wide handful of grain for the sparrows. The cloud-robed woman was gone, but a soft breeze stirred the leaves as if carrying her blessing onward.

Kongji was welcomed into a safe and happy home. Patzzi and her mother discovered that cruelty grows lonely, while generosity gathers friends in every furrow and pond. And when Kongji visited the old village, she always brought grain for the sparrows, hay for the ox, and the sweetest lettuce leaf for one very dependable turtle.
script_original:
옛날 옛적, 푸른 산과 논 사이에 콩쥐라는 마음씨 고운 아이가 살았습니다. 어머니가 세상을 떠난 뒤 아버지는 새 아내를 맞았습니다. 새어머니에게는 팥쥐라는 딸이 있었습니다. 새어머니는 부드러운 이불과 맛있는 떡은 모두 팥쥐에게 주고, 어렵고 힘든 일은 언제나 콩쥐에게 맡겼습니다.

콩쥐는 까치가 울기 전 일어나 물을 긷고, 마당을 쓸고, 밥을 지었습니다. 밤에는 등잔불이 꺼진 뒤에야 쉴 수 있었습니다. 그래도 콩쥐는 작은 벌레를 함부로 밟지 않았고, 굶주린 새에게 쌀 한 톨이라도 나누어 주었습니다. 팥쥐는 그런 콩쥐를 비웃었습니다. “착한 말이 일을 대신해 주지는 않아.” 콩쥐는 조용히 웃고 다시 손을 움직였습니다.

어느 따뜻한 날, 마을에 큰 잔치가 열렸습니다. 새어머니와 팥쥐는 고운 옷을 입고 나갈 준비를 했습니다. 새어머니는 콩쥐에게 부러진 호미를 내밀었습니다. “해가 지기 전에 돌밭을 모두 매라. 그리고 대문 옆 큰 독에 물을 가득 채워라.” 하지만 밭에는 돌이 가득했고, 독 밑에는 커다란 구멍이 나 있었습니다.

콩쥐는 손이 아프도록 일했지만 돌은 끝없이 나왔습니다. 마침내 나무 아래 앉아 눈물을 흘리자, 그늘 속에서 커다란 검은 소가 걸어 나왔습니다. “너는 배고픈 짐승에게 풀을 나누어 주었지. 오늘은 그 친절이 돌아올 차례란다.” 소는 힘센 어깨로 밭을 갈았습니다. 참새들은 고랑마다 내려앉아 조그만 돌까지 부리로 골라냈습니다.

콩쥐는 고맙다고 인사하고 우물로 달려갔습니다. 물을 아무리 부어도 독 아래로 줄줄 흘러나왔습니다. 그때 갈대 사이에서 거북이 한 마리가 기어 나왔습니다. “네가 전에 길 위의 나를 연못으로 옮겨 주었지.” 거북이는 단단한 등을 독의 구멍에 꼭 붙였습니다. 독에는 천천히 맑은 물이 차올라 작은 달처럼 반짝였습니다.

모든 일이 끝나자 구름빛 옷을 입은 여인이 나타났습니다. 여인은 비단신과 고운 저고리를 내밀며 말했습니다. “늘 다른 이를 기쁘게 한 마음도 오늘은 즐거워야지. 잔치에 가거라.” 콩쥐는 깊이 절하고 마을로 달렸습니다. 하지만 다리를 건너다 비단신 한 짝이 물에 빠지고 말았습니다.

젊은 원님이 갈대 사이에서 그 작은 신을 발견했습니다. 그는 마을 사람들에게 신의 주인을 물었습니다. 팥쥐는 발을 억지로 넣으려 했지만 맞지 않았습니다. 콩쥐가 신어 보자 가볍고 편안하게 꼭 맞았습니다. 콩쥐는 돌밭과 깨진 독, 소와 참새와 거북이에 관한 일을 숨김없이 이야기했습니다.

콩쥐는 떠나기 전에 밭으로 돌아가 도와준 친구들에게 하나씩 고마움을 전했습니다. 거북이를 독에서 조심스럽게 꺼내 연못으로 데려갔고, 검은 소에게는 싱싱한 풀을 베어 주었습니다. 참새들에게는 넉넉한 곡식을 뿌렸습니다. 구름빛 옷을 입은 여인은 보이지 않았지만, 나뭇잎을 흔드는 바람이 축복처럼 곁을 지나갔습니다.

새 집에서도 콩쥐는 예전의 힘든 날을 잊지 않았습니다. 일하는 사람에게 먼저 따뜻한 차를 건넸고, 아이들이 무거운 물동이를 들면 함께 들어 주었습니다. 좋은 옷과 넓은 방보다 소중한 것은 다른 사람의 수고를 알아보는 눈이라는 것을 잘 알고 있었기 때문입니다. 그래서 마을 사람들은 콩쥐를 찾아와 걱정을 나누었고, 콩쥐는 서두르지 않고 끝까지 들었습니다.

어느 봄날에는 거북이가 살던 연못 가장자리에 작은 돌다리를 놓았습니다. 아이들이 물을 건널 때 거북이와 물고기를 놀라게 하지 않도록 천천히 걷는 법도 가르쳤습니다. 친절은 한 번 베풀고 끝나는 일이 아니라 매일 다시 선택하는 일이라고 콩쥐는 생각했습니다.

원님은 콩쥐의 고운 모습보다 더 고운 마음을 알아보았습니다. 콩쥐는 안전하고 따뜻한 집에서 살게 되었습니다. 새어머니와 팥쥐는 못된 마음은 사람을 외롭게 하지만 친절은 밭과 연못 어디에서나 친구를 불러온다는 것을 배웠습니다. 콩쥐는 옛 마을을 찾을 때마다 참새에게 곡식을, 소에게 풀을, 믿음직한 거북이에게는 가장 싱싱한 상추 잎을 가져다주었습니다.

title: The Lady of the Lake
subtitle: a Welsh legend, about the Lady of Llyn y Fan Fach and three causeless blows
moral: Granny’s whisper: some promises are light to make and heavy to carry.
script_en:
High in the Black Mountain of Wales, beneath grey cliffs, lies a lonely lake called Llyn y Fan Fach. Its waters are dark and still, and the old people say that on quiet evenings you may see lights moving far below the surface, where the Tylwyth Teg, the Fair Folk, keep their shining halls.

Long ago a young shepherd pastured his flock beside that lake. One evening, as the sun went down, he saw a maiden sitting on a stone at the water's edge — the most beautiful maiden he had ever seen, with hair like dark water and a dress that shimmered like sunlight on scales.

His heart leapt, and being a simple lad, he did the first kind thing he could think of: he offered her his barley bread.

She looked at it and shook her head. “Hard-baked is thy bread,” she said, in a voice like water over stones. “I will not have thee.” And with a ripple she was gone.

The next evening he came again, and again she sat upon the stone. This time he offered bread his mother had left half-baked — and again she refused him. “Unbaked is thy bread,” she said. “I will not have thee.”

But his mother was a wise woman. “Take bread baked just enough,” she told him, “neither hard nor soft.”

On the third evening he offered it, and the lady smiled and took it from his hand. “I will be thine,” she said. “But hear my warning: if ever thou strikest me three blows without cause, I shall return to the lake forever, and take all my cattle with me.”

He swore he would never raise a hand to her. And from the lake there came a grand old man with a long white beard, who gave them as many cattle, sheep, and goats as the lady could count without drawing breath — and she counted by fives, one, two, three, four, five, until the meadows were full.

They married, and for years they were happy, and three fine sons were born to them.

But the warning hung over their happiness like a cloud. One day, at a christening, the lady wept — for she saw the sorrow waiting in the world for the little child. Her husband, meaning only to comfort her, tapped her shoulder and bade her hush. “That is the first causeless blow,” she said quietly.

Years later, at a wedding, she laughed — for she saw that all earthly joy must end. Again he tapped her shoulder in jest. “The second,” she whispered.

And at last, at a funeral, she sang for joy — for the dead was free of sorrow at last. Her husband tapped her a third time, saying, “Hush!”

She rose. She called her cattle by name, and the oxen left the plough standing in the field and followed her, dragging it behind them — the furrow they made can still be seen in that country. She walked into the waters of Llyn y Fan Fach, and the lake closed over her, and she was gone.

The shepherd grieved all his days. But their three sons grew up wise and kind, and their mother came to them in dreams and taught them the secrets of healing herbs. They became the Physicians of Myddfai, the most famous healers Wales has ever known — and that was the lady's last gift to the world above the water.
script_original:
Uchel ym Mynydd Du Cymru, o dan glogwyni llwydion, mae llyn unig o'r enw Llyn y Fan Fach. Mae ei ddyfroedd yn dywyll ac yn llonydd. Dywed yr hen bobl, ar nosweithiau tawel, y gellir gweld goleuadau'n symud yn ddwfn o dan yr wyneb, lle mae'r Tylwyth Teg yn cadw eu neuaddau disglair.

Ers talwm bu bugail ifanc yn pori ei braidd wrth y llyn. Un noson, wrth i'r haul fachlud, gwelodd forwyn yn eistedd ar garreg ger y dŵr. Hi oedd y ferch harddaf a welodd erioed, â gwallt fel dŵr tywyll a gwisg yn disgleirio fel heulwen ar glorian pysgod.

Neidiodd ei galon. Gan ei fod yn ŵr ifanc syml, gwnaeth y peth caredicaf y gallai feddwl amdano: cynigiodd ei fara haidd iddi.

Edrychodd hithau arno ac ysgwyd ei phen. “Rhy galed yw dy fara,” meddai mewn llais fel dŵr dros gerrig. “Ni allaf fod yn wraig i ti.” A chyda chrych ar y dŵr diflannodd.

Daeth yntau drachefn y noson nesaf, ac unwaith eto eisteddai hi ar y garreg. Y tro hwn cynigiodd fara hanner pob, ond gwrthododd hithau eto. “Heb ei bobi'n ddigonol yw dy fara,” meddai. “Ni allaf fod yn wraig i ti.”

Ond gwraig ddoeth oedd ei fam. “Dos â bara sydd wedi ei bobi'n union ddigon,” meddai, “heb fod yn rhy galed nac yn rhy feddal.”

Ar y drydedd noson cynigiodd y bara hwnnw. Gwenodd y forwyn a'i gymryd o'i law. “Byddaf yn eiddo i ti,” meddai, “ond gwrando ar fy rhybudd. Os rhoddi dri ergyd i mi heb achos, dychwelaf i'r llyn am byth, a bydd fy holl anifeiliaid yn dod gyda mi.”

Addawodd na fyddai byth yn codi llaw arni. Daeth hen ŵr urddasol â barf wen hir o'r llyn. Rhoddodd iddynt gymaint o wartheg, defaid a geifr ag y gallai'r wraig eu cyfrif mewn un anadl. Cyfrifodd fesul pump nes bod y dolydd yn llawn.

Priodasant, a buont yn hapus am flynyddoedd. Ganwyd tri mab iach iddynt.

Ond roedd y rhybudd yn hongian dros eu hapusrwydd fel cwmwl. Un diwrnod, mewn bedydd, wylodd y wraig oherwydd gwelai'r tristwch a allai aros am y plentyn bach. Gan fwriadu ei chysuro yn unig, cyffyrddodd ei gŵr â'i hysgwydd a gofyn iddi dewi. “Dyna'r ergyd gyntaf heb achos,” meddai'n dawel.

Flynyddoedd yn ddiweddarach, mewn priodas, chwarddodd hi, oherwydd gwyddai fod pob llawenydd daearol yn dod i ben. Cyffyrddodd ei gŵr â'i hysgwydd mewn cellwair. “Yr ail,” sibrydodd hi.

Yn olaf, mewn angladd, canodd hi o lawenydd am fod y marw wedi ei ryddhau o dristwch. Cyffyrddodd ei gŵr â hi am y trydydd tro, gan ddweud, “Taw!”

Cododd y wraig. Galwodd ei gwartheg wrth eu henwau. Gadawodd yr ychen yr aradr yn y cae a'i dilyn, gan lusgo'r aradr ar eu hôl. Dywedir y gellir gweld y rhych hyd heddiw. Cerddodd i ddyfroedd Llyn y Fan Fach; caeodd y llyn drosti, a diflannodd.

Bu'r bugail yn galaru drwy weddill ei oes. Ond tyfodd eu tri mab yn ddoeth ac yn garedig. Daeth eu mam atynt mewn breuddwydion a dysgu cyfrinachau perlysiau iacháu iddynt. Daethant yn Feddygon Myddfai, yr iachawyr enwocaf a fu yng Nghymru erioed. Dyna oedd rhodd olaf Arglwyddes y Llyn i'r byd uwchlaw'r dŵr.

title: The Lion’s Whisker
subtitle: an Ethiopian folktale, about patient love and the bravest whisker ever plucked
moral: Granny’s whisper: trust comes close one careful step at a time.
script_en:
Long ago in the highlands of Ethiopia, a woman married a kind widower whose young son had known much sorrow. She cooked his favorite foods and spoke gently, but the boy turned away. His grief had built a wall around him.

The woman went to a wise healer. “How can I make him love me?” she asked. The healer thought, then said, “Bring me one whisker from a living lion. Then I shall make you a medicine for his heart.”

She was frightened, but each evening she carried a bowl of food to a place where a lion came down from the hills. At first she left the bowl far away and hurried home. The lion waited until she was gone.

Night after night she returned. After many days the lion ate while she watched from a distance. After many more, he allowed her a little closer. She never rushed. She never reached before trust was ready.

At last the lion ate beside her. His golden breath stirred the grass. The woman raised one careful hand, touched his mane, and gently plucked a single whisker. The lion blinked, finished his meal, and walked back toward the hills.

Triumphant, she carried the whisker to the healer. He examined it — then tossed it into the fire. “Why?” she cried. “Do you know how long that took?”

“I do,” said the healer. “You approached a wild lion with patience. You brought food without demanding affection. You moved closer only when he was ready. Is the heart of a grieving child more dangerous than a lion?”

The woman understood. She went home and stopped trying to force the boy to love her. She left warm food near him. She listened when he wished to speak. She kept her promises. Days became weeks, and weeks became months.

One evening the boy sat beside her and placed his hand in hers. No magic medicine had opened his heart. Patience had. And the woman knew that the lion’s true gift was not the whisker she had taken, but the wisdom she had carried home.
script_original:
ከብዙ ዓመታት በፊት በኢትዮጵያ ደጋማ አካባቢ አንዲት ሴት ከአንድ ደግ ባልቴት ጋር ተጋባች። የባሏ ትንሽ ልጅ ብዙ ሀዘን አይቶ ነበር። ሴቲቱ የሚወደውን ምግብ ታበስልለትና በርኅራኄ ታነጋግረው ነበር፣ ግን ልጁ ከእሷ ይርቅ ነበር።

ሴቲቱ ወደ አንድ ጠቢብ ፈዋሽ ሄደች። “ልጁ እንዲያምነኝ ምን ላድርግ?” አለች። ፈዋሹም፣ “ከሕያው አንበሳ አንድ ጢም አምጪልኝ” አላት።

በየምሽቱ ለአንበሳው ምግብ ታመጣ ጀመር። መጀመሪያ ምግቡን ከሩቅ ትታ ትሄድ ነበር። ቀን ከቀን በትዕግሥት ቀረበች፤ ፈጥና አልዘረጋችም፣ እምነት እስኪዘጋጅ ጠበቀች።

በመጨረሻ አንበሳው ከአጠገቧ በላ። ሴቲቱ በጥንቃቄ አንድ ጢም ነቀለችና ወደ ፈዋሹ አመጣችው። እርሱ ጢሙን ወደ እሳት ጣለው። ሴቲቱ ተደነገጠች። “ይህን ለማግኘት ምን ያህል ጊዜ እንደፈጀ ታውቃለህ?”

“አውቃለሁ” አለ ፈዋሹ። “ወደ አንበሳው በትዕግሥት ቀረብሽ፣ ፍቅርን ሳትጠይቂ ምግብ ሰጠሽ። የሀዘንተኛ ልጅ ልብ ከአንበሳ ይበልጥ አደገኛ ነውን?” ሴቲቱ ተረዳች። ወደ ቤት ተመልሳ ልጁን አላስገደደችም። ትጠብቅ፣ ታዳምጥና ቃሏን ትጠብቅ ነበር። አንድ ምሽት ልጁ ከጎኗ ተቀምጦ እጁን በእጇ ውስጥ አኖረ። የልቡን በር የከፈተው አስማት ሳይሆን ትዕግሥት ነበር።

title: How Māui Slowed the Sun
subtitle: a Māori tale from Aotearoa, about courage, cooperation, and daylight shared fairly
moral: Granny’s whisper: daylight is brightest when many hands make room to share it.
script_en:
Long ago in Aotearoa, Tama-nui-te-rā, the great sun, hurried across the sky. He leaped from the eastern horizon and raced west before anyone could finish a day’s work. Hāngi stones were hardly warm when darkness fell. Fishing nets came home half-mended, and the kūmara gardens were left waiting.

Māui watched his people hurry from dawn until dusk. “The sun gives light,” he said, “but he keeps too much speed for himself.” His brothers shook their heads. No canoe could chase the sun. No spear could reach so high. Yet Māui asked them to trust a plan that would need every hand in the village.

People cut and softened strong harakeke, New Zealand flax, twisting its fibres into ropes. In some tellings, Māui’s sister Hina gave strands of her sacred hair to strengthen them. Aunties plaited. Children rolled cord between careful palms. The brothers tested every knot. By moonlight the long ropes lay coiled like sleeping eels.

Māui carried the enchanted jawbone of his grandmother, Murirangawhenua. He and his brothers travelled east through the night to the deep pit where the sun rested before morning. There they built low walls of clay to shelter themselves from the coming heat. Across the mouth of the pit they spread their ropes and tied a mighty noose.

Before dawn, Māui spoke a karakia, asking strength, steadiness, and right purpose for the work. Then the first fierce rays rose. “Pull!” cried Māui. The brothers leaned back together. The ropes tightened around the sun’s blazing hair. Tama-nui-te-rā struggled, and light flashed across the clay walls.

The heat was terrible, but nobody let go. Māui stepped forward with Murirangawhenua’s jawbone. He struck at the sun’s rays—not to destroy their giver, but to stop his wild racing. “Why do you hurry?” he called. “Our food cannot cook. Our work cannot be finished. Children scarcely have time to play before night.”

At last the sun grew tired. “Release me,” Tama-nui-te-rā said, “and I will cross the sky more slowly.” Māui made him promise. The brothers loosened the noose, though the rope marks remained streaming from the sun like long golden rays.

That morning the village waited. The sun climbed, warm and unhurried. The hāngi cooked through. Nets were mended, gardens tended, and children played beside the water before evening came. Māui did not claim the daylight as his own. Everyone had braided the ropes; everyone shared the gift. Even the smallest child knew a hand had helped.

Some winter days are still short, and summer days wander long. Yet when the sun moves gently overhead, people remember Māui, his brothers, Hina’s gift, Murirangawhenua’s jawbone, and the many hands that caught a racing light so there would be enough day for all.
script_original:
I ngā rā o nehe i Aotearoa, he tere rawa te haere a Tama-nui-te-rā i te rangi. Ka puea ake ia i te pae rāwhiti, kātahi ka oma ki te uru. Kāore anō ngā kōhatu o te hāngi kia wera, kua pō. Kāore anō ngā kupenga kia oti te raranga, kua ngaro te mārama.

I titiro a Māui ki tōna iwi e oma ana i te ata tae noa ki te ahiahi. Ka mea ia, “He koha te mārama a te rā, engari he nui rawa tōna tere.” Kāore ōna tuākana i whakapono i te tuatahi. Kāore he waka e whai i te rā, kāore hoki he tao e tae atu ki a ia. Heoi, i tono a Māui kia mahi ngātahi te kāinga katoa.

Ka tapahia te harakeke, ka whakangāwarihia ngā muka, ā, ka whiria hei taura kaha. I ētahi kōrero, ka hoatu e tōna tuahine a Hina ētahi whenu o ōna makawe tapu hei whakakaha i ngā taura. Ka whiri ngā whaea, ka miro ngā tamariki, ka whakamātau ngā tuākana i ngā here katoa.

Ka mauria e Māui te kauae tipua o tōna kuia, o Murirangawhenua. I te pō, ka haere rāua ko ōna tuākana ki te rāwhiti, ki te rua e moe ai te rā. Ka hanga rātou i ngā pātū uku hei whakaruru i te wera. Ka hora ngā taura ki runga i te waha o te rua, ka herea he māhanga nui.

I mua i te ata, ka karakia a Māui kia kaha, kia ū, kia tika te kaupapa. Ka ara ake ngā hihi mura tuatahi. “Kumea!” tā Māui karanga. Ka tō ngātahi ngā tuākana. Ka mau ngā taura ki ngā makawe kanapa o Tama-nui-te-rā. Ka kakari te rā, ka whiti te mura ki ngā pātū uku.

He tino wera, engari kāore tētahi i tuku. Ka whakatata atu a Māui me te kauae o Murirangawhenua. Ka patu ia i ngā hihi o te rā, ehara i te mea kia whakamate, engari kia mutu tōna oma. “He aha koe i tere ai?” ka karanga ia. “Kāore ā mātou kai e maoa. Kāore ngā mahi e oti. He iti rawa te wā tākaro a ngā tamariki.”

Ka ngenge te rā. “Tukua ahau,” ka mea a Tama-nui-te-rā, “ā, ka haere pōturi ahau i te rangi.” Ka tono a Māui kia oati ia. Ka wetekina te māhanga, engari ka noho ngā tohu o ngā taura hei hihi koura roa.

I taua ata ka tatari te kāinga. Ka piki te rā, he mahana, he ngāwari. Ka maoa te hāngi, ka oti ngā kupenga, ka tiakina ngā māra, ā, ka tākaro ngā tamariki i mua i te pō. Kāore a Māui i kī nāna anake te mārama. Nā te katoa ngā taura i whiri, nā te katoa hoki te koha.

He poto tonu ētahi rā o te hōtoke, he roa ētahi rā o te raumati. Engari, ina haere marire te rā i runga, ka maumahara te iwi ki a Māui, ki ōna tuākana, ki te koha a Hina, ki te kauae o Murirangawhenua, me ngā ringa maha i pupuri i te mārama kia nui ai te rā mō te katoa.

title: The Monkey and the Crocodile
subtitle: a wisdom tale from the Panchatantra of India, about friendship and thinking fast
moral: Granny’s whisper: keep your wits about you when the water gets deep.
script_en:
Long ago, on the bank of a wide brown river in India, there grew a great rose-apple tree, heavy with sweet purple fruit. And in that tree there lived a plump, cheerful monkey who ate rose-apples all day and dropped the pits into the river, plip, plop, plip.

One morning a great green crocodile came drifting down the river. The monkey called down, “Friend, you look tired. Would you like some of my fruit? It is sweeter than honey and cooler than the moon.” “I am not much of a fruit eater,” said the crocodile. “But I will try one.” He tried one, then another, then five. From that day on he came every morning, and the monkey and the crocodile became the best of friends, talking all day about the forest, the river, and everything.

One evening the crocodile carried home a pawful of fruit for his wife. She tasted it, and her eyes gleamed. “If this fruit is so sweet,” she said, “then how much sweeter must be the heart of the monkey who eats it all day long! Husband, I want to eat the monkey’s heart.”

The crocodile was horrified. “He is my friend!” But his wife cried and sulked and blew bubbles, and wore him down like water wears a stone, until at last he sighed and said, “Very well.”

The next morning the crocodile said, “Friend, my wife has heard so much about you that she begs you to come to our home for dinner. Hop on my back, and I will carry you across the river.” The monkey was delighted. He swung down onto the crocodile’s broad back, and off they went into the deep water.

But in the middle of the river, the crocodile slowed, and his head drooped, and he told the monkey the whole sad truth: that his wife wished to eat his heart, and so he was sorry, truly sorry, but he must take him to her. For a moment the monkey was so frightened he could not breathe. Then he looked at the far shore, and he made his voice as light as a leaf.

“Oh dear,” said the monkey. “Is that all? You should have told me at the start! We monkeys always leave our hearts hanging in our trees when we travel — hearts are so much trouble to carry around. If you take me back, I shall fetch mine at once, and gladly give it to your wife.”

“You would do that?” said the crocodile, turning around at once. “Good, good! Hold on tight!” And back they swam. The moment they reached the shallows, the monkey leapt into the branches, high, higher, highest, laughing until the leaves shook.

“Foolish crocodile!” he called down. “You had my friendship, and you traded it for a wish. Go home and tell your wife: the wisest heart in the forest stays on its own tree.” And the crocodile went home beneath the water, feeling very small, which is just the right size for anyone who has been greedy. And they say the rose-apples of that tree tasted sweeter than ever, because the monkey never took them — or his friends — for granted again.
script_alternate:
एक नदी के किनारे जामुन का बड़ा पेड़ था। उस पर एक चतुर बंदर रहता था। नदी में रहने वाला मगरमच्छ रोज़ किनारे आता, और बंदर उसे मीठे जामुन देता। धीरे-धीरे दोनों मित्र बन गए।

मगरमच्छ कुछ फल अपनी पत्नी के लिए ले गया। फल खाकर उसने सोचा, “जो बंदर रोज़ इतने मीठे फल खाता है, उसका हृदय कितना मीठा होगा!” उसने पति से बंदर का हृदय लाने को कहा। मगरमच्छ ने मना किया, पर अंत में दबाव में आ गया।

वह बंदर को अपनी पीठ पर बैठाकर बोला, “मेरी पत्नी ने तुम्हें भोजन पर बुलाया है।” नदी के बीच पहुँचकर उसने दुखी होकर सच बता दिया। बंदर डर गया, पर उसने बुद्धि नहीं खोई। उसने कहा, “अरे मित्र! तुमने पहले क्यों नहीं बताया? मैं अपना हृदय पेड़ की खोखल में छोड़ आया हूँ। वापस चलो, मैं उसे ले आता हूँ।”

मूर्ख मगरमच्छ उसे किनारे लौटा लाया। बंदर तुरंत पेड़ की ऊँची डाल पर चढ़ गया। “क्या कोई अपना हृदय शरीर से बाहर रखता है?” उसने कहा। “तुमने मित्रता को धोखा दिया, पर मेरी बुद्धि ने मेरी जान बचाई।”

मगरमच्छ लज्जित होकर लौट गया। बंदर ने सीखा कि मिठास बाँटना अच्छा है, पर विश्वास सोच-समझकर देना चाहिए। और नदी ने उनकी कहानी दूर तक पहुँचा दी।
alternate_note: Published Hindi text for a Panchatantra tale.

title: The Rabbit in the Moon
subtitle: a legend from Mexico, about a hungry traveler and a very small supper
moral: Granny’s whisper: small paws, enormous heart.
script_en:
Long, long ago, when the gods still walked the earth in Mexico, the great god Quetzalcoatl, the Feathered Serpent, splendid and wise, grew tired on a long journey. As evening fell he sat down to rest by the side of the road, hungry and weary.

A little rabbit came hopping by, eating the tender grass, and she stopped when she saw the traveler. “Good evening,” said the rabbit politely. “Why do you look so tired?”

“I have walked far,” said Quetzalcoatl, “and I have had nothing to eat. I am very hungry.”

The rabbit looked at the small pile of grass she had gathered. “I am only a rabbit,” she said, “and grass is all I have. It is not much of a supper for a traveler, but you are welcome to share it.”

“I cannot eat grass,” said the god gently.

The little rabbit thought for a moment. Then she stood up straight and said, “I am very small, but I do not want you to go hungry. So eat me. I am not much, but I am what I have.”

The god was silent. Then he bent down and lifted the rabbit in his hands, and his eyes grew wet. “You may be small, little rabbit,” he said, “but tonight no heart in the whole world is larger than yours. And I will not let the world forget it.”

Then the mighty Quetzalcoatl rose to his full height, and he lifted the little rabbit high, high up, high above the trees and the mountains, up to where the moon was rising, round and white and full. And he pressed her gently against the moon, so that her shape was printed there: long ears, soft body, up on her hind legs, nibbling the sky.

“There,” said the god, setting her down again on the grass. “You are only a rabbit, and your life will be short, as all our lives are. But from tonight until the end of the world, every child who looks up at the full moon will see your picture there, and remember what you offered to a hungry traveler on the road.”

And it is true. On the next clear night, when the moon is round and silver, find a child, or borrow one, and look up together. There she is, the little rabbit who gave everything she had, still standing in the moon, still reminding us that greatness is not measured in size, but in what you are willing to share.
script_alternate:
Hace muchísimo tiempo, cuando los dioses aún caminaban por los caminos de México, Quetzalcóatl tomó la forma de un viajero. Al caer la noche estaba cansado, hambriento y lejos de cualquier pueblo. Se sentó junto al sendero mientras la luna empezaba a subir.

Una conejita pasó comiendo hierba. «¿Por qué estás tan triste?», preguntó. El viajero le contó que no había comido en todo el día. La conejita acercó su pequeño montón de pasto. «Comparte mi cena.» Quetzalcóatl sonrió con ternura. «Los humanos no podemos comer hierba.»

La conejita pensó un momento. Miró el camino vacío, al viajero agotado y lo poco que tenía. Entonces se irguió y dijo: «No poseo nada más. Si mi hierba no puede alimentarte, cómeme a mí. No quiero que mueras de hambre.»

Los ojos del dios se llenaron de asombro. La levantó con ambas manos. «Eres pequeña, pero esta noche no hay corazón más grande que el tuyo. No te comeré; haré que el mundo recuerde tu generosidad.»

Quetzalcóatl alzó a la conejita hasta la luna redonda y blanca, y su silueta quedó marcada allí: las orejas largas, el lomo curvo y las patas recogidas. Luego la devolvió sana y salva a la tierra. «Tu vida será breve, como toda vida, pero cada niña, cada niño y cada viajero verá tu imagen y recordará que ningún regalo es pequeño cuando es todo lo que uno tiene.»
alternate_note: Published Spanish text for an Aztec legend.

title: The Golden Apple-Tree and the Nine Peahens
subtitle: a Serbian tale, about nine peahens and a prince who would not sleep
moral: Granny’s whisper: a true heart may lose the road, but it does not stop searching.
script_en:
Once upon a time there lived a king, and before his palace grew a marvelous tree — a golden apple-tree that blossomed, bore fruit, and ripened all in a single night. But every morning the branches were bare, and no one could tell who gathered the shining apples.

The king had three sons, and he asked the eldest to keep watch. The eldest lay down beneath the tree at dusk, full of brave plans — but just as the apples began to glow, sleep took him, and in the morning the tree was bare.

The second son fared no better. Then the youngest son said, “Father, let me try.” He carried his bed beneath the tree and slept until midnight — for he had set his heart on waking — and opened his eyes just as the whole palace lit up with the shining of the ripening apples.

At that moment nine peahens came flying through the night. Eight settled in the branches and began to eat, but the ninth alighted beside the prince — and in the blink of an eye she became a maiden so beautiful that the whole kingdom could not show her equal.

She talked with him kindly until after midnight, thanking him for the golden apples. And when she rose to go, he begged her to leave him one. She gave him two — one for him and one for the king his father — then turned back into a peahen and flew away with the others.

So it went for two nights more. But the elder brothers had spied on him, and jealousy gnawed them. They paid a witch to spoil his happiness, and on the third night she leapt from the shadows and cut a lock from the maiden's hair. The prince seized the witch and she was punished — but the peahens never came again.

The young prince grieved, and at last he set out into the world to find his beloved, with only his faithful servant for company.

Far away he came to a castle beside a lake, where a widowed queen lived with her daughter. The queen wished him to marry her daughter and stay — but his heart was elsewhere, and he would only ask where the nine peahens bathed at midday.

The queen, angry, bribed his servant with a little magic whistle: when the peahens came, he was to blow it, and the prince would fall into a deep sleep. Twice the prince slept while the ninth peahen bent over him, pleading for him to wake. On the third day — the last day the peahens would ever come — she wept and told the servant, “Tell your master to strike the head from the lower nail, and follow where it points, and he will find me.”

The prince woke, heard the message, and sent the false servant away. Alone, he struck the head from the lower nail of the whistle as she had said — and from it sprang a golden thread, floating on the wind. He followed it over mountains and through forests until he came to a hermit's hut.

The hermit listened to his tale and pointed to a road of white stone. “At its end stands the palace of the peahens,” he said. “Go with a true heart.”

At the road's end the prince told his story to the guard at the gate — and out ran a young empress, radiant as morning. It was she: the ninth peahen. They were married that very day, and the whole kingdom rejoiced.

One morning the empress had to go on a journey. She gave her husband the keys to twelve cellars. “You may open eleven,” she said. “But the twelfth you must never open — or sorrow will come of it.”

For a while he obeyed. But curiosity is a stubborn guest. One night he opened the twelfth door — and inside stood an iron-bound cask, and from within came a weak voice begging, “Water! Water! For pity's sake, a cup of water!”

His kind heart overcame his promise. He gave the voice three cups of water — and with a crash the iron bands burst, and out sprang a terrible dragon! It seized the empress and bore her away to its castle of black glass beyond the Iron Mountains.

But the prince did not despair. He sought the hermit again, who gave him sleeping herbs and wise counsel. For seven days the prince journeyed, until he reached the black glass castle. He waited until the dragon's snores shook the walls, crept in on silent feet, and led his beloved softly out by the hand.

They fled through the night while the dragon slept on, and by dawn they were safe. Back at her palace they planted a seed of the golden apple-tree in the courtyard — and every night it blossoms, bears fruit, and ripens, filling the palace with golden light.

And if you listen on a still night in Serbia, the old people say, you can hear nine peahens crying far away — and see a golden glow where the apple-tree blooms.
script_original:
Bio jednom jedan car, a pred njegovim dvorom raslo je čudesno drvo — zlatna jabuka koja bi u jednoj jedinoj noći procvetala, rodila i sazrela. Ali svakoga jutra grane su bile gole, i niko nije znao ko odnosi sjajne plodove.

Car je imao tri sina. Najstarijem je naredio da stražari. Princ je u sumrak legao pod drvo pun hrabrih namera, ali čim su jabuke počele da svetle, savladao ga je san. Ujutru su grane opet bile prazne.

Ni srednji sin nije prošao bolje. Tada najmlađi reče: „Oče, pusti mene da pokušam.“ Doneo je postelju pod drvo i spavao do ponoći, rešivši da se tada probudi. Otvorio je oči baš kad je ceo dvor zasjao od zlatnih jabuka koje su sazrevale.

Utom kroz noć dolete devet paunica. Osam ih slete na grane i poče da jede, a deveta se spusti kraj princa. U treptaju oka pretvorila se u devojku lepšu od svih u carstvu.

Ljubazno je razgovarala s njim do posle ponoći i zahvalila mu za zlatne jabuke. Kada je pošla, zamolio ju je da mu ostavi jednu. Dala mu je dve — jednu za njega, a jednu za njegovog oca cara. Zatim se ponovo pretvorila u paunicu i odletela sa ostalima.

Tako je bilo još dve noći. Ali starija braća su ga krišom posmatrala i zavist ih je izjedala. Platili su veštici da pokvari njegovu sreću. Treće noći iskočila je iz senke i odsekla pramen devojčine kose. Princ je uhvatio vešticu i ona je bila kažnjena, ali se paunice više nisu vratile.

Mladi princ je tugovao. Najzad je krenuo u svet da pronađe voljenu, a s njim je pošao samo njegov sluga.

Daleko od kuće stigao je do dvorca kraj jezera, gde je kraljica udovica živela sa ćerkom. Kraljica je želela da se princ oženi njenom ćerkom i ostane, ali njegovo srce je pripadalo drugoj. Samo je pitao gde se devet paunica kupa u podne.

Ljuta kraljica podmitila je slugu malom čarobnom zviždaljkom. Kada paunice dođu, trebalo je da dune u nju, pa bi princ pao u dubok san. Dvaput je princ spavao dok se deveta paunica naginjala nad njim i molila ga da se probudi. Trećeg dana, poslednjeg kada će paunice doći, zaplakala je i rekla sluzi: „Kaži gospodaru da udari glavu donjeg klina i pođe kuda ona pokaže. Tamo će me naći.“

Kad se princ probudio i čuo poruku, oterao je nevernog slugu. Sam je udario glavu donjeg klina na zviždaljci, kao što je devojka rekla. Iz nje se razvila zlatna nit i zaplovila na vetru. Pratio ju je preko planina i kroz šume sve do kolibe jednog pustinjaka.

Pustinjak je saslušao priču i pokazao put od belog kamena. „Na njegovom kraju stoji dvor paunica“, reče. „Pođi iskrena srca.“

Na kraju puta princ je ispričao svoju priču čuvaru kapije. Tada je istrčala mlada carica, blistava kao jutro. Bila je to ona, deveta paunica. Venčali su se istog dana i celo carstvo se radovalo.

Jednog jutra carica je morala na put. Dala je mužu ključeve od dvanaest podruma. „Jedanaest smeš otvoriti“, reče, „ali dvanaesti nikada, jer će iz njega doći nesreća.“

Neko vreme ju je slušao. Ali radoznalost je tvrdoglav gost. Jedne noći otvorio je dvanaesta vrata. Unutra je bilo bure okovano gvožđem, a iz njega je slabi glas molio: „Vode! Vode! Za milost, jednu čašu vode!“

Njegovo dobro srce nadjačalo je obećanje. Dao je glasu tri čaše vode. Uz prasak su popucali gvozdeni obruči, a iz bureta je iskočila strašna aždaja. Zgrabila je caricu i odnela je u svoj dvorac od crnog stakla iza Gvozdenih planina.

Princ nije očajavao. Ponovo je potražio pustinjaka, koji mu je dao uspavljujuće bilje i mudar savet. Putovao je sedam dana dok nije stigao do crnog dvorca. Sačekao je da hrkanje aždaje zatrese zidove, ušao na tihim nogama i nežno izveo voljenu držeći je za ruku.

Bežali su kroz noć dok je aždaja spavala, a do zore su bili bezbedni. U dvorištu njenog dvora posadili su seme zlatne jabuke. Svake noći ono cveta, rađa i sazreva, puneći dvor zlatnom svetlošću.

A ako oslušnete mirnu noć u Srbiji, kažu stari ljudi, možda ćete čuti kako devet paunica doziva iz daljine i videti zlatan sjaj tamo gde cveta jabuka.

title: The North Wind and the Sun
subtitle: an Aesop fable about persuasion, patience, and strength that does not need to shove
moral: Granny’s whisper: warmth often opens what force only closes tighter.
script_en:
High above the hills of ancient Greece, the North Wind rushed through the sky, rattling olive branches and chasing whitecaps across the sea. He was proud of his strength. When doors slammed or clouds scattered, he cried, “See how the whole world obeys me!”

The Sun rose nearby, warm and steady. “Strength has many forms,” the Sun said.

“None greater than mine,” boasted the North Wind. “I can bend trees, tumble roof tiles, and drive ships before me.”

Below them, a traveler walked along a winding road. He carried a small bundle and wore a thick cloak fastened at his shoulder. The North Wind pointed down. “Let us settle this. Whoever makes that traveler remove his cloak is stronger.”

The Sun agreed and slipped behind a cloud to let the Wind try first.

The North Wind drew a mighty breath. He blew across the road until dust flew and the traveler’s cloak snapped like a sail. But the traveler only pulled the cloth tighter. The Wind blew harder. He sent cold fingers around the traveler’s neck and tugged at every fold. The traveler lowered his head, fastened the cloak more securely, and wrapped both arms around his body.

“A little more,” muttered the Wind. He roared down from the mountains. Birds hid among the rocks. Leaves spun into the air. The traveler stopped behind a stone wall and held his cloak closed with all his strength.

At last the North Wind had no breath left for boasting. “Your turn,” he sighed.

The Sun came out from behind the cloud. At first, the Sun offered only a mild spring warmth. The traveler straightened and continued down the road. Then the Sun warmed the stones, the wild thyme, and the air itself. The traveler loosened the clasp at his shoulder.

The Sun shone a little more brightly—not fiercely, not to scorch, but enough to make the road pleasant. Soon the traveler smiled, took off his cloak, folded it over one arm, and rested beneath an olive tree.

The North Wind was silent. Looking down, he saw that his furious gusts had made the traveler cling to the cloak with all his might, while the Sun had given him room to choose. The contest had not been won by weakness, but by a different kind of strength.

“You are powerful,” said the Sun, “and winter needs your clear cold air. But when you try to force a person, they often hold tighter. Warmth can invite what force cannot command.”

The Wind considered this as he moved gently through the olive leaves. Far below, the traveler shared bread with another walker in the Sun’s kind light. From that day, the North Wind still blew when his season came, but he remembered that victory is not always won by pushing hardest. Sometimes the strongest touch is the one that lets another choose.

Expanded gently from Aesop’s public-domain fable “The North Wind and the Sun,” in the 1912 V. S. Vernon-Jones translation. Read the source.
script_original:
Ψηλά πάνω από τους λόφους της αρχαίας Ελλάδας, ο Βοριάς έτρεχε στον ουρανό, τίναζε τα κλαδιά των ελιών και σήκωνε κύματα στη θάλασσα. Ήταν περήφανος για τη δύναμή του. «Όλος ο κόσμος με υπακούει!» φώναζε.

Ο Ήλιος ανέβηκε δίπλα του, ζεστός και σταθερός. «Η δύναμη έχει πολλές μορφές», είπε.

Κάτω τους περπατούσε ένας ταξιδιώτης σε έναν στριφογυριστό δρόμο. Φορούσε βαρύ μανδύα. Ο Βοριάς τον έδειξε. «Ας δούμε ποιος είναι πιο δυνατός. Όποιος τον κάνει να βγάλει τον μανδύα του, κερδίζει.» Ο Ήλιος συμφώνησε και κρύφτηκε πίσω από ένα σύννεφο.

Ο Βοριάς φύσηξε δυνατά. Η σκόνη σηκώθηκε και ο μανδύας χτύπησε σαν πανί καραβιού. Ο ταξιδιώτης όμως τον έσφιξε περισσότερο. Ο άνεμος φύσηξε ακόμη πιο παγωμένα και τράβηξε κάθε πτυχή. Ο άνθρωπος έκλεισε καλά την πόρπη και τύλιξε τα χέρια γύρω από το σώμα του.

Ο Βοριάς βρυχήθηκε από τα βουνά. Τα πουλιά κρύφτηκαν και τα φύλλα στριφογύρισαν. Ο ταξιδιώτης στάθηκε πίσω από έναν πέτρινο τοίχο και κράτησε τον μανδύα με όλη του τη δύναμη. Στο τέλος ο Βοριάς δεν είχε άλλη πνοή. «Η σειρά σου», αναστέναξε.

Ο Ήλιος βγήκε από το σύννεφο. Πρώτα έδωσε μια ήπια ανοιξιάτικη ζεστασιά. Ο ταξιδιώτης ίσιωσε και συνέχισε τον δρόμο. Έπειτα ο Ήλιος ζέστανε τις πέτρες, το θυμάρι και τον αέρα. Ο ταξιδιώτης χαλάρωσε την πόρπη.

Ο Ήλιος έλαμψε λίγο περισσότερο, όχι για να κάψει αλλά για να κάνει τον δρόμο ευχάριστο. Σύντομα ο άνθρωπος χαμογέλασε, έβγαλε τον μανδύα, τον δίπλωσε στο χέρι και ξεκουράστηκε κάτω από μια ελιά.

«Είσαι δυνατός», είπε ο Ήλιος στον Βοριά, «μα όταν προσπαθείς να αναγκάσεις κάποιον, συχνά εκείνος κρατιέται πιο σφιχτά. Η ζεστασιά μπορεί να προσκαλέσει ό,τι η βία δεν μπορεί να διατάξει.» Από τότε ο Βοριάς θυμόταν πως μερικές φορές το πιο δυνατό άγγιγμα είναι εκείνο που αφήνει τον άλλον να επιλέξει.

title: The Legend of the Northern Lights
subtitle: an Inuit sky story, about spirits at play and lights that ask to be treated with respect
moral: Granny’s whisper: wonder is brightest when it travels with respect.
script_en:
In the far North, winter nights can stretch wide and deep. Snow softens every sound, stars burn close, and sometimes great ribbons of green, violet, and white begin to move across the sky.

In many Inuit communities, elders have told different stories about those lights. Some say they are the spirits of relatives and ancestors, traveling and dancing in the night. Some say the spirits are playing a game with a walrus skull, tossing it across the darkness like a ball.

One winter, a child named Nukka stood outside with her grandmother and watched the lights gather. They folded like curtains, then leaped from one horizon to the other. “Are they far away?” Nukka whispered.

“Far enough to be sky,” her grandmother said, “and close enough that we remember our manners.” She told Nukka never to shout at the lights or call them down in mockery. Beauty can be powerful, and old stories teach respect for what we do not command.

As they watched, the pale bands brightened. Nukka imagined swift players running over the stars, laughing as they chased their shining ball. She thought she heard a faint crackle, like dry snow under boots.

The child wanted to whistle, but remembered her grandmother’s words. Instead she tucked her mittened hand into the elder’s warm glove. Together they named those they missed and sent their love upward without asking the sky for proof.

The lights danced until the cold pinched their cheeks. Then they faded behind the mountains. The sky grew dark and calm again, but Nukka no longer felt the night was empty.

Whenever the aurora returned, she watched with wonder and respect. And when younger children asked what made the sky move, she shared the stories just as they had been shared with her: not as one single answer for every Inuit community, but as many bright ways of remembering that those who came before us are never entirely gone.
alternate_title: The Legend of the Northern Lights
script_alternate:
Dans le Grand Nord, les nuits d’hiver s’étendent longtemps. La neige adoucit chaque bruit, les étoiles paraissent proches et de grands rubans verts, violets et blancs se mettent parfois à danser dans le ciel.

Les communautés inuites racontent plusieurs histoires à leur sujet. Pour certains anciens, ce sont les esprits des parents et des ancêtres qui voyagent dans la nuit. D’autres disent que les esprits jouent avec un crâne de morse, lancé dans l’obscurité comme une balle.

Un soir, une enfant nommée Nukka regardait les lumières avec sa grand-mère. «Sont-elles loin?» demanda-t-elle. «Assez loin pour appartenir au ciel, répondit l’aînée, et assez proches pour que nous gardions nos bonnes manières.» Elle apprit à Nukka à ne pas se moquer des lumières ni à les appeler comme si on pouvait les commander.

Nukka imagina les joueurs courant parmi les étoiles. Elle voulut siffler, puis se souvint des paroles de sa grand-mère. Elle glissa plutôt sa mitaine dans la main chaude de l’aînée. Ensemble, elles nommèrent ceux qui leur manquaient et envoyèrent leur amour vers le ciel sans exiger de preuve.

Plus tard, Nukka transmit ces récits aux plus jeunes: non comme une seule réponse pour tous les peuples inuits, mais comme plusieurs manières lumineuses de se souvenir. L’émerveillement, disait-elle, brille davantage lorsqu’il marche avec le respect.
alternate_note: Published French (Québécois) text for a tale attributed to Inuit tradition.

title: The Parrot and the Merchant
subtitle: a tale from Rumi’s Masnavi, about a wordless lesson and the courage to set love free
moral: Granny’s whisper: a heart can love deeply without closing a cage door.
script_en:
In a city of gardens and blue-tiled courtyards lived a merchant who loved beautiful things. His dearest treasure was a green parrot with bright, watchful eyes. The bird lived in a polished brass cage, ate pistachios from the merchant’s hand, and spoke so wisely that visitors often forgot they were talking to a creature with feathers.

One spring, the merchant prepared a caravan for India. Before leaving, he asked everyone in his household what gift they wished him to bring home. One asked for silk, another for sandalwood, and a child asked for a painted wooden elephant.

Last of all, the merchant turned to the parrot. “And what shall I bring you, little friend?”

“Bring me no object,” said the parrot. “But when you see the free parrots of India, tell them that one of their kin lives in a cage in Persia. Ask if they have any message for me.”

The merchant promised. After many dusty roads, his caravan reached a green forest alive with birdsong. A flock of parrots flashed among the branches. The merchant called out his caged parrot’s greeting and described its comfortable life: the fine cage, the sweet fruit, and the safe courtyard.

At once, one wild parrot trembled, fell from its branch, and lay perfectly still on the ground. The merchant was stricken. “My poor message has broken its heart,” he said. He could do nothing, so he completed his trading and sadly began the journey home.

When the merchant returned, he distributed every present. Then the parrot asked, “What did my forest cousins say?”

The merchant hesitated. “One heard your message, shivered, and fell dead. I am sorry I ever spoke.”

His own parrot gave a small cry, shook from beak to tail, and dropped to the floor of the cage. The merchant opened the door in grief and lifted the still bird into his hands. In that instant the parrot sprang up, flew to a high garden wall, and spread its wings in the sunlight.

“So this was the message,” the merchant said, understanding at last.

“Yes,” replied the parrot gently. “My cousin taught without words: sometimes freedom begins when we stop performing the life that keeps us confined.”

The merchant could have been angry, but love spoke more clearly. He opened the courtyard gate. The parrot circled once above his old friend, then flew east toward the green horizon. Its feathers became a small green spark above the rooftops, and the merchant watched until even that spark disappeared.

Only then did he understand that the wild parrot had not died at all. It had sent a wordless lesson across the deserts: become still, and the keeper may open the cage himself. The merchant marveled that one bird’s silence had traveled farther than any shout. From then on, whenever he admired something beautiful, he asked himself whether loving it meant keeping it close—or helping it be free.

Retold from Jalal al-Din Rumi’s thirteenth-century Masnavi, Book I, “The Merchant and his Clever Parrot.” Read the public-domain translation.
script_original:
در شهری پر از باغ و حیاط‌های کاشی‌کاری، بازرگانی زندگی می‌کرد که دوستدار چیزهای زیبا بود. عزیزترین دارایی او طوطی سبزی بود با چشمانی روشن و هوشیار. پرنده در قفسی برنجی می‌زیست، از دست بازرگان پسته می‌خورد و چنان خردمندانه سخن می‌گفت که مهمانان گاهی فراموش می‌کردند با پرنده‌ای حرف می‌زنند.

بهار که رسید، بازرگان برای سفر به هندوستان آماده شد. از اهل خانه پرسید چه سوغاتی می‌خواهند. یکی ابریشم خواست، دیگری چوب صندل و کودکی فیل چوبی رنگ‌شده.

آخر از طوطی پرسید: «برای تو چه بیاورم؟» طوطی گفت: «چیزی نمی‌خواهم. وقتی طوطیان آزاد هندوستان را دیدی، بگو یکی از خویشانشان در قفسی در ایران زندگی می‌کند. بپرس آیا پیامی برایم دارند.»

بازرگان پذیرفت. پس از راهی دراز به جنگلی سبز رسید و پیام را برای گروهی طوطی بازگفت. ناگهان یکی از طوطیان لرزید، از شاخه افتاد و بی‌حرکت بر زمین ماند. بازرگان اندوهگین شد و گفت: «پیام من دل این پرنده را شکست.» سپس کارش را به پایان رساند و به خانه برگشت.

طوطی پرسید: «خویشانم چه گفتند؟» بازرگان با اکراه پاسخ داد: «یکی از آنان پیام تو را شنید، لرزید و مرد.» همان دم طوطی قفسی نیز فریادی کوتاه کشید، لرزید و کف قفس افتاد.

بازرگان با غم در قفس را گشود و پرندهٔ بی‌حرکت را در دست گرفت. ناگهان طوطی برخاست، بر دیوار بلند باغ نشست و بال‌هایش را در آفتاب گشود.

بازرگان گفت: «پس این بود پیام.» طوطی آرام پاسخ داد: «آری. دوستم بی‌واژه به من آموخت که گاهی آزادی زمانی آغاز می‌شود که نقشِ زندگیِ زندان‌ساز را دیگر بازی نکنیم.»

بازرگان می‌توانست خشمگین شود، اما محبت روشن‌تر سخن گفت. دروازه را گشود. طوطی یک بار بر فراز دوست قدیمی‌اش چرخید و به سوی افق سبز پرواز کرد. از آن پس بازرگان هرگاه زیبایی چیزی را می‌دید، از خود می‌پرسید: آیا دوست داشتن یعنی آن را نزدیک خود نگاه داشتن، یا کمک کردن تا آزاد باشد؟

title: Why the Piña Has a Hundred Eyes
subtitle: a Filipino folktale, about a mother’s tired wish and the fruit that remembers it
moral: Granny’s whisper: every old story grows warmer when we listen with care.
script_en:
Once, in a little house beside a wide green garden, lived a mother named Aling Rosa and her daughter, Pinang. Aling Rosa worked from morning until the lamps were lit. Pinang was cheerful and loving, but whenever her mother asked her to find something, she answered, “I cannot see it, Nanay.”

“The broom is beside the door,” her mother would say. Pinang looked at the ceiling, beneath the table, and inside a basket before returning empty-handed. “Where are my sewing scissors?” asked Aling Rosa. They lay bright and silver beside Pinang’s elbow, yet still she said, “I cannot find them.”

One rainy week, Aling Rosa became ill. She rested beneath a woven blanket while Pinang promised to cook rice. “The pot is on the shelf,” her mother called. Pinang searched noisily. “Where is the ladle? Where is the salt? Where are the matches?” Each thing stood in its usual place, but Pinang wanted her tired mother to name every step.

At last Aling Rosa’s head ached from answering. Without thinking, she sighed, “Oh, Pinang, I wish you had a hundred eyes, so you could find what is right in front of you.” The room became quiet. Aling Rosa closed her eyes and slept.

When she woke, the rain had stopped. The rice pot was cold, the kitchen was still, and Pinang was nowhere inside. Aling Rosa called from room to room, then along the road and through the garden. Neighbors helped search. No one found the girl.

Days passed. Aling Rosa recovered, but her heart felt heavy. One morning, while pulling weeds in the garden, she discovered a plant she had never seen. At its center grew a rough golden fruit. All across its skin were small diamond shapes, each one like a watchful eye.

Aling Rosa remembered her impatient wish. She held the strange fruit and whispered her daughter’s name. She cared for the plant tenderly, watering it and keeping insects away. The fruit was sweet when ripe, and its leafy crown stood up like Pinang’s untidy hair.

From then on, Aling Rosa paused before speaking when she was tired, and the neighbors taught their children to search carefully before calling for help. They did not tell the tale to frighten them. They told it so that seeing, listening, and helping could become habits practiced with love.

People began calling it pinya, in memory of Pinang. They told children that eyes are not only for looking; they are for noticing what needs to be done, seeing another person’s weariness, and finding kindness before someone must ask. And parents remembered that words spoken in anger can travel farther than we intend. So when a pineapple appears with its many little eyes, families tell the tale gently and look around together.
script_original:
Noong unang panahon, sa isang munting bahay sa tabi ng malawak at luntiang hardin, nanirahan ang inang si Aling Rosa at ang anak niyang si Pinang. Mula umaga hanggang magsindi ng ilawan ay nagtatrabaho si Aling Rosa. Masayahin at mapagmahal si Pinang, ngunit tuwing may ipinapahanap ang ina, lagi niyang sagot, “Hindi ko po makita, Nanay.”

“Nasa tabi ng pinto ang walis,” sasabihin ng ina. Titingin si Pinang sa kisame, sa ilalim ng mesa, at sa loob ng basket, saka babalik nang walang dala. “Nasaan ang gunting ko?” tanong ni Aling Rosa. Kumikinang iyon sa tabi ng siko ni Pinang, ngunit sasabihin pa rin niya, “Hindi ko po mahanap.”

Isang maulang linggo, nagkasakit si Aling Rosa. Nahiga siya sa ilalim ng hinabing kumot habang nangako si Pinang na magsasaing. “Nasa estante ang palayok,” tawag ng ina. Maingay na naghanap si Pinang. “Nasaan ang sandok? Nasaan ang asin? Nasaan ang posporo?” Nasa dati nilang lugar ang lahat, pero nais ni Pinang na sabihin ng pagod na ina ang bawat hakbang.

Sa wakas, sumakit ang ulo ni Aling Rosa sa kakasagot. Hindi nag-isip, napabuntong-hininga siya. “Naku, Pinang, sana ay magkaroon ka ng isang daang mata para makita mo ang nasa harap mo.” Tumahimik ang silid. Pumikit si Aling Rosa at nakatulog.

Nang magising siya, tumigil na ang ulan. Malamig ang palayok, tahimik ang kusina, at wala si Pinang sa loob ng bahay. Tinawag niya ang anak sa bawat silid, sa daan, at sa buong hardin. Tumulong ang mga kapitbahay sa paghahanap. Walang nakakita sa bata.

Lumipas ang mga araw. Gumaling si Aling Rosa, ngunit mabigat ang kaniyang puso. Isang umaga, habang nagbubunot siya ng damo, napansin niya ang isang halamang hindi pa niya nakita. Sa gitna nito ay may magaspang na dilaw na bunga. Sa balat ay maraming hugis-diyamante, at bawat isa ay parang matang nakamasid.

Naalala ni Aling Rosa ang kaniyang padalus-dalos na hiling. Hinawakan niya ang kakaibang bunga at ibinulong ang pangalan ng anak. Inalagaan niya ang halaman, diniligan ito, at inilayo sa mga kulisap. Nang mahinog, matamis ang bunga, at ang mga dahon sa ibabaw ay nakatayo gaya ng magulong buhok ni Pinang.

Mula noon, humihinga muna nang malalim si Aling Rosa bago magsalita kapag siya ay pagod. Tinuruan din ng mga kapitbahay ang mga anak na tumingin nang mabuti bago humingi ng tulong. Hindi nila ikinuwento ang alamat upang manakot. Ikinuwento nila ito upang maging ugali ang pakikinig, pagmamasid, at pagtulong nang may pagmamahal.

Tinawag ng mga tao ang bunga na pinya bilang alaala kay Pinang. Itinuro nila na ang mga mata ay hindi lamang para tumingin. Ginagamit ang mga ito upang mapansin ang kailangang gawin, makita ang pagod ng ibang tao, at mahanap ang kabutihan bago pa may humingi. Naalala rin ng mga magulang na malayo ang nararating ng salitang nasabi sa galit. Kaya kapag may pinya na maraming munting mata, marahang ikinukuwento ng pamilya ang alamat at sabay-sabay silang tumitingin sa paligid.
alternate_title: Kung Bakit May Isang Daang Mata ang Pinya

title: The Clever Qadi of Baghdad
subtitle: a Baghdad folk tale about careful listening, a disputed purse, and evidence hiding in plain sight
moral: Granny’s whisper: the truth often speaks softly, so a wise listener makes the room quiet.
script_en:
In old Baghdad, when lanterns glowed along the lanes and boats carried dates and spices down the Tigris, there lived a qadi known for listening longer than other people spoke. He did not hurry to display his cleverness. He let a question sit until the truth grew restless.

One morning two neighbors burst into his courtyard, each gripping one end of a leather purse.

“It is mine,” said Hasan, an oil seller. “I dropped it beside my stall.”

“It is mine,” said Karim, a cloth merchant. “I found it near the fountain after counting my coins.”

The purse held forty silver pieces. Neither man had marked them. Each described the same worn buckle, and every witness had arrived only after the shouting began.

The qadi asked Hasan what he had sold that morning. “Olive oil,” he replied. He asked Karim what he had sold. “Blue cloth and white linen.” Then the qadi set the purse on a low table.

“Perhaps the purse remembers,” he said.

The neighbors stared. The qadi asked for a basin of warm water. He emptied the coins into it one by one. At first nothing happened. Then a faint shining circle opened on the surface—one drop, then another, spreading thin as moonlight.

“Oil!” cried Hasan. “You see? The purse is mine.”

Karim folded his arms. “An oil seller touched it just now. That proves nothing.”

“A fair objection,” said the qadi.

He washed the coins, dried them, and asked both men to hold out their hands. Hasan’s fingers were clean because he had scrubbed before entering court. Karim’s fingertips, however, carried a pale blue stain from the cloth he handled. The qadi looked inside the purse’s seams with a small brass lens. There, caught beneath a stitch, lay a single blue thread.

Karim smiled in relief. Hasan shouted, “Cloth could cling to anything in the market!”

“Another fair objection,” said the qadi.

He called Hasan’s young apprentice. “When your master counts money, where does he keep it?”

“In a wooden box beneath the oil jars,” the boy answered. “He never carries a purse. He says purses are easy to lose.”

Then the qadi called Karim’s daughter, who brought the cloth accounts. Beside that morning’s sale was written: forty silver pieces received, placed in the mended leather purse.

The qadi returned the purse to Karim. Hasan lowered his head. He had seen it fall and hoped that shouting first would make the story his.

“You noticed the oil,” Hasan muttered, “but the oil was not enough.”

“One clue is a whisper,” said the qadi. “Two may be a conversation. Truth is safest when several honest things agree.”

Hasan apologized and later paid Karim for the morning he had lost. From then on, whenever neighbors brought a noisy quarrel to the courtyard, the qadi placed warm water on the table. People smiled at the old custom, then remembered to speak carefully—for in Baghdad, even a thread or a drop of oil might be listening.
script_original:
في بغداد القديمة، حين كانت الفوانيس تضيء الأزقة وتحمل القوارب التمر والتوابل في دجلة، عاش قاضٍ عُرف بأنه يستمع أكثر مما يتكلم. لم يكن يتعجل إظهار ذكائه، بل كان يترك السؤال ساكناً حتى يقلق الكذب وتظهر الحقيقة.

في صباحٍ ما دخل جارَان ساحته، وكل واحد منهما يمسك بطرف كيس جلدي. قال حسن بائع الزيت: «الكيس لي، سقط قرب دكاني». وقال كريم بائع القماش: «بل هو لي، فقدته قرب النافورة بعد أن عددت نقودي».

كان في الكيس أربعون درهماً. لم تكن على الدراهم علامة، ووصف الرجلان المشبك القديم نفسه. أما الشهود فلم يصلوا إلا بعد أن بدأ الصياح.

سأل القاضي حسن عمّا باعه في الصباح. قال: «زيت الزيتون». وسأل كريم فقال: «قماشاً أزرق وكتاناً أبيض». ثم وضع القاضي الكيس على مائدة قصيرة وقال: «لعل الكيس يتذكر».

طلب وعاءً من الماء الدافئ، وأسقط الدراهم فيه واحداً واحداً. بعد قليل ظهرت على سطح الماء دوائر رقيقة لامعة. صاح حسن: «زيت! أرأيت؟ الكيس لي!»

قال كريم: «لقد لمسه بائع الزيت الآن. هذا لا يثبت شيئاً». هز القاضي رأسه وقال: «اعتراض عادل».

غسل الدراهم وجففها، ثم طلب من الرجلين أن يمدّا أيديهما. كانت يدا حسن نظيفتين لأنه غسلهما قبل دخول المحكمة. أما أطراف أصابع كريم فكان عليها لون أزرق خفيف. نظر القاضي في خياطة الكيس بعدسة نحاسية صغيرة، فوجد خيطاً أزرق عالقاً تحت غرزة.

ابتسم كريم، لكن حسن قال: «الخيط قد يعلق بأي شيء في السوق!» فقال القاضي: «وهذا اعتراض عادل أيضاً».

استدعى صبيَّ حسن وسأله: «أين يحفظ معلمك نقوده؟» أجاب الصبي: «في صندوق خشبي تحت جرار الزيت. لا يحمل كيساً، ويقول إن الأكياس تضيع».

ثم جاءت ابنة كريم بدفتر الحساب. وفيه كُتب: بيع الصباح، أربعون درهماً، وُضعت في الكيس الجلدي المرقع. أعاد القاضي الكيس إلى كريم. خفض حسن رأسه؛ فقد رآه يسقط وظن أن من يصرخ أولاً يملك الحكاية.

قال القاضي: «الدليل الواحد همسة، والدليلان حديث، وتكون الحقيقة أكثر أماناً حين تتفق أشياء صادقة كثيرة».

اعتذر حسن ودفع لكريم ما خسره من وقت. ومنذ ذلك اليوم، كلما جاء خصمان بصياحٍ عالٍ، وضع القاضي وعاء الماء الدافئ على المائدة. فيبتسم الناس، ثم يتذكرون أن يتكلموا بحذر، ففي بغداد قد يكون خيط صغير أو قطرة زيت شاهداً صامتاً.

title: Sang Thong — The Golden Conch
subtitle: a Thai tale about hidden radiance, clear seeing, and a princess who trusts her own eyes
moral: Granny’s whisper: the truest gold is the goodness someone carries where costumes cannot reach.
script_en:
Long ago in a Thai kingdom, Queen Chantha gave birth not to an ordinary baby but to a shining golden conch. Jealous people whispered that the conch was a bad omen, and the queen was sent away from the palace. Still, she cared for it tenderly, keeping it near while she cooked and swept their small home.

Whenever the queen went to the forest, a little boy stepped from the conch. He washed the bowls, swept the floor, and cooked rice before slipping back inside. One day Chantha returned early and saw him. She embraced her son, Prince Sang Thong, and gently broke the empty shell so he would no longer need to hide.

But danger followed them, and the young prince had to journey alone. Deep in the forest he met a powerful ogress who loved him as her own child. She guarded a well whose water could turn him golden, a pair of flying shoes, and a marvelous disguise: the dark, rough face of Chao Ngo, the Wild Man. When Sang Thong was old enough to seek his path, she gave him these treasures and warned him to keep his true form hidden until a heart wise enough to see it appeared.

In another kingdom, the king invited princes to stand before his seven daughters. Each princess was to throw a garland to the husband she chose. Six garlands fell upon richly dressed men. The youngest princess, Rochana, looked past silk, jewels, and proud smiles. At the edge of the gathering stood Chao Ngo, quiet and awkward in his disguise. Yet Rochana saw a golden radiance around him. She placed her garland upon his shoulders.

The court laughed. Her father, ashamed of her choice, sent the pair to a humble hut and ordered difficult contests, hoping Chao Ngo would fail. First the sons-in-law were told to bring game from the forest. Then they were sent to bring fish from the river. Sang Thong put on his golden form and flying shoes in secret. He asked the creatures for only what was needed and returned with plenty, while the boastful princes came back tired and empty-handed.

At last the kingdom faced a challenge no one else could answer. Sang Thong stepped forward, laid aside the Wild Man’s mask, and revealed the golden prince beneath. Rochana smiled; she had known him all along.

The king bowed his head. He had judged by appearance, while his youngest daughter had judged by character. He welcomed them home and asked forgiveness. Sang Thong honored the queen who bore him, the forest mother who sheltered him, and the princess who truly saw him. And in the palace, children were taught that gold may shine brightly—but clear seeing shines brighter still.

A gentle retelling of Sang Thong (สังข์ทอง), Thailand’s traditional golden-conch tale, preserved in oral performance and in the early nineteenth-century royal drama associated with King Rama II. Story background.
script_original:
นานมาแล้วในอาณาจักรไทยแห่งหนึ่ง พระมเหสีจันทาให้กำเนิดหอยสังข์สีทองแทนทารกธรรมดา ผู้คนที่ริษยากระซิบว่าหอยสังข์เป็นลางร้าย พระนางจึงถูกขับออกจากวัง แต่ยังดูแลหอยสังข์ด้วยความรัก วางไว้ใกล้ตัวเสมอในบ้านหลังเล็ก

ทุกครั้งที่พระมารดาออกไปหาอาหาร เด็กชายคนหนึ่งจะก้าวออกจากหอยสังข์ เขาช่วยกวาดบ้าน ล้างถ้วย และหุงข้าว ก่อนจะกลับเข้าไปซ่อน วันหนึ่งพระนางกลับมาเร็วกว่าปกติและพบความจริง จึงกอดพระโอรสสังข์ทองและทุบเปลือกหอยที่ว่างเปล่า เพื่อไม่ให้ลูกต้องหลบซ่อนอีก

ต่อมาพระสังข์ต้องเดินทางตามลำพัง กลางป่าเขาพบนางยักษ์ผู้มีฤทธิ์ซึ่งรับเลี้ยงเขาเหมือนบุตร นางมอบบ่อเงินบ่อทอง รองเท้าวิเศษ และรูปเงาะป่าผิวคล้ำให้ พร้อมเตือนให้ซ่อนรูปทองไว้จนกว่าจะพบผู้ที่มองเห็นด้วยหัวใจ

ในอีกเมืองหนึ่ง กษัตริย์ให้พระธิดาทั้งเจ็ดเลือกคู่ด้วยพวงมาลัย หกองค์เลือกชายแต่งกายงดงาม แต่นางรจนา พระธิดาองค์เล็ก มองเลยผ้าไหมและเครื่องเพชรไปเห็นรัศมีทองภายในเจ้าเงาะผู้เงียบขรึม นางจึงคล้องพวงมาลัยให้เขา

ผู้คนหัวเราะ พระบิดาทรงละอายและส่งทั้งคู่ไปอยู่กระท่อม แล้วตั้งการทดสอบยาก ๆ ให้บรรดาเขยหาเนื้อจากป่าและหาปลาจากแม่น้ำ พระสังข์แอบถอดรูปเงาะ สวมรูปทองและรองเท้าวิเศษ ขอจากสัตว์เพียงเท่าที่จำเป็น แล้วกลับมาพร้อมอาหาร ส่วนชายที่โอ้อวดกลับมามือเปล่า

เมื่อบ้านเมืองเผชิญปัญหาที่ไม่มีใครแก้ได้ พระสังข์ก้าวออกมา วางหน้ากากเจ้าเงาะ และเผยร่างเจ้าชายทอง นางรจนาทรงยิ้ม เพราะนางรู้มาตลอด
