กษัตริย์ก้มพระพักตร์ ยอมรับว่าตนตัดสินจากรูปลักษณ์ แต่นางรจนาตัดสินจากความดี พระองค์ขออภัยและเชิญทั้งคู่กลับวัง พระสังข์ไม่ลืมพระมารดาผู้ให้กำเนิด แม่ยักษ์ผู้คุ้มครอง และเจ้าหญิงผู้มองเห็นตัวตนที่แท้จริง ตั้งแต่นั้น เด็ก ๆ ในวังจึงได้เรียนว่า ทองส่องแสงสวยงาม แต่สายตาที่เห็นคุณค่าภายในส่องสว่างยิ่งกว่า

title: Sedna — The Woman Who Became the Sea
subtitle: an Inuit story from across Inuit Nunangat, about the sea, respect, and the bonds between people and animals
moral: Granny’s whisper: what we receive from the living world must be met with gratitude.
script_en:
Long ago, when winter lay blue over the land and the sea breathed beneath its blanket of ice, a young woman lived with her father beside the Arctic shore. In different Inuit communities she is known by different names. Tonight, by this fire, we will call her Sedna.

Sedna was quiet and strong-willed. Many hunters came asking her to marry, but she did not wish to leave home. At last a stranger arrived wearing fine skins and promising a warm house, plenty of food, and soft lamps burning through every storm. His words sounded safe, and Sedna agreed to travel with him.

But across the water his promises vanished. His home was a cold nest on a rocky island, and he was not the generous hunter he had claimed to be. He was a storm-bird spirit, and his cries filled the sky. Sedna grew hungry and lonely. When her father heard her sorrow carried over the waves, he came in his small skin boat and took her homeward.

The bird spirit followed. Wings darkened the sky. Wind struck the sea until waves climbed like hills. Fearing that the little boat would overturn, Sedna’s father made a terrible choice: he pushed her into the water. Sedna caught the gunwale with both hands. In panic, he struck her fingers. As they fell into the sea, they changed—first into seals, then walruses, then the great whales who breathe clouds into the winter air.

Sedna sank beneath the waves. Yet the sea did not end her story. She reached the ocean floor, where her lost fingers had become every animal that feeds and clothes the people. There she became the powerful keeper of sea creatures, with long hair drifting in the currents and a lamp glowing in the deep.

When people hunted carelessly, wasted what they were given, or forgot to show thanks, the animals gathered close to Sedna and would not rise. Then an angakkuq, a spiritual helper, journeyed in song to her underwater home. Because Sedna had no fingers, the visitor gently combed the tangles from her hair and listened to her grief. When she felt remembered and respected, she loosened her hair, and seals and whales swam upward once more.

So elders taught that the sea is not a cupboard that never empties. Every animal is a gift, every hunt carries duties, and old hurts must be heard before balance returns. Hunters shared fairly, used what they took, and taught children never to boast over the animals that sustained them. On quiet nights, when the ice creaks and the northern lights fold above the horizon, families still remember the woman beneath the sea—fearsome, generous, wounded, and worthy of respect.
script_original:
ᐊᑯᓂᐅᔪᖅ, ᐅᑭᐅᖅ ᓄᓇᒥ ᑐᙵᕕᖃᖅᑎᓪᓗᒍ, ᓴᓐᓇ ᐊᑖᑕᒥᓂᒃ ᑕᕆᐅᑉ ᓯᒡᔭᖓᓂ ᓄᓇᖃᖅᐳᖅ. ᓴᓐᓇ ᓴᐃᒪᔪᖅ ᓴᙱᔪᕐᓗ ᐃᓅᕗᖅ. ᐊᖑᑏᑦ ᐅᓄᖅᑐᑦ ᓄᓕᐊᕆᔪᒪᔭᖓᑦ, ᑭᓯᐊᓂ ᐊᖏᙱᑦᑐᖅ.

ᐅᓪᓗᖅ ᐃᓚᖓᓂ ᖁᐸᓄᐊᖅ ᐃᓅᙳᐊᖅᓯᒪᔪᖅ ᑎᑭᑉᐳᖅ. ᐅᖃᖅᐳᖅ ᐃᒡᓗᖃᕐᓂᕋᖅᖢᓂ ᓂᕿᖃᕐᓂᕋᖅᖢᓂᓗ. ᓴᓐᓇ ᒪᓕᒃᐳᖅ. ᑭᓯᐊᓂ ᐅᖃᐅᓯᖏᑦ ᓱᓕᙱᑦᑐᑦ. ᕿᑭᖅᑕᒥ ᓂᒡᓚᓱᒃᑐᒥ ᓄᓇᖃᖅᐳᑦ, ᓴᓐᓇᓗ ᑳᒃᐳᖅ ᓄᒫᓱᒃᖢᓂᓗ.

ᐊᑖᑕᖓ ᑐᓴᖅᐳᖅ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᖅᑕᐅᓂᖓᓂᒃ. ᖃᔭᕐᒥᓄᑦ ᐃᑭᖅᖢᓂ ᓴᓐᓇ ᐊᐃᒃᐹ. ᐅᑎᖅᑎᓪᓗᒋᒃ ᖁᐸᓄᐊᖅ ᒪᓕᒃᐳᖅ. ᐊᓄᕆ ᓴᙱᔪᖅ ᐳᓪᓚᖅᐳᖅ, ᑕᕆᐅᕐᓗ ᐱᕐᓗᓕᖅᐳᖅ.

ᓴᓐᓇ ᐃᒪᕐᒧᑦ ᑲᑕᒃᐳᖅ. ᐃᒐᓛᖓᓂᒃ ᑎᒍᒥᐊᖅᐳᖅ. ᐃᓄᒐᖏᑦ ᐃᒪᕐᒧᑦ ᑲᑕᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ, ᓇᑦᑏᑦ, ᐊᐃᕖᑦ, ᐊᕐᕖᓪᓗ ᐆᒪᓂᖃᓕᖅᐳᑦ. ᓴᓐᓇ ᑕᕆᐅᑉ ᐊᑖᓄᑦ ᑭᕕᕗᖅ, ᑕᐃᑲᓂᓗ ᑕᕆᐅᑉ ᐆᒪᔪᖏᓐᓂᒃ ᐸᖅᑭᔨᐅᓕᖅᐳᖅ.

ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᐆᒪᔪᓂᒃ ᐊᑐᕐᓗᒃᐸᑕ ᖁᔭᓕᙱᒃᑯᑎᒡᓗ, ᐆᒪᔪᑦ ᓴᓐᓇᐅᑉ ᓄᔭᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᑲᑎᑉᐳᑦ. ᐊᖓᒃᑯᖅ ᐃᖏᖅᖢᓂ ᐃᒪᐅᑉ ᐊᑖᓄᑦ ᐊᐅᓪᓚᖅᐳᖅ, ᓄᔭᖏᓐᓂᒃ ᐃᓪᓕᕆᐊᖅᑐᖅᖢᓂ. ᓴᓐᓇ ᓈᓚᒃᑕᐅᒐᒥ ᐆᒪᔪᓂᒃ ᐊᓂᑦᑎᕗᖅ.

ᑕᐃᒪᐃᒻᒪᑦ ᑕᕆᐅᖅ ᐃᓱᖃᙱᑦᑐᖅ ᓂᕿᒃᑯᕕᐅᙱᑦᑐᖅ. ᐆᒪᔪᖅ ᐊᑐᓂ ᐃᓅᓯᖃᖅᐳᖅ, ᐃᓄᐃᓪᓗ ᖁᔭᓕᓗᑎᒃ ᐊᑐᖅᑕᕆᐊᖃᖅᐳᑦ. ᓴᓐᓇ ᑕᕆᐅᑉ ᐊᑖᓂ ᐃᖅᑲᐅᒪᔭᐅᕗᖅ—ᓴᙱᔪᖅ, ᑐᓂᓯᓲᖅ, ᐅᐱᒋᔭᐅᔪᕐᓗ.

title: The Shark and the Fisherman
subtitle: a Hawaiian legend, about a fisherman, a guardian shark, and care returned across the sea
moral: Granny’s whisper: care for the ocean, and remember that care may swim back.
script_en:
Long ago on Hawaiʻi, a fisherman paddled his canoe beyond the reef each morning. Before keeping any fish for himself, he placed the first catch back into the sea and said, “For the guardians of these waters.”

One day a large shark rose beside the canoe. Its dark fin cut the surface, but it did not strike. It took the offered fish gently, circled once, and vanished. The next morning it returned. Soon fisherman and shark knew one another’s rhythm: paddle, cast, first fish, quiet circle.

Other fishers warned him. “A shark is a shark.” The fisherman answered, “And the sea is the sea. Both deserve respect.” He never tried to touch or command the animal. He simply gave thanks and took only what his family needed.

Then came a morning when the sky changed too quickly. Wind rushed down from the mountains. Waves rose like dark walls. The canoe’s outrigger cracked, and the fisherman was thrown into the cold, churning water.

He kicked toward the overturned canoe, but the current pulled it away. Salt filled his mouth. Through the foam he saw a fin. The great shark moved beneath him, not with jaws open, but with its broad back rising close.

The fisherman laid one trembling arm across the shark. Steadily it swam, carrying him through the broken water toward the reef. Where the waves might have dashed him against coral, the shark turned and guided him into a calm channel.

People on shore ran into the shallows and pulled the fisherman to safety. Beyond them, the shark circled once. The fisherman lifted his hand in thanks, and the fin slipped under the shining water.

After that, the family taught every child to care for the sea, to waste no catch, and to remember the unseen bonds between an ʻohana and its ʻaumākua, an ancestral guardian. They said respect is not a bargain made for reward. It is a relationship tended day by day — like a canoe, like a net, like the first fish returned to the ocean.
script_original:
I ka wā kahiko ma Hawaiʻi, hoe aku kekahi lawaiʻa ma waho o ke āʻau i kēlā me kēia kakahiaka. Ma mua o kona mālama ʻana i kekahi iʻa, hoʻihoʻi ʻo ia i ka iʻa mua i ke kai me ka ʻōlelo, “No nā kiaʻi o kēia kai.”

I kekahi lā, piʻi mai kekahi manō nui ma ka ʻaoʻao o ka waʻa. ʻAʻole ia i hoʻouka. Lawe mālie ka manō i ka iʻa, kaʻapuni hoʻokahi, a nalowale. Hoʻi mai ia i nā kakahiaka he nui. Ua ʻike ka lawaiʻa a me ka manō i ko lāua ʻano: hoe, hoʻolei ʻupena, iʻa mua, kaʻapuni mālie.

A laila, hoʻololi koke ka lani. Pā mai ka makani mai nā mauna a kū aʻe nā nalu kiʻekiʻe. Haki ka ama, a hāʻule ka lawaiʻa i loko o ke kai anuanu. Huki aku ke au i kona waʻa.

Ma waena o ka huʻa, ʻike ʻo ia i ke kualā o ka manō. ʻAʻole i hāmama kona waha; hoʻokokoke mai kona kua ākea. Kau ka lawaiʻa i kona lima ma luna, a ʻau paʻa ka manō i ke kahakai. Alakaʻi ia iā ia ma kahi mālie o ke āʻau a hiki i ka poʻe o ke kauhale ke huki iā ia i ka palekana.

Kaʻapuni hoʻokahi ka manō. Hāpai ka lawaiʻa i kona lima me ka mahalo, a komo hou ka manō i ke kai. Mai ia lā aku, aʻo ka ʻohana i nā keiki e mālama i ke kai, e hoʻonele ʻole i ka lawaiʻa, a e hoʻomanaʻo i nā pilina me ka ʻaumākua. ʻAʻole he kūʻai ka mahalo; he pilina ia e mālama ʻia i kēlā me kēia lā.
alternate_title: Ka Manō a me ka Lawaiʻa

title: The Sparrows and the Elephant
subtitle: a Panchatantra friendship tale from India, about small allies, wise timing, and strength shared
moral: Granny’s whisper: no friend is too small to matter when every gift has its moment.
script_en:
In an old forest in India, a pair of sparrows built their nest on the broad branch of a tamarind tree. They lined it with soft grass, bits of cotton, and feathers that floated down from the sky. Before long, four pale eggs rested inside.

Each morning the sparrows sang to them. “Grow safely,” whispered the mother bird. “The forest is waiting.”

One hot afternoon, a wild elephant came crashing through the trees. He was not hungry or angry. He was simply careless. Wanting shade, he pushed against the tamarind trunk and snapped the branch. The nest fell. The little eggs broke on the ground.

The sparrows’ grief filled the leaves. Their friend Woodpecker heard them and came at once. “I cannot put the eggs together,” he said softly, “but I will not leave you alone.” He called his friend Bee, whose hum could soothe or distract, and Bee called Frog, who knew every pool and pit in the forest.

“We are tiny beside an elephant,” said the father sparrow.

“Tiny is not the same as powerless,” Frog replied. “We each know one thing well. Let us use those things in the right order.”

The next day they found the elephant resting in the heat. Bee flew close to his ear and hummed the sweetest, dreamiest song. The elephant closed his eyes and swayed, pleased by the music.

That was Woodpecker’s moment. Swift as two falling seeds, he darted forward and pecked at the elephant’s eyelids. The startled elephant stumbled away, unable to see. He trumpeted for water to cool his face.

Now Frog hid beside a deep, dry pit. “Croak, croak,” he called, making his voice sound cool and watery. The elephant followed the sound. Each time he came closer, Frog hopped to the far side and called again. Believing a pond lay ahead, the elephant stepped over the edge and tumbled into the pit.

The friends gathered above. They did not mock him. The mother sparrow spoke: “You broke our home because you believed small lives did not deserve your notice. Remember us.”

The elephant’s anger faded. He understood at last what his carelessness had cost. “I remember,” he said. “If you help me out, my strength will protect nests instead of breaking them.”

The animals brought vines. Elephant climbed free, and he kept his word. After that he walked gently beneath nesting trees, warned the herd away from low branches, and carried water to young saplings in the dry season.

The sparrows built again. Woodpecker shaped the branch, Bee brought fragrant fibers, and Frog sang from below. When the new chicks hatched, even Elephant stood at a respectful distance to hear their first thin peeps. Thus the forest learned that great strength needs careful eyes—and that four small friends, acting together, can teach a lesson no giant should forget.
script_original:
पुरा भारते कस्मिंश्चिद् वने चटकदम्पती तिन्त्रिणीवृक्षस्य शाखायां नीडं निर्मितवन्तौ। तस्मिन् नीडे चत्वारि अण्डानि आसन्। प्रतिदिनं तौ मधुरं गीतं गायन्तौ शिशूनां प्रतीक्षां कुरुतः स्म।

एकस्मिन् उष्णे दिने गजः वनमध्ये शीघ्रं चलन् आगतः। सः क्रुद्धः नासीत्, किन्तु असावधानः आसीत्। छायां प्राप्तुं सः वृक्षं प्राहरत्। शाखा भग्ना, नीडं भूमौ पतितम्, अण्डानि च भग्नानि।

चटकौ दुःखेन रुदितवन्तौ। तयोः मित्रं काष्ठकूटः आगत्य अवदत्, “अण्डानि पुनः कर्तुं न शक्नोमि, किन्तु युवां एकाकिनौ न भविष्यथः।” सः भ्रमरं आह्वयत्, भ्रमरः मण्डूकं च आह्वयत्।

मण्डूकः अवदत्, “वयं लघवः स्मः, परन्तु शक्तिहीनाः न। प्रत्येकस्य विशेषं कौशलम् अस्ति। उचितकाले तत् प्रयुञ्ज्महे।”

अन्यस्मिन् दिने गजः विश्रामं कुर्वन् आसीत्। भ्रमरः तस्य कर्णस्य समीपे मधुरं गुञ्जितवान्। गजः नेत्रे निमीलितवान्। तदा काष्ठकूटः शीघ्रं गत्वा तस्य नेत्रयोः आघातं कृतवान्। गजः द्रष्टुं न शक्तवान्, जलं च अन्विष्टवान्।

मण्डूकः गम्भीरस्य शुष्कगर्तस्य पार्श्वे उपविश्य “टर्र्, टर्र्” इति शब्दं कृतवान्। गजः तत्र सरः अस्ति इति मत्वा शब्दं अनुसृतवान्। सः गर्ते पतितवान्।

चटकी उपरि स्थित्वा अवदत्, “त्वया अस्माकं गृहं भग्नम्, यतः लघुजीवानां मूल्यं त्वं न अजानाः। अस्मान् स्मर।” गजः स्वदोषं ज्ञातवान्। “मां उद्धरत,” सः अवदत्, “मम बलं इतः परं नीडानि रक्षिष्यति।”

मित्राणि लताः आनयन्। गजः बहिः आगत्य प्रतिज्ञां पालितवान्। सः नीडयुक्तवृक्षाणां समीपे शनैः अचलत्, यूथं दूरं नीतवान्, शुष्ककाले वृक्षेभ्यः जलं च आनयत्।

चटकौ पुनः नीडं निर्मितवन्तौ। काष्ठकूटः शाखां सज्जीकृतवान्, भ्रमरः सुगन्धिततन्तून् आनयत्, मण्डूकः अधः गीतं गीतवान्। नवशावकानां प्रथमं शब्दं श्रोतुं गजः अपि दूरात् शान्तः स्थितवान्। एवं वनं ज्ञातवत्—महद् बलं सावधानतां याचते, लघुमित्राणां मैत्री च महत्कार्यं करोति।

title: Stone Soup
subtitle: a folktale from France, about a stone that fed a village
moral: Granny’s whisper: the magic ingredient is always each other.
script_en:
Long ago in a little village in France, there came a tired traveler with nothing in his pockets but a smooth round stone and a good helping of common sense. He was so hungry his stomach was talking to him, so he knocked on the first door. “Please,” he said, “might you spare a little food?” “Nothing here,” said the villager quickly. “We have hardly enough for ourselves.”

He knocked on two more doors, and heard the same song — nothing to spare, nothing at all, times are hard. But the traveler noticed a sack of carrots peeking from a window, and a cabbage tucked under a bench, and he smiled to himself.

So he walked to the middle of the village square, built a small fire, filled a great iron pot with water from the well, and set it to bubbling. Then, out of his pocket, he took the smooth round stone, polished it on his sleeve — polish, polish, polish — and dropped it into the pot with a magnificent plop.

A little girl came by. “What are you making?” she asked. “Stone soup,” said the traveler, tasting the warm water. “A soup made from a magic stone. It is nearly ready — though it would be even better with a carrot or two.” “I might know where a carrot is,” said the little girl, and she ran home and came back with three.

A baker came sniffing. “What is it now?” “Stone soup,” said the traveler, stirring. “It’s coming along nicely. It needs only a cabbage to be fit for a duke.” “A cabbage,” said the baker, thinking of the one under his bench. “Well. I suppose a duke should eat.” And away he fetched it.

And so it went. A farmer brought onions — “for flavor only.” A butcher brought soup bones — “they were going spare.” Somebody’s grandmother brought potatoes, somebody else brought salt, and the kind little girl brought a fistful of parsley, “because everything is better with something green.” Soon everyone in the village was standing around the pot, pretending they had not brought anything at all.

The traveler took out the stone — which looked exactly the same as it had that morning, for stones are steady folk — and set it carefully aside. Then he tasted the soup. “Friends,” he announced, “stone soup is done!” And out came bowls and spoons and loaves of bread, and that hungry village held a feast in the square that went on until the moon came up, with music and dancing besides.

As the traveler went on his way the next morning, the little girl ran after him. “Wait! You never told us the secret of the magic stone!” The traveler smiled and held it out to her. “There is no magic in the stone, little one. The magic was in the village — it simply needed somewhere to gather.” And he walked away down the road, leaving behind a pot, a stone, and a village that never quite managed to be strangers again.
script_original:
Un soir d’hiver, un voyageur arriva dans un village français, les bottes poussiéreuses et le ventre vide. Il frappa aux portes, mais partout on lui répondit qu’il n’y avait rien à partager. Pourtant, derrière les volets, il sentait l’odeur du pain et des oignons.

Le voyageur alla sur la place, remplit une grande marmite d’eau et alluma un feu. De sa poche, il sortit un caillou bien lisse, le lava soigneusement et le plongea dans l’eau. «Que préparez-vous?» demanda un enfant. «Une soupe au caillou, la meilleure du monde.»

Il goûta. «Presque parfaite! Une carotte ferait ressortir le goût du caillou.» L’enfant en apporta deux. Une voisine ajouta un chou, le boulanger un morceau de pain, puis vinrent des pommes de terre, des haricots, du sel et du persil. Chacun n’apporta qu’un peu, mais la soupe devint riche et parfumée.

Bientôt, on dressa des tables sur la place. Quelqu’un joua du violon. Des voisins qui s’étaient à peine parlé mangèrent ensemble sous les étoiles.

Le lendemain, le voyageur retira le caillou propre de la marmite. «Est-il magique?» demanda l’enfant. Il le posa dans sa main. «La magie n’a jamais été dans la pierre.» Après son départ, le village conserva le caillou sur un rebord de fenêtre, pour se rappeler qu’un petit don de chaque maison peut remplir la plus grande marmite.

title: How the Sun and the Moon Came to Live in the Sky
subtitle: a tale from Nigeria, about a generous invitation that outgrew the house
moral: Granny’s whisper: before you say everyone is welcome, dear, count everyone.
script_en:
Long ago, before Sun and Moon lived in the sky, they had a snug house on the earth. Sun was bright and busy, Moon was gentle and silver, and their dearest friend was Water, who lived with all his people in the rivers and sea.

Sun often went to visit Water. They talked beside the riverbank while fish flashed between them and frogs kept time. But Water never came to Sun’s house. At last Sun asked, “My friend, why do you never visit us?” Water replied, “I would gladly come, but my family is very large. Your house could not hold us all.”

“Then I shall build a larger house,” said Sun. Moon measured the rooms. Sun carried beams. Together they made the widest doorway, the tallest roof, and a hall so broad that their voices echoed. When it was finished, Sun hurried to Water. “Come tomorrow,” he said. “Bring everyone.”

The next day came a soft rushing at the door. Water called, “Are you certain it is safe for us to enter?” “Come in!” cried Sun and Moon. Water flowed over the threshold, clear around their ankles. Behind him came silver fish, crabs walking sideways, little turtles, water snakes, and bright river birds.

“There are more outside,” Water warned. “May they enter too?” Sun looked at Moon. Moon looked at the enormous hall. “Of course,” they said, for a promise is a promise. In came more fish, more frogs, and great creatures from the deep. Soon the water reached Sun’s knees.

“Still more are waiting,” said Water. “Shall they come?” Sun and Moon climbed onto their chairs. “Let them come.” Water rose to their waists, then their shoulders. They scrambled onto the table, then up the stairs, while a whale’s back passed through the hall below like a moving island.

At last Sun and Moon sat upon the roof with their feet tucked beneath them. Water lapped at the tiles. “One last time,” called their friend. “May the rest of my people enter?” Sun laughed, because what else could he do. Moon squeezed his hand. “Everyone,” they answered.

The water rolled over the roof, and Sun and Moon rose higher and higher until they reached the sky. There they found plenty of room. Sun made his home in the day, Moon made hers in the night, and Water spread shining over the earth below. And that, people say, is why Sun and Moon still live in the sky — bright hosts who once made room for the whole watery world.
script_original:
Ní ìgbà àtijọ́, kí Oòrùn àti Òṣùpá tó lọ gbé ní ọ̀run, wọ́n ní ilé tó dùn lórí ilẹ̀. Oòrùn máa ń tàn, Òṣùpá sì máa ń rọra bí fàdákà. Ọ̀rẹ́ wọn tó sún mọ́ wọn jù ni Omi, ẹni tó ń gbé pẹ̀lú gbogbo ẹja àti ẹ̀dá inú odò.

Oòrùn máa ń lọ bẹ Omi wò, ṣùgbọ́n Omi kò wá sí ilé wọn rí. Oòrùn béèrè pé, “Ọ̀rẹ́ mi, kí ló dé tí o kò fi wá bẹ wa?” Omi dáhùn pé, “Ẹbí mi pọ̀ gan-an. Ilé yín kò lè gba gbogbo wa.”

Oòrùn àti Òṣùpá kọ́ ilé ńlá kan. Wọ́n ṣe ilẹ̀kùn gbooro, òrùlé ga, àti gbọ̀ngàn tó tóbi. Ní ọjọ́ tí Omi dé, ó béèrè pé, “Ṣé gbogbo wa lè wọlé?” Wọ́n ní, “Ẹ wọlé!” Omi wọlé dé kokosẹ wọn, lẹ́yìn rẹ̀ ni ẹja, akan, ọ̀pọ̀lọpọ̀ àkèré àti ẹyẹ omi.

Àwọn mìíràn tún dúró lóde. Oòrùn àti Òṣùpá mú ìlérí wọn ṣẹ: “Kí gbogbo wọn wọlé.” Omi ga dé eékún, dé èjìká, dé orí. Wọ́n gun àga, gun tábìlì, nikẹyìn wọ́n gun orí òrùlé.

Omi bo ilé náà, Oòrùn àti Òṣùpá sì gòkè lọ sí ọ̀run, níbi tí ààyè pọ̀ sí. Oòrùn ń tàn ní ọ̀sán, Òṣùpá sì ń rìn ní alẹ́, Omi sì tan ká gbogbo ilẹ̀. Ìtàn yìí ń kọ́ wa pé ìlérí àlejò dára, ṣùgbọ́n ẹni tó pè gbogbo ènìyàn gbọ́dọ̀ mọ bí “gbogbo ènìyàn” ṣe pọ̀ tó.
alternate_title: Bí Oòrùn àti Òṣùpá Ṣe Lọ Gbé Ní Ọ̀run

title: Tenali Raman and the Brinjal Curry
subtitle: a beloved Tenali Ramakrishna wit tale from the Telugu storytelling tradition of Andhra Pradesh
moral: Granny’s whisper: a clever answer may escape trouble, but it is wiser not to steal the brinjals.
script_en:
In the days when Krishnadevaraya ruled the Vijayanagara kingdom, a cook served the royal court a curry made from tender purple brinjals grown in the palace garden. Tenali Raman tasted one spoonful, then another. The curry was so good that he spoke of nothing else all the way home.

His wife listened and said, “If the brinjals are truly so delicious, surely you brought one for your family.” Tenali stopped smiling. No one was permitted to take vegetables from the king’s garden. But the thought of that curry had already filled the kitchen. Late that night, Tenali slipped into the garden, picked two ripe brinjals, and hurried home.

His wife cooked them with tamarind, spices, and a little jaggery. Their young son was asleep on the roof terrace, where the night air was cool. “Wake him,” she said. “It would be unkind to eat such a feast without him.” Tenali knew a child might repeat the whole adventure in the morning, but he also knew his wife was right.

He carried a pot of water upstairs and sprinkled it gently over the sleeping boy. “Wake up!” Tenali whispered. “A sudden rain has come. Come inside before you are soaked.” The drowsy child stumbled downstairs, ate the brinjal curry with great pleasure, and went back to sleep believing he had escaped a midnight shower.

At dawn the royal gardener found the missing brinjals. The king’s minister suspected Tenali and questioned him before the court. Tenali calmly denied knowing anything about the garden. “Ask his son,” said the minister. “Children always tell the truth.”

The boy was brought in. “What did you eat last night?” asked the minister. “Brinjal curry,” he answered at once. The court murmured. Then the boy added, “Father woke me because it was raining. My clothes were wet, and we ate inside while the rain fell.”

The minister smiled triumphantly, but the king looked through the open windows at the dry courtyard. Not a drop of rain had fallen for weeks. “The child was dreaming,” the minister said at last, embarrassed. “Then a dream cannot prove a theft,” replied Tenali. The king laughed, for he recognized his poet’s clever hand even when he could not prove where it had been.

Tenali went home with a warning not to let his appetite wander into the royal garden again. His wife saved him the last spoonful of curry. And their son kept insisting that the strangest rainstorm in Vijayanagara had fallen from a perfectly clear sky.

Retold with respect from the long-lived Tenali Ramakrishna oral-story tradition of Andhra Pradesh, in which the sixteenth-century Telugu poet is remembered for wit that exposes pride and untangles trouble.
script_original:
విజయనగర సామ్రాజ్యాన్ని శ్రీకృష్ణదేవరాయలు పాలిస్తున్న రోజుల్లో, రాజభవనంలోని తోటలో పండిన లేత ఊదారంగు వంకాయలతో వంటవాడు రుచికరమైన కూర వండాడు. తెనాలి రామకృష్ణుడు ఒక ముద్ద రుచి చూశాడు, మరొక ముద్ద తిన్నాడు. ఇంటికి చేరేంతవరకు ఆ వంకాయ కూర రుచినే పొగుడుతూ వచ్చాడు.

అతని భార్య విని, “అంత రుచిగా ఉంటే మనకోసం ఒక వంకాయైనా తీసుకురాలేదా?” అని అడిగింది. తెనాలి నవ్వు ఆగిపోయింది. రాజుగారి తోటలోని కూరగాయలను ఎవరూ తీసుకెళ్లకూడదు. అయినా ఆ కూర రుచి మాటల్లోనే ఇంటి వంటగదిని నింపేసింది. ఆ రాత్రి అందరూ నిద్రపోయాక తెనాలి తోటలోకి మెల్లగా వెళ్లి, రెండు పండిన వంకాయలు కోసుకుని ఇంటికి వచ్చాడు.

అతని భార్య చింతపండు, మసాలాలు, కొద్దిగా బెల్లం వేసి వంకాయ కూర వండింది. వారి చిన్న కొడుకు చల్లని గాలి కోసం మేడమీద నిద్రపోతున్నాడు. “బాబును లేపండి,” అంది ఆమె. “ఇంత మంచి కూరను వాడికి పెట్టకుండా మనమే తినడం బాగోదు.” పిల్లవాడు ఉదయం జరిగినదంతా చెప్పేస్తాడేమోనని తెనాలి ఆలోచించాడు. అయినా భార్య మాట సరేననిపించింది.

తెనాలి ఒక చెంబు నీళ్లు తీసుకుని మేడపైకి వెళ్లాడు. నిద్రలో ఉన్న బాబుపై మెల్లగా నీళ్లు చల్లాడు. “లే బాబూ! ఒక్కసారిగా వాన మొదలైంది. తడిసిపోకముందే లోపలికి రా,” అన్నాడు. నిద్రమత్తులో ఉన్న బాలుడు కిందికి వచ్చి వంకాయ కూరను ఆనందంగా తిన్నాడు. ఆపై అర్ధరాత్రి వాన నుంచి తప్పించుకున్నాననుకుంటూ మళ్లీ నిద్రపోయాడు.

తెల్లవారగానే తోటమాలి వంకాయలు కనిపించకపోవడం గమనించాడు. రాజుగారి మంత్రి తెనాలినే అనుమానించి సభలో ప్రశ్నించాడు. తోట విషయం తనకు తెలియదని తెనాలి ప్రశాంతంగా చెప్పాడు. “అతని కొడుకును అడగండి,” అన్నాడు మంత్రి. “పిల్లలు నిజమే చెబుతారు.”

బాలుణ్ని సభకు తీసుకొచ్చారు. “నిన్న రాత్రి ఏం తిన్నావు?” అని మంత్రి అడిగాడు. “వంకాయ కూర,” అని బాలుడు వెంటనే చెప్పాడు. సభలో గుసగుసలు మొదలయ్యాయి. వెంటనే బాలుడు, “వాన పడుతుంటే నాన్న నన్ను లేపారు. నా బట్టలు తడిశాయి. వాన పడుతుండగా మేము ఇంట్లో కూర తిన్నాం,” అన్నాడు.

మంత్రి గెలిచానని చిరునవ్వు నవ్వాడు. కానీ రాజు కిటికీలోంచి ఎండిపోయిన ప్రాంగణాన్ని చూశాడు. ఎన్నో వారాలుగా ఒక్క చినుకూ పడలేదు. “బాలుడు కల కని ఉంటాడు,” అని మంత్రి చివరకు సిగ్గుతో అన్నాడు. “అయితే ఒక కల దొంగతనానికి సాక్ష్యం కాలేదు కదా,” అన్నాడు తెనాలి. తన కవి తెలివి ఇందులో ఉందని రాజుకు అర్థమైంది; ఆయన గట్టిగా నవ్వాడు.

ఇకపై తన ఆకలి రాజుగారి తోటలోకి వెళ్లకుండా చూసుకోమనే హెచ్చరికతో తెనాలి ఇంటికి వచ్చాడు. అతని భార్య చివరి ముద్ద వంకాయ కూరను అతనికోసం దాచింది. వారి కొడుకు మాత్రం నిర్మలమైన ఆకాశం నుంచి విజయనగరంలోనే విచిత్రమైన వాన పడిందని చాలాకాలం చెప్పుకుంటూనే ఉన్నాడు.

ఆంధ్రప్రదేశ్‌లో తరతరాలుగా చెప్పబడుతున్న తెనాలి రామకృష్ణుని జానపద కథల సంప్రదాయం ఆధారంగా గౌరవపూర్వకంగా పునఃకథనం. పదహారవ శతాబ్దపు తెలుగు కవి తెనాలి రామకృష్ణుడు తన చమత్కారం, సమయస్ఫూర్తికి ప్రసిద్ధుడు.

title: The Three Sillies
subtitle: an English folktale, about a mallet in the rafters and worries that have not happened
moral: Granny’s whisper: do not borrow tears from troubles that have not happened.
script_en:
Once in England a young man went to supper with his sweetheart and her parents. The girl went down to the cellar for cider. There, stuck in a beam above the stairs, she saw an old wooden mallet.

“Suppose I marry,” she thought, “and suppose we have a little boy, and suppose he comes for cider, and suppose that mallet falls on his head!” She sat on the step and wept.

Her mother came looking for her. When she heard about the future little boy and the mallet, she sat down and wept too. Then the father came. Soon all three were sobbing beneath the perfectly still mallet.

The young man found them and stared. “I will travel,” he said, “and if I meet three people sillier than you, I shall return and marry your daughter.”

At the first village he saw a woman trying to pull her cow up onto a thatched roof with a rope. “There is lovely grass up there,” she explained. “Would it not be easier to cut the grass and carry it down?” he asked. The woman blinked. That was one.

Next he found a man jumping again and again into his trousers, which stood open on the floor. “It is exhausting,” puffed the man. The traveler showed him how to sit and put in one leg at a time. That was two.

Farther on, people crowded around a pond, dragging rakes through the water. “The moon has fallen in!” they cried, pointing to its reflection. “We must pull it out.” A cloud crossed the sky, the reflection vanished, and everyone cheered. That was three — and perhaps several more.

The young man returned to his sweetheart’s house. The family was still in the cellar, though the mallet had not moved. He took it down and laid it safely on the floor.

“I have seen greater silliness,” he said, “but let us not compete with it.” So they dried their eyes, brought up the cider, and celebrated. Whenever anyone began worrying about a long chain of maybes, the family looked at the old mallet by the hearth — and solved the one real problem first.
script_alternate:
Un jeune Anglais dînait chez sa fiancée et ses parents. La jeune fille descendit chercher du cidre à la cave. Au-dessus de l’escalier, elle vit un vieux maillet coincé dans une poutre. «Si je me marie, si j’ai un fils, s’il vient chercher du cidre et si le maillet lui tombe sur la tête!» Elle s’assit et pleura.

Sa mère la rejoignit, entendit cette longue chaîne de «si», et se mit à pleurer aussi. Puis le père arriva. Bientôt, tous les trois sanglotaient sous le maillet parfaitement immobile.

Le jeune homme les trouva. «Je voyagerai, dit-il. Si je rencontre trois personnes plus sottes que vous, je reviendrai me marier.» Il vit d’abord une femme qui tirait une vache sur un toit pour lui faire manger l’herbe du chaume. Il lui montra qu’on pouvait couper l’herbe et la descendre. Voilà la première.

Il rencontra ensuite un homme qui sautait dans son pantalon posé au sol. Puis des villageois qui fouillaient un étang avec des râteaux, croyant que le reflet de la lune était la lune tombée dans l’eau. Voilà la deuxième, la troisième, et peut-être davantage.

Le jeune homme rentra. La famille pleurait encore. Il décrocha le maillet et le posa par terre. «J’ai vu plus sot, mais ne cherchons pas à gagner le concours.» Ils séchèrent leurs larmes, burent le cidre et fêtèrent les noces. Désormais, lorsqu’une inquiétude bâtissait une tour de peut-être, ils résolvaient d’abord le seul problème réel.
alternate_note: Published as ‘Practice in: Français’ — French practice text for an English tale.

title: Tiddalick the Frog
subtitle: a Gunnai Kurnai Dreaming story, respectfully retold in English from a living oral tradition
moral: Granny’s whisper: every old story grows warmer when we listen with care.
script_en:
In the time when the land and its creatures were finding their ways, Tiddalick was the largest frog anyone had ever seen. He sat beside a bright billabong beneath the gum trees, listening to reeds whisper and dragonflies skim the water. One morning he woke with a thirst that seemed bigger than the whole sky.

Tiddalick bent his head and drank. He drank past the cool shallows, past the lily roots, and past the deep place where fish hid. He drank until the creek stopped singing and the billabong became cracked earth. His round belly swelled like a hill after rain, but not one drop was left outside him.

The animals came from every direction. Kangaroo found no water for her joey. Emu pecked at dry mud. Wombat’s favorite pool was dust. Even the insects grew quiet. “Tiddalick has swallowed all the water,” said wise Owl. “We must make him open his mouth.”

They decided to make the frog laugh. Kookaburra told her funniest story and laughed at every part, but Tiddalick only blinked. Kangaroo bounced backward, tripped over his tail, and landed in a bush. Tiddalick’s cheeks did not move. Emu danced with knees high and wings flapping. Still the frog sat solemn and tight-lipped.

One by one, the animals tried. Wombat rolled downhill like a furry stone. Frill-necked Lizard puffed his collar until it looked like a bright umbrella. Tiddalick stared ahead, holding the water inside.

At last tiny Eel wriggled onto the dry ground. She twisted left, looped right, tied herself in a loose knot, then tried to untie herself while pretending this was exactly what she had planned. A small sound escaped Tiddalick: “Hmph.” Eel wriggled faster, slipped beneath her own tail, and popped upright like a bent twig.

Tiddalick’s eyes widened. His mouth trembled. Then he laughed—a deep, rolling laugh that shook the leaves. Water burst from his mouth in a sparkling rush. It filled the cracks, ran along the creek, and spread through the billabong. Fish flickered again. Kangaroo’s joey drank. Frogs sang all around the shore.

For a while no one spoke. They simply listened to water finding its old pathways. Tiddalick lowered his eyes. He could not put the morning back, but he could choose differently next time. He moved aside so the smallest animals could drink first.

Tiddalick’s belly became small, and his thirst became ordinary. The animals welcomed the water carefully and shared it. This story belongs to a living Aboriginal tradition, carried by people and Country long before it reached printed pages. When it is told, we remember that water is life, greed leaves everyone thirsty, and even the smallest creature may carry the gift that restores the world.
script_alternate:
Acknowledgement: Tiddalick is shared as a Gunnai Kurnai Dreaming story. It comes from a living Aboriginal oral tradition, not from one fixed “original” written script. This second English telling keeps that oral character in mind and invites families to listen for the land, water, animals, and community at the heart of the story.

Listen now. In the old time, when every track and waterway carried a lesson, Tiddalick sat beside the billabong. He was a great frog, broad as a rock and quiet as the shade. One morning a huge thirst woke inside him. He leaned down and began to drink.

He drank the shining edge of the pool. He drank the cool middle. He drank where the reeds grew and where the little fish turned. He drank the creek that fed the billabong. Soon the mud cracked, the reeds bent, and not a single drop remained for anyone else. All the water was held inside Tiddalick’s swollen belly.

Kangaroo came with her joey. Emu came from the plain. Wombat, Kookaburra, Lizard, Owl, Eel, and many smaller creatures gathered. They could not live without water. Owl said, “The water must come out through Tiddalick’s mouth. We will make him laugh.”

Kookaburra began with a story and laughed so loudly that echoes answered from the trees. Tiddalick did not smile. Kangaroo bounced in circles and tumbled into a bush. Tiddalick only blinked. Emu stretched his neck, stamped his feet, and danced until dust rose around him. Still the frog kept his mouth closed.

Wombat rolled. Lizard spread a collar bright as sunrise. The animals tried every silly sound and crooked step they knew. Tiddalick watched, round and serious, while the dry Country waited.

Then Eel moved forward. She was small beside the others, but she had an idea. Across the dust she wriggled, folded, looped, and knotted herself. She pretended to be surprised by her own tail. Tiddalick made one little snorting sound. Eel wriggled again, twisted the wrong way, and sprang straight as a stick.

Tiddalick could hold back no longer. He opened his mouth and laughed. The laugh rolled across the ground, and the water rolled with it. Out it came, filling the creek, soaking the earth, and returning to the billabong. The animals drank, the fish moved, and the frogs began their evening song.

For a quiet moment everyone listened as water found the old creek bed. Tiddalick moved away from the deepest pool and let the smallest creatures drink first. The choice did not erase his greed, but it showed that a lesson can begin with making room.

Tiddalick was no longer enormous. The others did not waste the water they had regained. They shared it and watched over it together. Remember the lesson carried in this telling: water joins every life; taking everything harms the whole community; laughter can loosen what greed has held tight; and a small helper should never be overlooked.

This second English telling keeps that oral character in mind and invites families to listen for the land, water, animals, and community at the heart of the story.

title: Timun Mas — The Golden Cucumber
subtitle: a Javanese tale about courage, good counsel, and four small gifts used at exactly the right time
moral: Granny’s whisper: brave feet run best when a steady mind tells them where to go.
script_en:
In a village in Central Java lived a kind widow called Mbok Srini. She worked carefully, shared what she could, and longed for a child to fill her quiet home with laughter. One evening a giant named Buta Ijo appeared at the edge of the forest and offered her a golden cucumber seed.

“Plant it,” he said. “You will find the child you wish for. But when she is grown, she must come with me.”

Mbok Srini was frightened, yet her longing overcame her caution. She planted the seed. Soon a vine spread across her garden, bearing one cucumber that gleamed like gold. Inside lay a baby girl. Mbok Srini named her Timun Mas—Golden Cucumber—and loved her more with each passing season.

Years went by. Timun Mas grew brave, thoughtful, and quick on her feet. Mbok Srini remembered the promise with dread. When Buta Ijo’s heavy steps shook the ground, she begged for more time. Then she hurried through the forest to seek a wise hermit.

The hermit gave her four small packets: cucumber seeds, needles, salt, and shrimp paste. “Give these to Timun Mas,” he said. “Tell her to be calm and use them one by one.”

When the giant returned, Timun Mas ran. Buta Ijo thundered after her, knocking branches aside. She opened the first packet and scattered cucumber seeds. At once, a wide field of tangled vines sprang up. The giant stopped to tear through them—and to gobble the cucumbers—but soon he was chasing her again.

Timun Mas threw the needles behind her. They became a dense bamboo forest with sharp, towering stems. Buta Ijo pushed through, grumbling as the bamboo snagged his clothes. Still he came on.

Next she cast the salt. The ground rolled into a shining sea. Timun Mas crossed in a small wave, light as a leaf, while the giant splashed and struggled. At last he reached the far shore.

Only one packet remained. Timun Mas breathed slowly and tossed the shrimp paste onto the earth. It became a deep, bubbling marsh. Buta Ijo stepped in and sank to his knees. The more wildly he fought, the deeper the mud held him. Timun Mas did not stop to boast. She kept running until the forest grew quiet behind her.

At sunset she reached home. Mbok Srini held her close and apologized for the promise made in fear and loneliness. Timun Mas forgave her, and together they planted ordinary cucumbers—green, crisp, and meant only for sharing.

From then on, Mbok Srini made no bargains with shadows, and Timun Mas kept the empty packets as a reminder: courage is not having no fear. It is carrying good counsel, choosing the right moment, and taking the next sure step toward home.

Retold from Timun Mas, a traditional Javanese folktale associated with Central Java. Story background and traditional variants.
script_alternate:
Di sebuah desa di Jawa Tengah tinggallah seorang janda baik hati bernama Mbok Srini. Ia rajin bekerja dan suka berbagi, tetapi sangat merindukan seorang anak. Suatu petang raksasa Buta Ijo muncul di tepi hutan dan memberinya sebutir benih mentimun emas.

“Tanamlah benih ini,” katanya. “Kau akan memperoleh anak yang kau dambakan. Namun ketika ia dewasa, ia harus ikut denganku.” Karena sangat berharap, Mbok Srini menyetujuinya. Dari benih itu tumbuh sebuah mentimun berkilau seperti emas, dan di dalamnya terdapat bayi perempuan. Ia menamainya Timun Mas.

Tahun-tahun berlalu. Timun Mas tumbuh menjadi gadis yang berani, bijaksana, dan lincah. Mbok Srini semakin takut mengingat janjinya. Ketika langkah Buta Ijo mengguncang tanah, ia meminta waktu lalu pergi menemui seorang pertapa.

Pertapa itu memberikan empat bungkusan kecil: biji mentimun, jarum, garam, dan terasi. “Berikan kepada Timun Mas,” pesannya. “Suruh ia tetap tenang dan menggunakannya satu per satu.”

Saat Buta Ijo datang lagi, Timun Mas berlari. Raksasa itu mengejarnya sambil menyingkirkan dahan-dahan. Timun Mas menabur biji mentimun. Seketika tumbuh ladang luas penuh sulur. Buta Ijo berhenti untuk menerobos dan memakan mentimun, tetapi kemudian kembali mengejar.

Timun Mas melempar jarum. Jarum berubah menjadi hutan bambu yang rapat dan tajam. Buta Ijo menerobos sambil menggerutu. Lalu Timun Mas menabur garam. Tanah berubah menjadi lautan berkilau. Ia menyeberang seringan daun, sedangkan raksasa itu berenang dengan susah payah.

Tinggal satu bungkusan. Timun Mas menarik napas dan melemparkan terasi. Tanah menjadi rawa yang dalam dan mendidih. Buta Ijo terperosok sampai lutut; semakin keras ia meronta, semakin dalam lumpur menahannya. Timun Mas tidak berhenti untuk menyombongkan diri. Ia terus berlari hingga hutan kembali sunyi.

Saat matahari terbenam, Timun Mas tiba di rumah. Mbok Srini memeluknya dan meminta maaf atas janji yang dibuat dalam ketakutan dan kesepian. Timun Mas memaafkannya. Bersama-sama mereka menanam mentimun biasa untuk dibagikan. Timun Mas menyimpan bungkusan kosong sebagai pengingat: keberanian bukan berarti tidak takut, melainkan mendengarkan nasihat baik dan mengambil langkah yang tepat menuju rumah.
alternate_note: Published Bahasa Indonesia text for a Javanese folktale.

title: Why the Turtle’s Shell Is Cracked
subtitle: a folktale from Nigeria, about a sky-feast and a very hard landing
moral: Granny’s whisper: a clever tongue will not fly you home.
script_en:
Long ago in Nigeria, in the time when birds and beasts talked together like neighbors, there lived a turtle who was very clever and very fond of good food.

One season a great hunger came over the land. The yams dried up, the rivers ran low, and every creature grew thin. Every creature, that is, except the birds, who stayed round and glossy. Turtle could not understand it, until his friend Parrot let the secret slip: the birds had been invited to a great feast, high up in the sky, in the land above the clouds.

“A feast!” cried Turtle. “Take me with you!” “You?” laughed Parrot. “You have no wings.”

But Turtle would not give up. At last the birds took pity on him, and each bird gave him one feather, until Turtle had two grand wings of every color: red from Parrot, blue from Kingfisher, grey from Dove. He practiced flapping, and on the day of the feast, up they all flew together, into the clouds.

On the way, clever Turtle made a speech. “Friends,” he said, “when important people visit the sky, they take new names. My new name shall be All of You.” The birds chuckled, and agreed to take names as well.

When they arrived, the hosts of the sky brought out dish after dish: pepper soup, roasted yams, sweet palm wine. And before anyone could taste a bite, the hosts said, “This feast is for all of you.”

Turtle raised a claw. “You heard them. For whom is this feast?” “For all of you,” chorused the birds politely. “And I am All of You,” said Turtle, and down he sat and ate the very best of every dish, while the birds picked at the crumbs he left. The birds grew angrier and angrier.

When the feast ended, each bird flew to Turtle and, without a word, took back its feather. Then one by one they all flew home, leaving Turtle standing on a cloud with empty claws, a very full stomach, and no wings at all.

“Parrot!” called Turtle. “Fly to my wife! Tell her to spread every soft thing in the house under the sky, so I can jump down!”

Now Parrot was still very cross. So instead he flew down and told Turtle’s wife, “Bring out every hard thing in the house: the hoes, the stones, the pots, and pile them up below!” Which she did.

Turtle looked down, saw something piled up, and assumed the best. He jumped. Down, down, down he tumbled, and crash! He landed on the pile of hard things, and his beautiful smooth shell broke into pieces.

The medicine man glued it back together as best he could, but the shell was never smooth again. And that is why, to this day, every turtle carries a shell of patches and cracks. A reminder, the grandmothers say, that a clever tongue may win you a dinner, but it will not fly you home.
script_original:
N’oge gara aga, Mbe bụ onye aghụghọ ma na-achọkarị ihe karịa nke ya. Otu ụbọchị, nnụnụ gwara ya na a ga-enwe nnukwu oriri n’eluigwe. Mbe enweghị nku, ya mere ọ rịọrọ nnụnụ ọ bụla ka o nye ya otu nku. Ha kwenyere, mee ya nku abụọ mara mma, ma ha dọrọ ya aka ná ntị ka ọ ghara ime aghụghọ.

Tupu ha efega, Mbe kwuru ka onye ọ bụla họrọ aha ọhụrụ maka oriri ahụ. Ya onwe ya họrọ aha “Unu Niile.” Mgbe ha rutere n’eluigwe, ndị ọbịa kwuru, “Nri a bụ maka unu niile.” Mbe biliri ozugbo sị, “Aha m bụ Unu Niile; ya mere nri niile bụ nke m.” Ọ rie nke kacha mma, hapụrụ naanị ntakịrị maka nnụnụ ndị nyere ya aka.

Nnụnụ were iwe. Otu otu, ha weghachiri nku ha. Mbe enweghịzi ụzọ isi laghachi n’ala. Ọ gwara otu nnụnụ ka ọ gwa nwunye ya ka o dobe ihe dị nro n’ala, ka ọ daba n’elu ya. Ma nnụnụ ahụ gwara nwunye Mbe ka o dobe nkume na ite siri ike.

Mbe si n’eluigwe daa. Ọkpụkpụ ya kụrụ nkume ma gbawaa n’ọtụtụ ebe. Nwunye ya kpọrọ ndị na-agwọ ihe, ha jikọtara iberibe ya ọnụ. Mbe lanarịrị, ma akara mgbawa ahụ nọgidere n’ọkpụkpụ ya.

Ọ bụ ya mere, ka ndị nne ochie na-ekwu, ọkpụkpụ mbe ji nwee ọtụtụ ahịrị. Ha na-echetara anyị na amamihe na-enweghị obiọma na-aghọ aghụghọ, nakwa na onye na-eji onyinye ndị enyi ya emegbu ha nwere ike ịla n’ụlọ naanị ya.
alternate_title: Ihe Mere Mbe Ji Nwee Mgbawa n’Ọkpụkpụ Ya

title: Vasilisa the Brave
subtitle: a Russian wonder tale, about a little doll, a dark forest, and courage that listens
moral: Granny’s whisper: courage often speaks in a very small voice.
script_en:
Once, in a village at the edge of a deep Russian forest, lived a girl named Vasilisa. Before her mother died, she gave Vasilisa a tiny wooden doll. “Keep her hidden,” her mother said. “When trouble comes, give her a crumb to eat and ask her advice.”

Vasilisa’s father later married a proud woman with two daughters. They gave Vasilisa the hardest work, yet every task was finished by morning, for at night the little doll ate her crumb and whispered what to do.

One autumn evening, the stepmother put out every flame in the house. “There is no fire,” she said. “Go to Baba Yaga in the forest and ask for a light.” Everyone knew Baba Yaga was a fearsome witch, but Vasilisa wrapped bread in her kerchief, slipped the doll into her pocket, and went.

The forest grew black. A rider dressed in white passed, and dawn glimmered. A rider in red passed, and the sun rose. At last a rider in black passed, and night fell. Then Vasilisa saw a fence of bones and, behind it, a hut standing on chicken legs.

Baba Yaga flew down in a great mortar, sweeping away her tracks. “I smell a human child!” she cried. Vasilisa bowed. “My family sent me to ask for fire.” The witch narrowed her eyes. “Work for me, and perhaps you shall have it.”

She ordered Vasilisa to sort poppy seeds from dust, wash a mountain of cloth, cook supper, and clean the whole yard before dawn. When Baba Yaga slept, Vasilisa fed the doll. “Do not fear,” whispered the doll. “Rest, and morning will help us.” By sunrise every task was done.

The witch returned and grumbled. “Who helps you?” Vasilisa answered carefully, “My mother’s blessing.” Baba Yaga shuddered. “No blessings in my house! Take your fire and go!” She thrust a glowing skull-lantern onto a stick and pushed Vasilisa through the gate.

All the way home the skull lit the safe path. When Vasilisa arrived, its fierce light drove every cruel shadow from the house. Afterward Vasilisa went to live with a kind old woman in town. With the doll’s guidance and her own patient hands, she wove cloth so fine it reached the palace, where her skill and honest heart brought her a joyful new life.

And Vasilisa kept the tiny doll all her days — not because brave people never feel afraid, but because the bravest know when to listen to love carried quietly beside them.
script_original:
Жила-была у края тёмного русского леса девочка Василиса. Перед смертью мать подарила ей маленькую деревянную куколку. «Береги её, — сказала мать. — Когда придёт беда, дай ей крошку хлеба и спроси совета».

Отец Василисы женился снова. Мачеха и её дочери заставляли девочку выполнять самую тяжёлую работу. Но ночью куколка съедала крошку и тихо подсказывала, что делать, и к утру всё было готово.

Однажды мачеха погасила в доме огонь и послала Василису за пламенем к Бабе-яге. Девочка взяла хлеб, спрятала куколку и вошла в лес. Она увидела белого всадника — рассвело; красного — взошло солнце; чёрного — наступила ночь. Наконец показалась избушка на курьих ножках, окружённая забором из костей.

Баба-яга велела до утра перебрать зёрна, выстирать гору белья, сварить ужин и убрать двор. Василиса накормила куколку. «Не бойся, отдыхай», — прошептала та. К рассвету вся работа была сделана.

«Кто тебе помогает?» — спросила ведьма. «Материнское благословение», — честно ответила Василиса. Баба-яга испугалась: «Не нужны мне благословения!» Она дала девочке светящийся череп на палке и вытолкнула за ворота.

Огонь осветил Василисе дорогу домой и прогнал злые тени из её жизни. Позже она поселилась у доброй старушки и стала прекрасной ткачихой. Куколка оставалась с ней всегда — не потому, что храбрые никогда не боятся, а потому, что настоящая храбрость умеет слушать тихий голос любви.

title: The Lion and the Clever Rabbit
subtitle: a wisdom tale from the Panchatantra of India, about a roar and its echo
moral: Granny’s whisper: the quiet ones are doing the thinking.
script_en:
Long ago in a forest in India there lived a lion who was strong and fierce, and terribly, terribly greedy. Every day he killed more animals than he could ever eat, just for the joy of killing. The animals gathered and held a meeting, and at last they went to the lion with a plan.

“Great king,” they said, bowing low, “hunting must be so exhausting. Let us make it easy for you. Every day, one of us will come to your cave at noon, all by himself, and you shall eat him without lifting a paw.” The lion liked this very much. “An excellent arrangement,” he said. “But mind you keep your promise, or I shall eat you all at once.”

And so, each day, one animal went to the lion’s cave, and the forest lived in fear, counting the days.

At last it was the turn of a small rabbit. The little rabbit sat and thought, and thought, and then he smiled, for cleverness is worth more than claws. He hopped slowly to the lion’s cave, arriving long past noon.

The lion was furious. “You are late! And you are no bigger than a mouthful! Where have you been?”

The rabbit bowed so low his ears touched the ground. “Forgive me, great king. Five rabbits set out this morning, but on the way we met another lion, who said that he was king of this forest, and that you were nothing but a house cat. He ate our four brothers. I begged him to let me go, so I could tell you what he said.”

The lion roared so loudly the leaves trembled. “Another lion? In my forest? Take me to him at once!”

“Follow me,” said the rabbit, and he led the lion all the way to an old well with stone walls. “He lives down there. Be careful, great king. He is fierce.”

The lion crept to the edge of the well and looked down. There, in the dark water, he saw a lion looking back at him, for still water shows every creature its own face. He opened his mouth to roar, and the lion in the well opened his mouth too. He roared with all his might, and the sound came echoing back, as if the other lion were roaring louder.

That was too much. The lion leaped into the well to tear his enemy to pieces, and down he went with a mighty splash. And he never came out again.

The little rabbit hopped home, and when the animals heard what he had done, they danced around him until the moon came up. And that is why the grandmothers say: you do not need to be the biggest creature in the forest. You only need to be the one who thinks.
script_alternate:
बहुत समय पहले भारत के एक जंगल में एक शक्तिशाली और लालची सिंह रहता था। वह रोज़ ज़रूरत से अधिक जानवर मारता। डरे हुए पशुओं ने उससे कहा, “महाराज, हम प्रतिदिन स्वयं एक जानवर आपके भोजन के लिए भेजेंगे। कृपया बाकी जंगल को चैन से रहने दें।” सिंह मान गया, पर उसने देर होने पर सबको खाने की धमकी दी।

एक दिन एक छोटे खरगोश की बारी आई। वह रास्ते में सोचता रहा और जान-बूझकर दोपहर के बहुत बाद सिंह की गुफा पहुँचा। भूखा सिंह गरजा, “तुम इतने देर से क्यों आए? और तुम तो एक कौर से भी छोटे हो!”

खरगोश ने झुककर कहा, “महाराज, हम पाँच खरगोश चले थे। रास्ते में दूसरे सिंह ने हमें रोका। उसने कहा कि वही इस जंगल का राजा है। उसने चार को खा लिया और मुझे आपको चुनौती देने भेजा।” यह सुनते ही सिंह क्रोध से काँप उठा। “मुझे अभी उसके पास ले चलो!”

खरगोश उसे एक पुराने गहरे कुएँ तक ले गया। “वह नीचे छिपा है,” उसने कहा। सिंह ने पानी में झाँका और अपना ही प्रतिबिंब देखा। वह गरजा, तो कुएँ से उसकी गूँज वापस आई। सिंह समझा कि दूसरा सिंह उसे ललकार रहा है। वह उसे पकड़ने के लिए कुएँ में कूद पड़ा और फिर बाहर न आया।

छोटा खरगोश जंगल लौट आया। सभी पशु आनंद से नाचे। तभी से बुज़ुर्ग कहते हैं: जंगल में सबसे बड़ा होना आवश्यक नहीं; कठिन समय में शांत मन से सोचना ही सच्ची शक्ति है।

title: The Wonderful Birch
subtitle: a folktale from Finland, about a wish spoken to a birch stump
moral: Granny’s whisper: a loving promise can take root in the most unexpected place.
script_en:
Long ago, in a little village at the edge of Finland's great northern forest, there lived a kind woman who had everything she needed except the one thing her heart wanted most: a child of her own.

One spring morning she walked out to the meadow, where an old birch stump stood silver in the sun. She laid her hand upon it and whispered, “If only I had a daughter — even if she were no more than a birch tree, I would love her.”

The forest was listening.

Before the summer ended, a daughter came to her — a little girl with skin as pale as birch bark and hair that shone like new leaves in sunlight. The woman named her Koivunen, “little birch,” and loved her more than words can tell.

Koivunen grew gentle and bright, and every day she drove the family's cows out to the meadow, singing as she went, while the white birches bent above her like tall, kind grandmothers.

But deep in the woods lived an old noita, a wise-woman of the wilds whose heart had grown hard and envious. One evening she watched the girl singing among the cows, and jealousy rose in her like cold water in a well.

The next morning, when Koivunen came to the meadow, the noita was waiting. With a wave of her staff she turned the girl into a slender silver birch, and in her place she set her own sullen daughter, bidding her drive the cows and say nothing.

The mother soon knew something was wrong — this girl did not sing, and her eyes were cold. But she could not prove what her heart felt, and she wept quietly at night.

Now, a young shepherd from the village often cut firewood at the meadow's edge. One winter day he noticed the slenderest birch weeping bright drops of sap, though the air was freezing. “Poor tree,” he said, and he cut one small splinter from its side to carve a spindle for his mother — no more than the tree could spare.

That night something strange happened. When the boy woke, the spindle was finished — carved smooth and fine — though he had barely begun it. The next night it was the same: his work done for him while he slept, the cottage swept, the porridge warm.

On the third night he only pretended to sleep. At midnight, by moonlight, he saw a maiden step out of the wood of the spindle — pale as birch bark, hair like new leaves — and take up his tools with gentle hands.

“Who are you?” he whispered.

She told him everything: the wish, the noita, the birch. “The spell can only be broken,” she said, “if one who loves me holds my hand until the sun rises, and does not let go.”

The boy took her hand in his. All night he held it — through the hooting of owls and the sighing of the wind — and when the first light touched the meadow, the wood softened, and Koivunen stood before him, whole and laughing and crying all at once.

The noita's spell was broken. The sullen false daughter fled back to the woods, and the old noita, her power spent, was never seen again.

Koivunen ran home to her mother, and there was such rejoicing in the little village that the cows lowed and the birches rustled. In time she married the shepherd boy, and they lived kindly all their days.

And the people of Finland say that to this day, when the wind moves through the birch trees on a summer evening, you can hear them whispering her name.
script_original:
Kauan sitten pienessä kylässä Suomen suuren pohjoisen metsän laidalla asui lempeä nainen. Hänellä oli kaikki tarpeellinen, paitsi se, mitä hänen sydämensä eniten kaipasi: oma lapsi.

Eräänä kevätaamuna hän käveli niitylle, jossa vanha koivunkanto hohti hopeisena auringossa. Hän laski kätensä sen päälle ja kuiskasi: ”Kunpa minulla olisi tytär — vaikka hän olisi vain koivupuu, rakastaisin häntä.”

Metsä kuunteli.

Ennen kesän loppua nainen sai tyttären. Tytön iho oli vaalea kuin koivun tuohi ja hiukset kiilsivät kuin uudet lehdet auringossa. Nainen antoi hänelle nimeksi Koivunen, pieni koivu, ja rakasti häntä enemmän kuin sanoin voi kertoa.

Koivusesta kasvoi lempeä ja valoisa tyttö. Joka päivä hän ajoi perheen lehmät niitylle ja lauloi kulkiessaan. Valkoiset koivut kumartuivat hänen ylleen kuin pitkät, ystävälliset isoäidit.

Syvällä metsässä asui kuitenkin vanha noita, erämaan tietäjänainen, jonka sydän oli kovettunut ja tullut kateelliseksi. Eräänä iltana hän näki tytön laulavan lehmien keskellä, ja kateus nousi hänessä kuin kylmä vesi kaivossa.

Seuraavana aamuna noita odotti niityllä. Hän heilautti sauvaansa ja muutti Koivusen hoikaksi hopeakoivuksi. Tytön paikalle hän lähetti oman synkän tyttärensä ja käski tämän paimentaa lehmiä ja pysyä vaiti.

Äiti huomasi pian, että jokin oli vialla. Tämä tyttö ei laulanut, ja hänen katseensa oli kylmä. Äiti ei pystynyt todistamaan sitä, minkä sydämessään tiesi, ja siksi hän itki hiljaa öisin.

Kylän nuori paimen hakkasi usein polttopuita niityn reunalla. Eräänä talvipäivänä hän huomasi kaikkein hoikimman koivun vuodattavan kirkkaita mahlapisaroita, vaikka ilma oli jääkylmä. ”Voi sinua, puuparka”, hän sanoi. Hän leikkasi kyljestä vain pienen säleen, ei enempää kuin puu saattoi antaa, ja aikoi veistää siitä äidilleen värttinän.

Yöllä tapahtui kummia. Kun poika heräsi, värttinä oli valmis, sileäksi ja kauniiksi veistetty, vaikka hän oli tuskin aloittanut. Seuraavana yönä kävi samoin: työ valmistui hänen nukkuessaan, tupa lakaistiin ja puuro odotti lämpimänä.

Kolmantena yönä poika vain teeskenteli nukkuvansa. Keskiyöllä hän näki kuunvalossa neidon astuvan esiin värttinän puusta. Neito oli vaalea kuin koivun tuohi, hänen hiuksensa olivat kuin uudet lehdet, ja hän tarttui työkaluihin hellin käsin.

”Kuka sinä olet?” poika kuiskasi.

Neito kertoi hänelle kaiken: äidin toiveen, noidan ja koivun. ”Loitsu murtuu vain, jos joku, joka rakastaa minua, pitää kädestäni auringonnousuun asti eikä päästä irti.”

Poika otti hänen kätensä omaansa. Hän piti siitä kiinni koko yön pöllöjen huhuilun ja tuulen huokausten halki. Kun ensimmäinen valo kosketti niittyä, puu pehmeni, ja Koivunen seisoi hänen edessään kokonaisena, nauraen ja itkien yhtä aikaa.

Noidan loitsu oli murtunut. Synkkä valetytär pakeni takaisin metsään, eikä voimansa menettänyttä noitaa enää koskaan nähty.

Koivunen juoksi kotiin äitinsä luo. Pienessä kylässä riemuittiin niin suuresti, että lehmät ammuivat ja koivut humisivat. Aikanaan Koivunen meni naimisiin nuoren paimenen kanssa, ja he elivät lempeästi kaikki päivänsä.

Suomessa kerrotaan yhä, että kun tuuli liikuttaa koivuja kesäiltana, niiden voi kuulla kuiskaavan Koivusen nimeä.

title: The Mitten
subtitle: a Ukrainian winter tale about hospitality, patience, and making room
moral: Granny’s whisper: A little warmth grows larger each time it is shared.
script_en:
On the coldest morning of winter, an old grandfather walked through the forest with his dog trotting behind him. Snow rested on the pine branches, the path shone blue in the early light, and each breath rose like a little cloud. As the grandfather reached into his pocket for a handkerchief, one warm red mitten slipped from his belt and fell beside the path. He did not notice. The dog did not notice either, and soon their footprints disappeared among the trees.

A tiny mouse found the mitten first. She circled it, touched the soft wool, and peeked inside. “A house with no door and no owner,” she whispered. “May I call it home?” She wriggled into the thumb, curled her tail around herself, and was soon wonderfully warm.

Before long, a frog came hopping through the snow. “Who lives in this mitten?” he called. “I do—the little mouse. And who are you?” “A frog with very cold feet. Is there room for one more?” The mouse shifted closer to the thumb. “Come in, if you enter gently.” The frog tucked himself beside her.

Then came a hare, whose long ears were pink with cold. After the hare came a fox with a snowy brush of a tail. After the fox came a gray wolf, quiet as moonlight. Each one asked, “Who lives in this mitten?” Each time the animals named themselves, then paused before saying, “Come in, but mind your elbows, paws, and tail.” The mitten stretched wider and rounder, yet its red stitches held.

Last came a wild boar, snuffling a path through the drifts. The mitten rose and fell as everyone made room. “There cannot be space,” said the wolf. “There is a little,” said the mouse, “if kindness sits close.” So the boar squeezed inside, and seven warm breaths misted the wool.

Just then a bear lumbered from the birches. “Who lives in this mitten?” he rumbled. The animals answered from smallest to largest. The bear sighed. “I have walked all night. Might I rest one paw inside?” The mouse considered the seams. “One paw, then. Slowly.” But when the bear felt that lovely warmth, his nose followed, then his shoulders, then all of him. The mitten swelled as big as a haystack. One stitch gave a tiny squeak.

Far down the path, the grandfather felt the wind on his bare hand. “My mitten!” he cried, and turned back. His dog ran ahead, nose low to the snow. Soon the dog saw the enormous red shape trembling beside the path and barked in astonishment.

Out sprang the mouse, the frog, the hare, the fox, the wolf, the boar, and the bear—each in such a hurry that the snow flew like feathers. They vanished safely among the trees. The mitten shrank to its ordinary size, though it was rather rumpled and one seam had opened.

The grandfather picked it up and smiled at the many tracks around it. That evening, his grandchild darned the loose seam with strong red thread. From then on, the grandfather tied both mittens to a cord. And whenever winter pressed hard against the windows, the family remembered the little woolen house that had held an entire forest because everyone had made just a little more room.

This original retelling follows the Ukrainian cumulative folktale Рукавичка, recorded in nineteenth-century folklore collections.
script_original:
Найхолоднішого зимового ранку дід ішов лісом, а позаду біг його пес. Сніг лежав на соснових гілках, стежка синіла в ранковому світлі, і кожен подих здіймався маленькою хмаркою. Коли дід поліз до кишені по хустинку, одна тепла червона рукавичка зісковзнула з пояса й упала край стежки. Дід не помітив. Пес теж не помітив, і незабаром їхні сліди зникли поміж дерев.

Першою рукавичку знайшла маленька мишка. Вона обійшла її навколо, торкнулася м’якої вовни й зазирнула всередину. «Хатка без дверей і без господаря, — прошепотіла вона. — Чи можна мені тут оселитися?» Мишка вмостилася у великому пальці, обгорнула себе хвостиком і відразу зігрілася.

Незабаром по снігу прискакала жабка. «Хто-хто в цій рукавичці живе?» — запитала вона. «Я, мишка-шкряботушка. А ти хто?» — «Жабка-скрекотушка з дуже холодними лапками. Чи знайдеться місце ще для однієї?» Мишка посунулася. «Заходь, тільки обережно». І жабка примостилася поруч.

Потім прибіг зайчик із почервонілими від холоду вухами. За зайчиком прийшла лисичка з пухнастим засніженим хвостом. За лисичкою — сірий вовк, тихий, мов місячне світло. Кожен питав: «Хто-хто в цій рукавичці живе?» Звірі називали себе й казали: «Заходь, тільки бережи наші лапи, боки та хвости». Рукавичка розтягувалася дедалі ширше, але червоні стібки трималися.

Останнім прийшов дикий кабан, прокладаючи рилом стежку в заметах. Усі посунулися. «Місця вже немає», — сказав вовк. «Трошки є, — відповіла мишка, — якщо доброта сяде тісненько». Кабан утиснувся всередину, і сім теплих подихів огорнули вовну парою.

Тут із березняка вийшов ведмідь. «Хто-хто в цій рукавичці живе?» — загуркотів він. Звірі відповіли від найменшого до найбільшого. Ведмідь зітхнув: «Я йшов усю ніч. Чи можна хоч одну лапу погріти?» Мишка глянула на шви. «Одну лапу. І повільно». Та за лапою потягнувся ніс, за носом — плечі, а тоді й увесь ведмідь. Рукавичка роздулася завбільшки зі стіг сіна, і один стібок тихенько пискнув.

Тим часом дід відчув холод на голій руці. «Моя рукавичка!» — вигукнув він і повернув назад. Пес побіг попереду, принюхуючись до снігу. Побачивши величезну червону грудку біля стежки, він здивовано загавкав.

Вискочили мишка, жабка, зайчик, лисичка, вовк, кабан і ведмідь — так швидко, що сніг злетів угору, мов пір’я. Усі щасливо сховалися між деревами. Рукавичка знову стала звичайною, тільки трохи пом’ятою, а один шов розійшовся.

Дід підняв її й усміхнувся, побачивши довкола безліч слідів. Увечері онука заштопала шов міцною червоною ниткою. Відтоді дід прив’язував обидві рукавички до шнурка. А коли зима тулилася до вікон, родина згадувала маленьку вовняну хатку, що вмістила цілий ліс, бо кожен посунувся ще трішечки.

title: The Fairy in the House
subtitle: a Basque lamia tale about welcome, gratitude, and the price of an unkind farewell
moral: Granny’s whisper: Some blessings arrive quietly, and leave when kindness does.
script_en:
In a white farmhouse among the green Basque hills lived a woman who spun flax beside the fire each evening. Her wheel whispered chirrin, chirrin while rain tapped the shutters and her husband stacked the last logs for the night. Their pantry was modest, but there was bread on the board, a little ham hanging from a beam, and peace beneath the roof.

One evening, just as the spindle began to turn, a lamia stepped out of the chimney shadow. She was small and bright-eyed, with hair that shone like wet river stones. “Good evening, mistress of the house,” she said. The woman’s hands paused, but she remembered that a guest at the hearth must be offered food. She cut a thin slice of ham, warmed it in the pan, and set it before the lamia.

The fairy ate, nodded politely, and left before the embers dimmed. The next evening she returned. And the next. Each time, the woman shared what she had. Each morning afterward, the flax seemed easier to spin, the hens laid well, and the loaf lasted a little longer than expected. The house was never rich, but nothing necessary ran out.

After many weeks, however, the woman grew tired of the unannounced visitor. “I wish our evenings belonged to us again,” she told her husband. “I do not know how to ask a fairy to leave.” Her husband thought he could solve the matter by making the lamia uncomfortable. He wrapped himself in his wife’s shawl, sat at the wheel, and tried to spin.

The wheel did not whisper chirrin, chirrin. Under his heavy hands it clattered firgilun, fargalun. When the lamia arrived, she tilted her head. “Your spinning has a different song tonight.” “I am tired,” the husband answered, keeping the shawl low over his face. He set the pan over the fire and offered to warm the usual slice of ham.

But he handled the pan roughly. It struck the hearth, sparks jumped, and a splash of hot fat flew toward the lamia. She leapt back with a cry and ran into the dark yard. At once, many other lamias gathered around her, asking who had hurt her. Startled and ashamed, she answered only, “I hurt myself.”

“Then you must tend the hurt yourself,” said the others, and together they disappeared toward the stream. The first lamia never returned to the farmhouse.

At first the couple were relieved. No chair scraped unexpectedly. No tiny knock sounded after sunset. Yet the flax began to knot. A fox found the hens. Damp spoiled the grain. Nothing dreadful happened all at once; rather, the house’s good fortune ebbed away as quietly as water slipping between stones.

Only then did the couple understand that the nightly slice of ham had never been simply a burden. It had been part of a friendship, and the ease in their home had grown from welcome given freely. They repaired the hearth, set a clean stool beside it, and left a small portion of supper there for travelers seen and unseen.

The lamia did not come back. Some unkindness cannot be called home merely by wishing. Still, the couple became gentler with every guest who crossed their threshold. Their household was never as prosperous as before, but warmth slowly returned—not fairy luck this time, but the steady blessing made whenever people share what they have.

Original English retelling after “The Fairy in the House,” collected in the Basque Country by Wentworth Webster and published in Basque Legends (1877). A full Basque text has not been invented.

Etxeko lamia is the Basque title used here for “The Fairy in the House.” This retelling is presented in English rather than offering an unverified Basque translation.

title: Uthlakanyana
subtitle: a Zulu trickster episode about listening closely and using wit instead of strength
moral: Granny’s whisper: A careful ear can find a doorway where strength sees only a wall.
script_en:
Uthlakanyana was small enough to be overlooked and quick enough to notice everything. One evening, while crossing the hills, he heard a deep boo-boo-boom rolling over the grass. Around the bend came a great cannibal carrying an enormous musical calabash beneath one arm. Each step shook a thunderous note from it.

“Good evening, Uncle,” said Uthlakanyana in his sweetest voice. The cannibal stopped. “How can I be your uncle?” “Surely you remember your sister’s smallest child.” But this cannibal had heard of the little trickster. “I know who you are,” he said. “You are Uthlakanyana, and your clever tongue will not catch me.”

Uthlakanyana admired the calabash. “Then at least let me carry your instrument for one hill.” The cannibal gripped it tighter. “No. I will lend you nothing.” He strode on, and the booming faded behind him.

Uthlakanyana continued until he found another cannibal at a lonely hut, softening a hide by pounding it. This one had not heard the warnings. “Come in, sister’s child,” he said. “Help me work.” Uthlakanyana sat down and began to pound in rhythm.

Soon the first cannibal’s calabash sounded in the distance: boo-boo-boom. Uthlakanyana stopped and widened his eyes. “Did you hear that?” The second cannibal listened, then pounded faster, pretending not to worry. The hide thumped. The calabash answered more loudly: BOO-BOO-BOOM.

“It is coming nearer,” whispered Uthlakanyana. Now both stepped outside. On one hill stood the cannibal with the calabash. On another stood Uthlakanyana and his new host. “Who are you, making such a terrible noise?” shouted the second cannibal.

The first was tired and cross from carrying his load. He called back a proud name and boasted, “I gulp wild greens whole. As for a man, I swallow him without even chewing.” The second cannibal heard only the boast. He forgot that he was a frightening creature himself. With a yelp, he ran over the far hill and did not look back.

Uthlakanyana waited until the booming cannibal reached the hut. “Uncle,” he said, “the one who fled kept me here as a child. If you truly are braver, perhaps I should live with you instead.” The first cannibal puffed out his chest. He had distrusted Uthlakanyana before, but victory made him careless. “Very well,” he said. “You are much smaller than I am. You may stay.”

The next morning the cannibal went hunting and ordered Uthlakanyana to guard the hut. Uthlakanyana looked at the great doorway, the heavy calabash, and the path between the hills. He understood that boastful creatures often frighten one another better than anyone else can. He took food for the road, left the calabash where it would boom in the wind, and slipped away while the hills were still blue with dawn.

Behind him, the instrument called boo-boo-boom into the empty valley. One cannibal hid from the sound. The other hurried home to protect it. And Uthlakanyana, too small to win by force, walked safely between them—listening, thinking, and smiling at the way a single loud boast had opened the road.

Original English retelling of an episode in the Uthlakanyana cycle recorded in Henry Callaway’s Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus (1868). A full modern isiZulu translation has not been invented.

title: How Glooscap Named the Animals
subtitle: a Wabanaki story with a Passamaquoddy source, about names, gifts, and knowing one’s measure
moral: Granny’s whisper: A true name does not make us bigger; it helps us become who we are.
script_en:
When the world was still young, the forests were full of footsteps but few names. Wings crossed the dawn. Paws pressed the riverbanks. Antlers moved between the spruce trees like branches walking. Glooscap traveled through this lively country, greeting each being as a relative and listening for the work each would do.

He called the animals together beside a wide river. “Tell me what you hope to be,” he said. “Then I will give each of you a name to carry.” The animals rustled closer. Some had quiet wishes. Others had wishes much larger than themselves.

Bear came first, strong-shouldered and serious. “Make me so fearsome that every creature flees before me,” Bear said. Glooscap looked at Bear’s broad paws, his patience at the berry patch, and the warm den he would dig before winter. “You will be powerful,” Glooscap answered, “but strength will not be your only gift. You will know when to roam and when to rest. You will teach that even the mighty need seasons of stillness.” He gave Bear a name suited to that life.

Next hurried Squirrel, flicking a splendid tail. “Make me the largest animal in the forest,” Squirrel begged. “Let my steps shake the hills.” Glooscap smiled. “Your body will remain small, because smallness will help you leap where others cannot. You will plant more trees than you remember, hiding seeds for winter. The forest will rise from work you forget you did.” Squirrel considered this and held his tail a little higher.

Moose stepped from the shallows, tall and solemn. “Give me speed enough to outrun every hunter.” Glooscap saw how Moose’s long legs crossed bog and snow. “You will have great strides,” he said, “and also ears that catch the softest warning. Your size will ask you to walk with care, for the smallest nesting bird shares the path.” Moose bowed his heavy head.

Beaver slapped the water impatiently. “Give me rule over the whole river.” Glooscap picked up a peeled stick from the shore. “Not rule,” he said. “Responsibility. Your teeth will cut wood, your paws will shape mud, and your houses will slow the water. Ponds will shelter fish, frogs, ducks, and reeds. What you build must make room for others.” Beaver studied the current, already imagining a dam.

One by one the animals came. Glooscap did not name them for empty wishes or loud boasts. He named them for the gifts folded inside them and for the duties those gifts required. Some left delighted. Some needed time to understand. Yet as each name was spoken, the forest seemed to recognize its owner.

At last Glooscap stood alone beside the evening river. Around him, Bear searched for a winter den, Squirrel buried a seed, Moose stepped gently through the reeds, and Beaver carried a branch toward the bank. Their names did not make them more important than one another. The names helped each remember a place in the living world.

And so, when people heard wings, paws, splashing tails, or hooves among the trees, they did not hear strangers. They heard neighbors with gifts, limits, and work of their own. A good name, Glooscap had shown, is not a crown. It is a promise about how one will live among all the others.

Original English retelling after “How Glooskap Named the Animals,” identified as Passamaquoddy in Charles G. Leland’s The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884). Kluskap is a preserved Mi’kmaq form of the culture hero’s name; no Mi’kmaq story text has been invented.

title: Sina and the Eel
subtitle: a Samoan tale about friendship, farewell, and the gift remembered in every coconut
moral: Granny’s whisper: Love may change its shape and still offer shade, water, and remembrance.
script_en:
In a village near the sea lived a young woman named Sina. Each morning she walked beneath breadfruit trees to a clear freshwater pool. There she washed, filled a gourd for her family, and listened to the little springs bubbling through the stone. One day, a small eel appeared between the water plants and watched her with bright, gentle eyes.

Sina did not chase it away. She dropped a few crumbs from her food, and the eel ate them. The next day it returned. As weeks passed, Sina and the eel became familiar companions. She called it Tuna. When Sina sang beside the pool, Tuna traced circles under the surface. When rain made the path slippery, Tuna waited until she arrived safely.

Tuna grew larger. At first Sina was pleased to see her friend thriving, but soon the eel was so big that it startled other people who came for water. Children hurried back to the village. Elders warned that a creature of such size could no longer remain in the little pool.

Sina felt torn between affection and fear. She visited a farther spring, hoping Tuna would stay behind. But the eel followed through hidden channels beneath the ground and rose to greet her. She went to another village; again Tuna appeared in the water. At last Sina understood that their friendship was reaching a change neither of them could avoid.

Tuna spoke to her in the quiet way of beings from the oldest stories. “Do not be afraid,” the eel said. “My time in this form is nearly finished. I will not follow you farther. When I am gone, take my head and plant it in the earth near your home. Care for that place, and from it will grow a gift.”

Sina wept, for this was not the promise she wished to hear. Yet Tuna asked her to remember their mornings together and to trust that farewell was not the same as forgetting. Sina carried out her friend’s request with tenderness. She chose a sunny patch of soil, planted what Tuna had given, and kept the ground soft with water.

Days passed. Then a green shoot pushed through the earth. It became a slender palm, taller and taller, until its leaves opened above the roofs. Among them grew round fruit unlike any the village had seen. The hard shells held sweet flesh and cool, clear water—a drink waiting high above the salty sea.

On each coconut were three marks: two like eyes and one like a mouth. When Sina lifted a coconut to drink, it seemed that Tuna’s face looked back at her. She remembered the bright eyes in the pool, the circles beneath her songs, and the promise that friendship could become a gift.

The villagers planted the new fruit along the shore. Coconut palms gave them drink, food, fiber, vessels, shade, and wood. Canoes traveling from island to island carried coconuts with them, and each new tree leaned toward wind and water.

Sina still missed Tuna. Love did not erase the sadness of parting. But whenever she opened a coconut, she shared the first drink with someone nearby. In that way, Tuna’s final gift never belonged to one person alone. It traveled from hand to hand, cool as the old spring, while the palms whispered above the village that what is cherished may return in a new and generous form.

Original English retelling of the Samoan tradition of Sina and Tuna, informed by published accounts and modern Samoan oral-history records. A full Samoan translation has not been invented.
